points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author states that he composed the book at the repeated request of a senior figure of the dawa, to gather into one place what lies scattered through the books of the saints and their learned callers — the paired and authoritative books, the brief compositions on Sharia matters, and expansive treatments of juristic paths and legal opinions — so that their contents would be made more accessible.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author names the book إسعاف الطالب في جميع المطالب ('The Student's Aid in All Demands') and dates the start of composition to the seventh of Rajab al-Asabb in the year 1051 of the Prophetic migration.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author writes from within the Tayyibi Ismaili tradition, invoking the Prophet, 'Ali, Fatima al-Batul, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, the pure Imams, and the caller of his own age, the dai Jafar ibn Sulayman and his successor the dai Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, in service to the Imam al-Tayyib.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author disclaims personal credit: whatever in the work is correct derives from the substance of his patron the caller and his successor, while whatever is a slip or error comes from his own shortness of reach.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: Reporting from 'some of the noble books', the author states that faith has eight levels (مراتب).

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The first of the eight levels of faith is charity (الإحسان) toward parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the nearby neighbor, the companion at one's side, the traveler, and those whom one's faith obligates one to care for — a level the author says is established in the Book of God.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The quoted source asserts that whoever undertakes the worship of God and the call of the People of the House without knowledge and without action cannot rightly bear the name of faith, and holds no bond with God nor covenant or honor with His guardian, having departed from faith.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author announces that he will next treat the distinction between faith (iman) and Islam — what each encompasses — and what lies beyond them.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: Quoting the fourth of the Mustansiriyya Councils (the Councils of Exposition and Wisdom), the author reports that the Imams of religion are seven, recurring in the world as the days of the week recur until the rising of the Qa'im, while twelve proofs (hujjas) are spread throughout the world — and this constitutes knowledge of the sum of the limits (hudud) of the testimony.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author distinguishes knowing the limits of the testimony from fulfilling the rights owed to those limits: the latter consists of upholding seven obligations of religion and twelve practices incumbent upon the God-fearing, mirroring the seven Imams and twelve proofs.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The seven obligations of religion are guardianship (walaya), purity (tahara), prayer (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting (sawm), pilgrimage (hajj), and struggle (jihad).

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The twelve practices are honoring parents, maintaining kinship ties, protecting the neighbor, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, truthfulness in one's home, good conduct with one's spouse, kindness to dependents, spreading the greeting of peace, feeding others, keeping the bond among the brethren, and visiting the sick — and the author states these twelve are not obligatory upon women.

points.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
points.text: The author cites 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts that the Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects and this community will divide into seventy-three, of which one is in the Garden and the rest in the Fire.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Foster-Suckling, reads the Qur'anic phrase 'God is his master, and Gabriel, and the righteous of the believers' as designating 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and woman.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: On the same authority, 'and their father was righteous' is taken to mean an Imam, and 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' to mean the Imams among God's servants, so that 'the righteous' in scripture is a technical designation for the Imams.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: The Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah, in a Friday sermon, likened himself in the physical world to the Pen in the spiritual world, setting four ranks beneath him each preceded by a spiritual rank guiding it upward, so that the earthly hierarchy faces and inscribes what it derives from the spiritual world as a pen inscribes a tablet.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In the account from Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, the king of Rum sends a messenger with money to test Muhammad's successor with three questions: what is not God's, what is not with God, and what God does not know.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: Abu Bakr and 'Umar both fail the test and, rather than admitting ignorance, accuse the questioner of disbelief — a failure 'Abdullah ibn Abbas explicitly criticises before directing the company to 'Ali.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali answers that what is not God's is a partner, what is not with God is injustice, and what God does not know is that the Messiah is His son — citing 'Do you inform God of what He does not know?' — the point being that what does not exist is not an object of divine knowledge.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: The Roman envoy responds by professing that there is no god but God, that Muhammad is His Messenger, and that 'Ali is his guardian (wali), and 'Ali has al-Hasan and al-Husayn distribute the money among the Muslims.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In the narration from Abu al-Jarud via al-Harith al-Awar, Muawiya secretly sends a Syrian to 'Ali in al-Rahba with eleven questions relayed from Ibn al-Asfar, who had promised to follow and pay tribute to whoever could answer them.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali detects the stranger as an outsider before he speaks, grants him safety for wartime acts on the principle that 'when war lays down its burdens, there is no harm in it,' and denounces Muawiya and the nation that severed his kinship and denied him his right.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: 'Ali defers the answering to al-Hasan, who resolves all eleven questions — including that truth and falsehood are four fingers apart (what the eye sees is true, what the ear hears is largely false), that the moon's light was once like the sun's until God erased it per the verse on the two signs, and that the hardest of ten things ascends from stone through iron, fire, water, cloud, wind, angel, Angel of Death, death, to the command of God.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: Ibn al-Asfar, receiving the answers through Muawiya, testifies that they could only come from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message and refuses Muawiya even a single dirham — a foreign witness against Muawiya's claim.

points.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
points.text: In a further narration, 'Ali resolves 'Umar's four unasked questions: true dreams occur while the soul is loosed in the kingdom and false ones as it returns (per the verse on God taking souls in sleep), instinctive love and hatred trace to souls created two thousand years before bodies that knew or rejected one another in the air, and forgetting comes from a film over the heart like the film of the moon — after which 'Umar concedes 'You have spoken truly, O Abu al-Hasan.'

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author, citing the twenty-third of the Mustansiriya councils, states that the revelation of peace divides into seven sections above (from God and His angels) and twelve sections below (from human beings).

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The seven higher forms of peace are enumerated from Qur'anic verses: God's own 'Peace be upon you'; 'O Noah, descend in peace from Us'; 'their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace'; 'they will be met therein with greeting and peace'; the angels' entering with peace from every gate; the command that believers pray for and submit to the Prophet; and 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin'.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The author identifies Yasin as the Prophet Muhammad, and therefore 'the family of Yasin' as the family of Muhammad, making the seventh Qur'anic peace a peace upon the Imams of the Prophet's house.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: In the twenty-fourth assembly it is stated that the offering of peace is an obligatory Sunnah of Islam expressing affection and submission, and that al-Salam is one of the names of God, possessed of majesty and honor.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Among the twelve human forms, the first four are named: the greeting of the people of the right hand ('Peace be upon you for your patience'), the greeting on entering houses/the mosque, the peace concluding the prayer, and the believer's 'peace' when addressed by the ignorant.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The Sunnah fixes an order of precedence in initiating the greeting: camel-rider to horse-rider, horse-rider to donkey-rider, donkey-rider to the walker, the walker to the one standing, and the one standing both initiates and returns it.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The return of a greeting is divided into three kinds — the virtuous reply (greeting back with something better), the complete reply (responding in kind, per 'return it with something better, or return it as it is'), and the just reply.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The just reply applies to dhimmis, who do not initiate the greeting; if one does, the answer is 'And upon you', because some were reported to say 'al-sam alaykum' (death be upon you) instead of 'al-salam alaykum', so that whoever said good receives its like and whoever said evil receives its like.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: The Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah is reported to pray on Sunday for the lower borders, the five — the spokesman, the foundation, the culmination, the successor, and the wing — and on Saturday over the seven days and twelve months.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Saints of the religion are reported to pray across the days of the week for the proclaimers and their gates, the imams of their stations, their proofs and preachers, and specifically for the seven proclaimers, seven culminations, seven caliphs and twelve successors, asking to be admitted to every good granted them and spared every evil they were spared.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: Amir al-Mu'minin in his Four Hundred Counsels commands returning a greeting with something better or in kind, shaking the hand of an enemy who dislikes it (citing 'Repel with that which is better...'), and replying to 'May God greet you with peace' with 'You are the peace of God, and the finest of abodes and stations'.

points.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
points.text: From the book of questions of Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi with answers from Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, it is ruled that peace should be proclaimed aloud to shaykhs and teachers (better than the Indian custom of bowing or lowering the head), while audibility in returning greetings or in blessing a sneezer is a courtesy and not an obligation — except that returning a greeting itself is required, whether aloud or silently.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen, in the book of the Esoteric Nursing, interprets the Quranic verse 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' as referring to the Imams among God's servants.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: On the verse promising to make 'those made weak in the land' Imams and heirs, Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen identifies 'those made weak' as the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, weakened in the person of Ali himself, who is the proof (hujja) of Muhammad, the earth being his likeness.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Al-Muizz li Din Allah, in his Sunday supplication, ranks beneath the Foundation (al-Asas) the Terminus (al-Mutimm) facing Israfil, beneath the Terminus the After (al-Lahiq) facing Michael, and beneath the After the Wing (al-Janah) facing Gabriel.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Al-Muizz states that these three ranks deliver to the respondents from the Speaker and the Foundation in the corporeal world, just as three deliver from the two principles — the Pen and the Tablet — in the spiritual world; the author glosses these three as the Grandfather (al-Jadd), the Opener (al-Fath), and the Imagination (al-Khayal), identified with Israfil, Michael, and Gabriel.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: In his Friday supplication al-Muizz enumerates the hudud as Speaker, Foundation, Terminus, After, Wing, Authorized (ma'dhun) and Respondent (mustajib), together with twelve proofs ranked across twelve regions (jaza'ir), which the author links to the Quranic 'over it are nineteen.'

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Sayings ascribed to Ali in the supplication of victory and awe invoke numbered groups — six transmitted, seven beheld, nine signs, ten words, twenty-one, eight encircling the Throne, eleven prostrating, twelve bowing — and seven Imams, seven successors, seven witnesses, seven substitutes.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali is reported in the Four Hundred Manners as saying that whoever holds fast to the Imams joins the truth and whoever holds to another way is undone.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali prohibits exaggeration (ghuluw) concerning the Imams, requiring believers to say 'we are servants under a Lord' while permitting them to say of the Imams' excellence whatever they wish — a boundary that condemns excess without limiting praise of merit.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali teaches that both errors are remediable through the Imams: the one who exaggerates returns to them, and they themselves raise up the one who falls short (al-muqassir).

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Ali's commandments to the Imams' followers require working as the Imams work, relying on pious restraint (wara'), avoiding those who revile them, not praising them openly before the enemy, truthfulness, patience, and not burdening the Imams with intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Further maxims from the Four Hundred Manners warn that disputation bequeaths doubt, that speech is to be reckoned among deeds, that sin withholds sustenance, that the best deed of the believer is awaiting the relief (intizar al-faraj), and that blessed is he admonished by another's example.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: Muhammad bin Tahir's supplication seeks nearness to God through the Imams' gates, proofs, preachers, authorized ones, respondents of their cycles, and all who follow or shelter with them.

points.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
points.text: The nineteenth Mustansiriya council divides the commanded ties of kinship into seven and twelve, identifying the seven as the Imams of the religion — the 'kin' whose affection the Quran names as the Prophet's only reward — recurring like the days of Friday.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, warns believers not to despise weak brothers (whoever despises a believer is belittled and detested by God and will not be joined with him on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), not to force a brother to ask when his need is already known, and to visit, be tender, and give freely rather than be like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali is quoted as saying the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother, so that a brother's slip is met with guidance, counsel and gentleness rather than a group banding against him, and discord is condemned because it leads a person away from the path.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Ali forbids backbiting on the authority of the Qur'anic rebuke 'Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?', and urges that meeting believers with a handshake and a bright face causes the burdens each carried to lift by the time they part.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: A recorded question from Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi about the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt and food when one lacks them at the moment (though able to buy) was answered by Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris bin al-Hassan bin Abdullah al-Ala: there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: In the seventeenth Mustansiriya council, righteousness toward parents is named the first of the twelve practices that correspond to the number of the letters of the testimony, the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses having already been explained.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: From the two Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward both parents, the council draws the point that in both places it is the mother's deed alone (carrying in hardship, weakness upon weakness) that is laid to the child's account, so she whom God distinguished by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The eighteenth council divides righteousness toward parents into seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and identifies three pairs of parents: the bodily parents who caused his form to come into being and nourished him, the two parents in religion who caused his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), and the two fathers of the community who convey the divine sciences (the Prophet and the legatee, and the Imams of their progeny), citing 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community.'

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The seal of righteousness toward parents is a person's righteousness toward his own soul: making the truth plain to it and establishing it therein, magnifying it so as to awaken its longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it and rescuing it from what has bound it.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twelve manners toward parents are listed: honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering one's voice, magnifying and not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility in mercy, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, not opposing their command, saying no word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights that God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to come out from what He forbade and enter into what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The nineteenth council divides relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers, al-ashiqqa'; paternal half-brothers, banu al-'allat; maternal half-brothers, al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and defines the commanded tie as keeping the bond, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, or abandon — and Ali states there is no binding oath in the severing of kinship.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: The twentieth council, building on parents and kinship, divides safeguarding the neighbor into seven ranks graded by how many rights each holds — the kin-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship, faith), the kin non-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship), the believing stranger-neighbor (neighborliness, faith), the companion at your side who differs in religion and creed (neighborliness), the companion aboard ship (right of nearness), the one who shares your litter, and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding of all.

points.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
points.text: Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into or eavesdropping on the neighbor's house, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement he asks for, not acting haughtily when higher in station nor envying when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being called the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, forbids silence until nightfall except in the remembrance of God, forbids reverting to desert life after the migration, and holds that a man of sound mind does not recite the Quran in a state of ritual impurity until he purifies himself for it.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib warns believers not to let the Murjiah overcome them with their opinion, marking a category of teachers whose word must be refused.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: In the book of questions of Sheikh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, the questioner asks whether al-Sadiq's reported licensing of al-Shafii — cited from Hamid al-Din's al-Hadi wal-Mustahdi, al-Numan's al-Daaim, and Idris ibn al-Hasan's Zahr al-Maani — meant al-Shafii later changed like al-Mughirah and Abu al-Khattab, or whether ignorant men falsely claimed his school as others falsely claimed the Imamate of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and Abdullah ibn Muawiyah.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: The answer given is qualified, not general: al-Sadiq had indeed granted al-Shafii license, but solely on account of al-Shafii's acknowledgment of the excellence of the Ahl al-Bayt and for no other reason.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Asked how the Prophet's saying that whoever looks into his brother's book without permission is as one looking into the Fire can stand when members of a school freely read one another's books, the answer distinguishes the book of inner truth (haqiqa), which may be looked into only by permission of the one who granted access, from all other books, where refraining is mere good manners and not binding.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: A borrower who finds damage or disorder in a borrowed Quran or other book may repair it without the owner's permission, but is under no obligation to do so.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Books of the dawah left by a deceased man may not be used to settle his debts even when his other goods are insufficient, because they belong to the dawah and are not inherited property.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Yemeni callers answering Indian sheikhs rule that those licensed to read religious benefits may read to women through a screen so the woman hears without being seen, and that no man may be alone with a woman unless another woman is with her or another man with him.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: The obligatory knowledge no believer may leave unlearned is enumerated as: knowledge of God's oneness and His transcendence above likeness, above the stripping of attributes, and above nonexistence; acknowledgment of all messengers first to last and of their delivery of the message; acknowledgment of Muhammad as Seal of the Prophets and affirmation of what he brought; acknowledgment of the Imams of his progeny whose guardianship and obedience God joined to His own in 'Obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you'; and recognition of the Imam of the age with submission to his command and taking knowledge from him.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: This obligatory knowledge rests on the premise that God has never left the earth without a proof against His servants and an Imam calling to His obedience, supported by 'On the day We shall call every people by their Imam' and 'You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide'; whoever affirms this is bound to follow the guide, ask the people of remembrance, and take from them, and his rank is raised in proportion to what he then learns.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali holds that the worth of every man is what he has mastered of knowledge, and the Messenger of God holds that seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim man and woman.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Ali forbids measuring religion by analogy, declaring that a people will come who do so and that they are religion's enemies, the first analogical reasoner having been Iblis; instead, discourse one does not recognize must be referred back to the Imams and suspended there.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan in Mafatih al-Nimah reports al-Sadiq drawing a distinction between referring an obscure teaching back to the Imams — bringing it to them so they may establish its proof and disclose its interpretation — and throwing it back at them by calling it false and turning away.

points.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
points.text: On concealment and precaution, Ali warns that whoever divulges the Imams' secret will be made by God to taste the cold of iron.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The author cites a Book of Question and Answer arranged by the order of the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, in which the questions come from teachers of the Indian lands and the answers from the summoners (duat) of the Yemeni lands.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Answering an Indian question, the Yemeni respondent rules that the prohibition on urinating beneath fruit-bearing trees covers both trees on which fruit is actually present and trees whose property it is to bear fruit.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The respondent rules that although greeting and speaking are forbidden to one in a state of hadath, once he has risen from that place — having cleansed himself with a stone or otherwise — he may be greeted, must return the greeting, and may speak.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The respondent permits reusing a stone or clod of earth previously used for cleansing after urination, once it has dried, provided no impurity and no moisture are evident upon it.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as listing the nullifiers of ablution: sleep, whatever issues from the front or rear passage (whether a stone or wind), an enema, fainting, insanity, and the disappearance of the glans into the front passage of a living or dead person.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Tawil al-Daaim is cited for the rule that one who interrupts his ablution may build upon what he has already done, so long as the water has not dried upon the limbs already washed.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is also cited for the concession that one whose hands are amputated above the elbows, leaving nothing of them, is released from the obligation of washing the hands.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The Trusted of the Imam, the Banner of Islam (al-Muayyad), in the fifth council of his Majalis al-Bayan and Majalis al-Hikma (the Councils of al-Mustansiriyya), teaches that Islam is built upon seven obligations to which twelve practices are attached, and that each individual obligation likewise contains its own seven obligations and twelve practices.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: In that council walaya is named the first and most excellent of the obligations, and it is stated that in every allusion made by these numbers the ranking of the friends of God is the utmost aim and intention.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The seven obligations of the lesser purity (ablution) are given as pure water, intention, washing the face, washing the hands, wiping the head, wiping the feet, and order — order being that one begins with what God began by mentioning.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The twelve practices of ablution are enumerated as istinja, washing the hands before entering them into the vessel, pronouncing God's name on sitting down, rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, moving the ring so water reaches beneath it, combing water through the beard, wetting the eyes, giving the right limbs precedence over the left, wiping the ears inside and out, the second and third washings of the face (the first being the obligation), and the siwak.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: The greater purity — washing of the whole body — is likewise divided into seven obligations (washing from janabah, from menstruation, of the unbeliever entering Islam, of one recovering from unconsciousness, from the blood of nifas, after immersion in impurity, and of the dead, this last being an obligation on the living until one of them performs it) and twelve practices (Friday; al-Fitr; al-Adha; ihram; entering the Haram; entering the Kabah; entering Madinah; the day of Arafah; the nights of the nineteenth, twenty-first and twenty-third of Ramadan; and after washing the dead).

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, commands cleansing with water from foul odor and prescribes set invocations on entering the privy and on looking at what has passed from one, the latter grounded in the Prophet's report that an angel turns the servant's neck so he looks at it and asks: this is what you were eager for — consider where you took it from and what it has come to.

points.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
points.text: Ali is also cited in the same context for the rule that when sleep mingles with the heart, ablution becomes obligatory.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: A ruling reported in the question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam holds that prayer is not permitted while a man knowingly carries impurity, so one who prayed having forgotten the istinja must wash and repeat the prayer.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The same source rules that uncovering oneself for wudhu or washing in a screened place where no one sees is permissible and the purity obtained is valid, the concealment reported of some Imams being a matter of excellence of manners rather than obligation.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah lists twelve manners of the wudhu governing the privy, including entering with sandals and the left foot first, covering the head, not facing or turning the back to the qiblah, leaning on the left leg, not lingering, cleansing with the left hand using three fresh stones rather than dung or worn bone, keeping silent within, and leaving with the right foot first.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Kitab al-Idah reports the Prophet saying Gabriel commanded him on God's behalf to wash the two hollows beside the chin in ablution — the sides of the tuft below the lower lip — these being "the neglected place."

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The author reports sayings of Ali ibn Abi Talib from his Four Hundred Manners on purification, including that rinsing the mouth and drawing in water is Sunnah purification of mouth and nose, that istinja with cold water cuts off piles, that ablution after purity is ten good deeds, and that one should say the basmalah and the prayer to be among the repentant and the purified before touching water.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The questions and answers distinguish the istinja as both a Sunnah practice that must not be deliberately abandoned — whose omission through forgetfulness does not spoil wudhu or require repeating a prayer already performed — and as obligatory insofar as the removal of impurity is itself obligatory.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: For one with a wound or boil that water cannot touch, the answer given is that he wipes over bandages and coverings for wudhu, and performs tayammum if removal would harm him through cold or injury or if he is sick; for the greater purification he pours water in a stream, and performs tayammum if he fears for himself, whether traveling or at home.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: On water, the rulings hold that abundant water above the Shariah measure which overpowers impurity remains purifying, whereas a vessel whose water has shown a quality of impurity becomes impure and is not restored by pouring more water in a stream unless it rises above the measure after the vessel is purified; running water and a pool eight cubits in length and breadth remain valid.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Used water and used dust are declared pure and purifying, so that purification with them is permitted once and many times, against the practice of ordinary people who do not permit a second use.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The saying "whoever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him" is interpreted to mean that water purifies and is not itself purified, and likewise the knowledge of the Imam: whomever it does not purify, nothing else will.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Majalis al-Bayan enumerates seven obligations of wudhu (pure water, intention, washing face, washing hands, wiping head, wiping feet, and the Quranic order), twelve of its Sunnah acts, seven obligatory forms of ghusl, twelve Sunnah forms of ghusl, and twelve places where prayer is disliked.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah reports the Prophet forbidding wiping over the socks and forbidding the abandonment of saying the basmalah aloud, and Ali is quoted that there is no dissimulation in drinking intoxicants or in wiping over the socks.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl in al-Risalah al-Maknunah divides purity and filth into two kinds: outward purity by outward water cleansing urine and excrement, and inward purity by inward water — which is knowledge — cleansing the inward filth of doubt and ignorance.

points.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
points.text: The same author reads the seven elements of wudhu as seven bounds — three Sunnah (rinsing the mouth, drawing in water, istinja), two washings and two wipings, one of each bounded and one unbounded — and takes the face, containing the seven openings, as bearing the meaning of the Speaker, since a person is known by his face just as no one is known except through his prophet and there is no deliverance except by turning toward him.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: The section's material is drawn from a compiled book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, with further material from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, al-Risala al-Maknuna, Tawil al-Shariah, and the Four Hundred Manners of Ali ibn Abi Talib.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Against the report in some Shariah books that one who performs tayammum out of fear of cold must later wash and repeat the prayer, the answering dai rules that whoever fears water will harm him — resident or traveler, weak man or sick — performs tayammum, prays, and owes nothing further and no repetition.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Doubt itself triggers obligation: one who revives from unconsciousness not knowing his condition, and one who wakes finding traces of semen (wet or dry) without recalling emission, must perform the ghusl.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Asked for the inner likeness of ghusl from janabah, since marital relations are a likeness of imparting and receiving, the answer given is that the washing is a likeness of the removal of doubt, and doubt arises only at the moment of imparting and receiving.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: For the one in janabah and the menstruating or post-natally bleeding woman, removing hair or nails is disliked — better left until purification — and neither may deliberately recite the Quran, nor Quranic matter embedded in supplications or books, nor the basmalah with the intention of Quranic recitation.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Al-Risala al-Maknuna grounds ghusl in Quran 'if you are junub, purify yourselves' and the Prophet's 'beneath every hair is janabah', and glosses junub as 'one far from a thing', concluding that the obedience of one in janabah is void and false.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Ali is reported in the Four Hundred Manners as forbidding the Muslim to sleep while junub or without purity (using tayammum if no water), because the believer's spirit ascends to God, who blesses it and either forms it beautifully if its term has come or returns it to the body with trusted angels.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Vomit does not render impure what it falls upon (though washing the place is better), and ground once urinated upon becomes ruled pure for prayer and tayammum when the impurity's substance and smell are gone — since sun and light purify it — provided it is not ground set aside as a privy.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Ali's ruling that touching a corpse 'after it has grown cold' obliges ghusl is interpreted to mean after it has become impure, so contact with its moisture makes the living person impure, while the corpse-washer's own washing is from the Sunnah.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Items that cannot be rubbed or wrung three times are purified by passing the hand over them until impurity and smell are gone, then lifting from the water and letting it drip, repeated three times; heavier items are trodden with the feet and pressed out, likewise three times.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: A Muslim nursing woman's milk is pure for her and others (Walid Izz al-Din Maad ibn Abdullah ibn Ali), since milk is like saliva and every Muslim's saliva is pure; and small amounts of impurity — wet hair, the milk or butter of filth-eating animals, egg white — are excused.
entities: Izz al-Din Maad ibn Abdullah ibn Ali

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Despite the verse 'the polytheists are nothing but impurity', the Imams permitted prayer in garments polytheists have made so long as they have not worn them or visible impurity has not appeared — including cloth sprinkled with impure water during weaving that has since dried — whereas what they have bleached or washed with soap is pure only by washing.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Against the common people's view that a large garment whose ends do not move together may be prayed upon at its pure part, the dai rules that prayer upon a partly impure garment or bedding is not permitted at all; tayammum covers ritual impurity, not impure garments, and the sick man must have his garments washed by another.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Idris ibn al-Hasan, answering Sheikh Yusuf ibn Ismail al-Samti al-Hindi, rules that whatever ground tayammum is not valid from may not be prayed upon (citing 'the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a purification'), and that the Indian scruple against sweeping houses and shops at night is unreliable and blameless to violate.
entities: Yusuf ibn Ismail ibn Ibrahim al-Samti al-Hindi

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: A vessel licked by a dog — and likewise by a pig — is washed seven times, one of them with earth; and if impurity falls into one of two indistinguishable vessels, neither may be used and one performs tayammum and prays.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: Ali's Four Hundred Manners are cited for a body of cleanliness practices as Sunnah and purification — trimming the mustache and nails, washing the head with mallow, depilatory paste every fifteen days, plucking the armpits, feast-day bathing, washing garments, avoiding dogs, not relieving oneself on roads or into standing water or the wind (for water and air have their folk), and cleansing foul odor since God hates the servant who offends those sitting near him.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: In answers of Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris to Sheikh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi, Ali's saying 'whomever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' is interpreted esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and so is the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, God does not purify.

points.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
points.text: On long uncombed hair, Hasan ibn Idris rules there is no defect if it is parted into two halves, though leaving it unparted is unfitting, and doing so deliberately in defiance of the ruling voids the prayer.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author reports that using a split bamboo cane or similar to scrape the tongue after the siwak, as most people of India do, is permitted, since the siwak itself is the mainstay; he also records that one must not clean between the teeth with a knotted stalk of dried grass, and that using the siwak while in janaba (major ritual impurity) is disliked.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author cites Sharh al-Akhbar defining rayhan as every fragrant plant, with the myrtle (al-as) singled out by that name, and Ta'wil al-Da'a'im defining it as the tips of sweet-scented plants at blossoming — a comprehensive name for fragrant plants, most often given to myrtle because it is the most lasting and strongest.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author quotes Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred points of etiquette that the tooth-stick pleases the Lord, sweetens the mouth, and belongs to the sunna.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Tayammum requires dust: on a smooth rock fixed in the ground it is valid only if dust lies on it, not otherwise.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author draws the distinction that tayammum is not permitted to a settled (non-traveling) person except for cause, whereas a traveler far from water, or unable to reach it before the prayer time lapses, or endangered in person or property by going to it, performs tayammum.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: A traveler who forgets an owed ghusl from a night of Ramadan and finds no water may use tayammum for both prayer and fast; likewise a woman purified from menses before sunset in Ramadan, or a man with a nocturnal emission, who fear harm from washing, may perform tayammum and fast without making up the day.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author records a series of tayammum cases: one who dies on a journey without water is given tayammum; one who fears illness from ablution performs tayammum; a menstruating traveler's wife once pure may do tayammum and become lawful to her husband; an imam in janaba with water for only one may do tayammum and lead others who have done so; a man with water only for ablution but impurity on his garment washes the garment and does tayammum; a junub with water insufficient for ghusl does tayammum at noon and uses the water for ablution at afternoon prayer since he is by then pure; where a corpse and a junub compete for one washing's water, the junub washes and the corpse is given tayammum; and a Christian or Zoroastrian wife purified from menses on a journey is taught the tayammum by her husband.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Citing Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, the author adds that finding water breaks the tayammum and returns the man to janaba, that a new convert without water performs tayammum and prays, that one made impure while sleeping in the Prophet's mosque should perform tayammum before passing through it or the sanctuary, and that a sound person performs tayammum on behalf of an invalid who cannot.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author records that one in minor impurity may do tayammum for the funeral prayer if he fears missing it; that one who prayed with tayammum while forgetting water in his baggage repeats with ablution if time remains but is discharged if the time has gone out; that al-Muntakhaba directs one who finds no earth to beat felts and garments and use that dust even if none is seen to fly; and that Ta'wil al-Da'a'im requires a man trapped in a crush to pray with tayammum and then repeat the prayer once he can reach water.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: In a reported case two men performed tayammum together and only one prayer was valid: the man who asked to be taught prayed validly, while his teacher, who struck the earth for him, did not, because he formed no intention for himself — establishing that intention (niyya) is indispensable.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author rules that the dung of any animal not lawful to eat is impure, so neem oil pressed from stones passed through crows' droppings may not be eaten, sold, or bought, even though no impurity is visible in it.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: Where a liquid such as honey, clarified butter, olive oil or sesame oil holds an animal with flowing blood that has died in it, it may not be eaten nor fed to animals lawful to eat, though soap may be made from it and sold only if the buyer is told of its corruption, and a garment washed with such soap must be rinsed with pure water; reports add that it may be fed to dogs and non-edible beasts, that a pot with a dead mouse has its broth poured off and its meat washed and eaten, and that food is still edible if one or two grains of mouse droppings are removed but not if three come out.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author reconciles the report that the leavings of a menstruating woman, a Jew, a Christian, beasts of prey and riding animals do no harm with the ruling that a dog's lapping is impure by appealing to moisture and to water above the legal limit, and elsewhere holds that the leavings of a Jew, Christian, Magian or cat falling into a small vessel leave it valid for purification so long as no saliva is apparent.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: On unbelievers' foodstuffs the author distinguishes the prohibition of their slaughtered animals — forbidden only because God's name is not pronounced and the animal is not turned to the qibla — from their other food, which is lawful in itself but defiled wherever they have touched it with their moisture or wet implements, so that avoidance is obligatory when an alternative exists but need removes the restriction except for their slaughter and their moisture.

points.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
points.text: The author cites Hasan ibn Nuh's questions to Husayn ibn Idris that the slaughter of the People of the Book may be eaten if a Muslim observed the qibla and the divine name, and cites the Yemeni masters' answers to Hasan al-Hindi that eating the cooking of a serving girl careless about ritual purity is permitted; and holds that betel with a small harmless amount of lime, like water with a little earth, is not forbidden unless gross and harmful.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: The section is built from a question-and-answer compilation arranged according to the chapter order of Qadi al-Numan's Daaim al-Islam, supplemented by letters and rulings of later dignitaries.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: On circumcision the rule given is that no uncircumcised person is left so in Islam even at eighty years of age, and the same insistence is extended to the circumcision of girls (khafd) for a woman who has grown old.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Qadi al-Numan, answering his district governor al-Khattab ibn Wasim, qualifies the rule: a man born circumcised — as some prophets are reported to have been — is exempt, and one whose glans or most of it is already exposed is not compelled, though it is recommended for a young man that remaining skin be cut away.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: A reported saying of Ali instructs women not to take the girls' circumcision to the utmost but to leave something of it, which the answer glosses as better for the husband's inclination toward her; a further opinion holds that the prayer and the marital intercourse of an uncircumcised woman are nonetheless valid, the sunna being merely to hasten to it.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Hair of the head must be parted into two halves from front to back — the Indian custom of parting toward the middle is rejected — and deliberate defiance of this ruling is said to corrupt the prayer, while mere negligence does not.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Trimming is permitted only from the two sides of the beard (al-aridayn) and body hair may be shaved, shortened or plucked freely, but nothing may be removed from the beard itself.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Defined terms are supplied for the Prophet's prohibition on a menstruating woman taking up a qassa or jumma: the jumma is hair plaited from the side locks to the nape, the qassa is cutting the head's hair leaving about a quarter at the front, and the qunzua — hair gathered with portions left standing — is likewise forbidden.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Engraving the skin with henna dye is forbidden, but dyeing the teeth, filing uneven teeth level (for women), and piercing the ears of women and infant girls for ornaments are all permitted, and Indian popular scruples about spouses sharing one comb or about combing on Friday night are dismissed as having no reliance placed upon them.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Henna for a man is not sinful but is judged unfitting: it is better for him to leave it absent a cause, since henna, like jewelry, was appointed for women.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, writing from Yemen in his letter al-Sayf al-aqta fi ibtal al-bida, argues that God placed men's adornment in the beard and women's in the length of their head hair, so that a woman's shaving of her head — or even of the edges around the crown and the temples — is a disfigurement of her form and an inversion of the divinely appointed order.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar's proof for that prohibition is an a fortiori argument from Qadi al-Numan's ihram rulings: since the bald man passes the razor over his head while the woman released from ihram only cuts from the ends of her hair and shaves none of it, shaving can never be lawful for her as a standing custom.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar condemns a double inversion of practice: girls are being circumcised within ten to forty days when Ali forbade it before seven years, while boys' circumcision — commanded to be hastened, ideally on the seventh day — is deferred, in some regions to nearly twenty years, a delay shamed by the People of the Book who circumcise on the seventh day in obedience to Moses.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: Jafar rules that girls' circumcision must be done in concealment — known only to the girl, the operator and a few household women — and that the public gatherings, hospitality and call to prayer used for it in Yemen belong only to the purification of male children and offend against modesty, which the Prophet made part of faith.

points.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
points.text: The author reports that he himself put questions from the Island of Hind to Jafar in Yemen, who ruled that a girl dying below seven is not to be circumcised since the set limit may not be transgressed — a ruling Muhammad ibn Fahd al-Mukarrami independently confirms — whereas a male child who dies uncircumcised is, by preferred sunna, circumcised after death.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The author states that the material in this section is drawn largely from a previously mentioned book of questions and answers whose compiler arranged it following the chapter order of دعائم الإسلام.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The answer given is that if impure garments, carrion skins, or skins of beasts of prey cling to the body while either is wet, the body must be washed, and the same applies to garments washed by the hands of polytheists.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On the authority of تأويل الدعائم, the goat's hair is not to be shorn except after slaughter — if shorn while the animal is alive it counts as carrion — a ruling stated to apply to the goat in particular, whereas sheep's wool may be shorn for use while the animal lives.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The answer regarding wool, fleece or hair shorn from a lawful animal while alive is that prayer is not permitted in it until it has been washed, yet the material itself is not impure.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Concerning vessels made of carrion skins in Waghar used to transport ghee or oil to Ahmedabad, the answer is that the contents become impure and one may not pray in a garment they touch, that selling or buying the ghee or the soap made from it is permitted provided the buyer is told it is impure, but that selling or buying the carrion skins themselves is unlawful.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: From مختصر المصنف: a broken bone may be patched only with the bone of a properly slaughtered animal whose flesh is eaten; one who used carrion bone, non-edible animal bone, or human bone must remove it and repeat every prayer, compelled by the ruling authority if known, but it is not removed after death if he died in ignorance.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On menstruation, the husband may touch the whole body of the menstruating woman short of intercourse, though it is better he avoid what is beneath the wrapper worn from navel to knees, for fear the fluid reach her womb.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The texts set the least of menstruation at three days, the most at ten days, and the least of purity at ten days; blood beyond ten days makes the woman a mustahadah if she is in doubt, while a certain woman who distinguishes menstrual blood from istihadah blood may continue to abstain without making up prayers.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On the term of nifas the author reports divergent positions: Hasan ibn Nuh and several books reckon it by the woman's accustomed duration; a book of the Sharia of the people of the House gives a minimum of twenty days, a middle of forty and a maximum of sixty; and al-Numan's المنتخبة has her wait up to two months and then, if blood persists, count herself mustahadah and make up the abandoned prayers and fasts by precaution.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The author gives his own decisive ruling that the postpartum woman, once clean of blood, becomes pure after twenty days, thereafter relying on her custom and judging any excess blood as istihadah if its character has changed.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: The mustahadah is defined as a woman whose blood does not cease but is distinguishable — thick and turbid in menstruation, thin otherwise — so that she abstains from prayer, the mosque and her husband while the menstrual blood is present, and resumes all of these with ablution for each appearance of the remaining flow.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: From تأويل الدعائم: a man who approaches a menstruating woman must seek forgiveness and repent, with charity recommended; the same falls on the woman if she consented, nothing on her if compelled, and if she concealed her menstruation the sin falls on her alone and not on the unknowing husband.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: In the answer of Hasan ibn Idris to Shaykh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghuri al-Hindi, nifas may be less than forty days though forty must be reckoned, and Muhammad ibn al-Fahd held that blood seen after ten days makes a woman a mustahadah who washes (or performs tayammum) for each prayer time as she is able.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: Hasan ibn Idris answers that neither the menstruating woman nor the one in janaba may recite any portion of the Quran, whether in supplications or books, nor recite the basmala with the intention of Quranic recitation.

points.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
points.text: On istibra: marriage to a woman with whom one has fornicated requires prior clearing of the womb; مختصر المصنف sets the withdrawal at two months; كتاب الأخبار transmits forty-five nights for a mature woman who has not menstruated and nine months for such a virgin deflowered by the seller; and by the maxim "the child belongs to the bed and the fornicator gets the stone," the fornicator has no claim in the child's lineage.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author cites Ali ibn Abi Talib's 'four hundred precepts' to establish prayer's merits and conditions: night prayer benefits body and earns God's pleasure, the worshipper receives only that portion of prayer to which he attended, and laziness, drowsiness, looking aside, and toying with the beard are to be avoided.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Quoting Ali, prayer is 'the offering (qurban) of every godfearing person' and no deed is more beloved to God than prayer, so worldly affairs must not distract from its appointed times, God having reproached in Q107 those 'neglectful of their prayer' — i.e., heedless of its times.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: From a book of legal riddle-questions the author reports three cases: the drunkard for whom prayer is impermissible (Q4:43) yet who is not excused for omitting it; the emigrant whose prayer behind a bedouin (a'rabi) is invalid since bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy; and the swimmer unable to reach land, who owes an obligatory prayer without bowing or prostration.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: On precedence, the answer given is that one who remembers missed prayers (al-fawa'it) during a current prayer's time must pray the missed ones first if time allows, and he sins if, with room in the time and no hindrance, he neglects them for the current prayer.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The section systematically distinguishes ada (performance within its time) from qada (making up after the time has passed), applying the distinction to sunnah and nafilah prayers — e.g., remaining sunnah is made up once its time (before the obligatory prayer) has passed, and the optional prayer is ada so long as its time has not lapsed.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The sunnah of Maghrib is the stated exception to the rule that sunnah precedes the obligatory prayer: it is prayed after the obligatory Maghrib and still counts as ada, provided nothing separates the two, or if a slight interruption occurred and the congregation had not finished it.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: One who abandons the prescribed prayer for a long period without excuse is 'not counted a Muslim' during that period and none of his lawful deeds is accepted — citing the Prophet's 'between the servant and disbelief is only the abandonment of prayer' and Ali's 'prayer is the pillar of religion, the first deed God examines' and 'no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer'.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: The author qualifies that 'disbelief' here means only that his deeds are not accepted, since he stands in a disbeliever's position; in practice — poll tax, killing, enslaving his offspring, ritual impurity, his slaughtered meat — his ruling remains that of a Muslim, because the two testimonies place him within the rulings of Islam.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Upon sincere repentance (tawba nasuh, Q66:8) the abandoner becomes truly Muslim and his deeds are accepted; he need not make up the prayers missed before repenting (though he is rewarded if he does), but deliberately broken Ramadan fasts from that period require both making up and expiation.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: A contrasting case is drawn: one otherwise constant in prayer who misses obligatory prayers out of necessity may not perform the sunnah or optional prayers of the current time until he has first made up the missed obligatory prayer.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Prayer at the end of the time with certainty is better than at its beginning with doubt; prayer performed before the time has entered must be repeated; missed prayers may be made up whenever remembered except at sunrise, the meridian, and sunset, and voluntary prayer at those moments is makruh on Friday and other days alike.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, in the book of the interpretation of the Sharia, defines the five times by hidden indications — Dhuhr when a shadow equals its object, 'Asr when double, Maghrib at the setting of the disc, Isha' al-Akhirah at the vanishing of the white twilight, Fajr from daybreak to near sunrise — and notes the times are hidden while the prayers are manifest, making ten: five outward and five inward.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Al-Nu'man further sets prayer's four boundaries — time, qibla, wudu, intention — and its seven obligatory elements: takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, glorification, tashahhud, and sealing.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah is reported as ruling that the Fajr prayer belongs neither to the night nor the day prayers — for if it were of the night the faster could still eat, and if of the day its recitation would not be aloud — it being the middle prayer of five, and no prayer follows it because it is a call after a call with no call after it.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inward Nursing, gives the witr as three units with fixed surahs (al-A'la, al-Kafirun, al-Ikhlas) and the qunut after rising from bowing, followed after a separation by two units prayed seated reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas specifically, then the dawn prayer of four units — two voluntary and two obligatory — identified as the middle prayer of Q2:238.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim, answering Muhammad 'Ali ibn Salih al-Badri from Yemen to Hind in 1145 AH, rules that making up prayer follows the rule of the fast — only men make up on behalf of men — and that an aged man too weak to make up prays what he can while another makes up on his behalf with expiation.

points.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
points.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd ibn Salah's epistle rules that a bequest for making up a deceased's missed worship is applied in order — obligatory prayer portions, then shaf' and witr, then the sunan — with prayer advanced before the obligatory fast if the wage is insufficient.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Answering a question about a man appointed by a tyrannical sultan as prayer leader, muezzin or teacher on a salary drawn from the port levy or jizya, the compiled answer is that such money comes from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) and is lawful for him to consume only if it is administered according to the judgment of one appointed by the friends of God.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Idah reports from Jafar ibn Muhammad ibn Ali that giving the call while walking or mounted is permissible provided that at the moment of the testimony one faces the qibla, while the author states that the books attributed to the Ahl al-Bayt agree that the iqama is valid only while standing on the ground.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf instructs the muezzin to say inwardly, after the twofold testimony to Muhammad's messengership, 'I bear witness that Ali is the friend of God,' and after 'Come to the best of deeds,' 'The family of Muhammad are the best of humankind.'

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf further holds that one present in the mosque at the call should not leave before praying, except for a necessity with intent to return in time or to perform ablution, and if he misses the congregation he prays alone or with another congregation without fault.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Tawil al-Sharia holds that the muezzin may give the adhan without purity but the iqama requires purity, that he faces the qibla and forms intention first, and that the supererogatory prayer is joined to the adhan while the obligatory prayer is prayed only after the iqama.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Idris ibn Sayyidina Hasan records in the sixth part of Uyun al-Akhbar that in the caliphate of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah the muezzins added to the call the testimony that 'our mawla Ali is the friend of God' and the proclamation that Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind and their kindred the best of kindred, in confirmation of the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir, 'Whoever's master I am, Ali is his master.'

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Against the claim, related from Abu Bakr, that 'we are the kindred of the Messenger of God,' the text holds that Ibn Abbas identified the near kindred as Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn alone, and that Abu Bakr's only link to the Prophet was the remote one of Quraysh, a point supported by al-Kumayt's verse naming Banu Hashim as the Prophet's clan.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The common objection is stated: many concede that Muhammad is the best of humankind but deny it of Ali, since humankind includes the prophets.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The first answer to that objection is that all Muslims agree, on the verse 'You were the best community brought forth for the people,' that Muhammad's community surpasses earlier communities which themselves contained prophets and favoured friends of God — so the same comparative logic must be granted for Ali.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Supporting reports are cited: the hadith of the two weighty things from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, likening the Book and the Prophet's kindred to Noah's ark in which boarding means salvation and holding back means drowning, and the saying 'Ali is the best of humankind, and whoever refuses this has disbelieved.'

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The narrated confrontation at al-Gharafa has al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah adjudicate between the preacher of Atfih, who rejected the new call, and the dai who gave it, by getting the preacher to confirm as sound the reports that al-Hasan and al-Husayn are the masters of the youth of the Garden, that their father is better than the two of them, and that the people of the Garden are youths who do not grow old.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: Al-Hakim's syllogism concludes that since Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus are in the Garden but are not its youths, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn are masters of its youth while their father is better than they, it is established that Ali is the best of humankind together with the Prophet — whereupon the shaykh assented and al-Hakim told the dai to give the call as he wished, for none would oppose him.

points.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
points.text: The author announces that he will next reproduce in full the epistle of his sayyid and mawla and father Muhammad ibn Fahd, entitled al-Muriba amma jarat bihi al-mubahatha, which frames the dispute between those who hold the added words of the call impermissible and unnarrated and those who hold them commanded by the Noble Book and binding on whoever obeys those whose command must be obeyed.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The section is framed as a recorded debate: one jurist challenges another over why his school alone says in the call to prayer 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred,' and the respondent undertakes to answer.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The respondent's first reply is that by Quran 41:46 and 6:164 the formula, if righteous, benefits only its users and, if wrong, harms only them, so no other group is burdened by it — a reply the questioner accepts while still demanding a plain proof.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The questioner concedes as established that Muhammad is the best of human beings because he is master of the messengers, but denies that Ali's likeness to him in that excellence is established, and demands proof — so only Ali's rank is actually in dispute.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof one argues from the Purification verse (33:33) that the people of the household are equal to the Prophet in purity, and since Ali is the most excellent of them and the Prophet's guardian and successor, likeness to the Prophet is established for him.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proofs two, three and six argue from 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin' (37:130), 'You are the best community brought forth for humankind' (3:110), and 'those who believe and do righteous deeds are the best of creation' (98:7) that these verses address the Prophet's household, and since Ali is first and most excellent among them he is the best of human beings.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof four reasons that God granted Moses's request for Aaron as minister, brother, sharer in his task and holder of joint authority, and that since God's way admits no change or alteration (35:43, 17:77) and Muhammad was told to follow earlier prophets' guidance, Muhammad was obliged to appoint Ali in the same role — confirmed by the hadith 'Ali stands to me in the station of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.'

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proof five argues from the Guardianship verse (5:55–56), read as revealed concerning Ali, that he shares with the Messenger guardianship over the believers, a station only the best of human beings after the Messenger could hold — reinforced by the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir Khumm, 'Whoever's master I am, this Ali is his master.'

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: Proofs seven and eight argue from 3:33–34 (God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran) and 44:30–32 (God chose the Children of Israel above the worlds) that, since Muhammad is more excellent than all prophets, his family surpasses the family of every prophet in every era, and Ali is the most excellent of that family.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: An objection is reported from opponents of the school: that Umar's removal of 'Hayya ala khayr al-amal' from the adhan is unproven from their books, was in any case a sound exercise of judgment, and that if it were an error then adding 'I testify that our master Ali is the guardian of God' would equally be an error, since adder and subtractor are alike.
entities: Ashhadu anna mawlana Aliyyan waliyy Allah

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The author replies that even conceding both addition and subtraction to be error, the two are not of equal degree, for four reasons: the subtractor misled vastly more people; he preceded al-Hakim by over four centuries and the earlier misleader is more culpable; he not only subtracted but added the ugly sentence 'prayer is better than sleep,' setting prayer against sleep as though comparing a sword to wood; and he dropped the Prophet's phrase from all five prayers while attaching his own only to the dawn prayer.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: The author rejects as void slander the ascription of the guardianship phrase to al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, noting that the Twelver Shia, though differing from him in school, also use it in the call to prayer.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
