points.text: Against the claim that Umar's subtraction is absent from the opponents' books, the author answers that the disputed soundness and fabricated reports of Sahih al-Bukhari, the other five, and al-Mishkat relieve the people of truth of any need to refute them, and that al-Qadi al-Numan's narration from Jafar al-Sadiq predates those compilations, which may well have suppressed the report to avoid censure.

points.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
points.text: On the origin of the added phrase, the author holds that the testimony to guardianship issued from Ali himself about himself once the office passed to him after the Prophet, just as the Prophet testified to his own prophethood and God testified concerning His own oneness (3:18).

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The compilation cites the Prophet's saying that the earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification except the bathhouse, the cemetery, and the latrine, and the answer affirms that in the outward sense of the Sharia one does not pray in those places at all and no mosque is built beside graves.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: A decisive distinction is drawn between a mosque given over to public use (waqf) and one kept private: a private mosque within a house may be pulled down, relocated or absorbed into the house, while a publicly dedicated mosque may not be demolished by its owner, though nothing is owed if it collapses on its own.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: A man building a congregational or other mosque on his own property does as he wishes and need not seek the governor's permission.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The 'neighbor of the mosque' is defined as one who hears the call to prayer, and while the prayer of any man without congregation counts as a single prayer, it is specifically disliked for the neighbor of the mosque to pray alone at home without an excuse.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The greeting prayer of the mosque is owed only in a mosque open to the people, not in a private place of prayer, and not while an obligatory prayer is owed or outside the times when supererogatory prayer is permitted.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: The compilation's answer holds that one who leaves the mosque for a need and returns prays the greeting again, whereas Muhammad ibn al-Fahd rules in his epistle that going out only to the mosque's courtyard or forecourt does not require repeating it, since those areas lie within the mosque's bounds.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Two imams do not lead the same prayer at one time in one assembly, and the leading of prayer is not held in one mosque more than once — except that an imam whose state is broken may appoint a substitute, and a separate congregation praying on the roof is permitted.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Both the Q&A compilation and Muhammad ibn al-Fahd resolve the grave-and-mosque problem by order of construction: if the mosque or domed structure was built first and burial followed, prayer in it is permitted, but if it was built on account of a pre-existing grave it takes the ruling of a cemetery and prayer in it is never permitted.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: One ignorant of the qibla exerts his judgment and prays; if he learns of his error during the prayer and time is short he turns toward the House and completes it provided he was between east and west, but if his back was to the Kaaba only repetition suffices — and if two (or four) directions are equally confused he prays toward both together.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Tawil al-Daaim rules that bringing weapons into mosques is not permitted in the outward sense except for the imam of the mosque on Friday, while Ali is quoted forbidding praying with a sword before one because the qibla is a place of safety.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Majalis al-Bayan lists twelve places where prayer is disliked: cemetery, slaughterhouse, bathhouse, latrine, resting places of camels, facing a sleeping person, without a screen, wet impure ground, upon food, places of worship, churches, and Magian houses unless sprinkled with water.

points.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
points.text: Al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya grades prayer in seven ascending ranks of merit: the house counts as one prayer, the market mosque twelve, the tribal mosque twenty-five, the congregational mosque one hundred, the Farthest Mosque one thousand, the Mosque of the Messenger ten thousand, and the Sacred House of God one hundred thousand.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The compiler states that twelve categories of men may not lead prayer — the sick leading the healthy, the leper, the one with white leprosy, the madman, one on whom a prescribed penalty has been carried out, the child of adultery, the bedouin leading emigrants, the fettered leading the unfettered, one who performed dry ablution leading those who used water, the mute leading speakers, a traveler leading residents, and one hostile to the Prophet's household leading its followers — while each of these may lead others in his own condition.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Reported from Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, precedence in leading prayer follows a ranked order — earliest in emigration, then best reciter, then most learned in jurisprudence, then eldest — with the owner of a mosque having better right in his mosque, and the Imam or whomever he appoints having the strongest right of all, while a woman leading women stands among them rather than ahead.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The compiler defines the محدود, whose leadership is barred, as one upon whom the prescribed legal penalty has actually been carried out, and defines the barred 'fettered' man as one bound on the legs or anywhere else.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: A slave learned in jurisprudence may lead when no one more learned is present, and he leads whoever is below him in rank even if they are free men — though when the slave's master is present in the slave's own dwelling the master has the stronger right to lead.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Taqiyya licenses modification but not abandonment of ritual elements: one may omit ربنا لك الحمد before outsiders, and may recite the basmala aloud only so far as to hear himself, but such omission is forbidden for any cause other than taqiyya.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: An imam whose recitation is so distorted that it alters the meanings of the Quran — as by a wrong vowel turning a verse of mercy into one of punishment — may not lead and spoils the prayer, whether the defect comes from lost teeth or ignorance of the points of articulation; and one who recites well is obliged to lead when the people call on him.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Sources differ in degree on the blind imam: al-Ikhtisar and al-Qadi al-Numan permit his leading when there is need and he is set straight, but not as a standing imam, while al-Muntakhaba adds that he may lead only if set straight on a given day; Mukhtasar al-Athar reports that the People of the House disliked his imamate along with that of the leper, the child of adultery, the castrated, the owned slave, the bedouin, the penalized, and the madman.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Two imams are not to be gathered in one undivided place unless the later one is the more excellent — as when a higher licence-holder prays a second congregation of the same prayer in the same house — while a partition removes the objection entirely.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: A follower must never precede the imam in any act, returning to his prior position if he does so by forgetfulness, and the Prophet is reported in al-Majalis al-Hatimiyya as warning that whoever raises his head before the imam risks God transforming his head into a donkey's.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: If an imam's ablution breaks, the prayer is saved only if a substitute is put forward at that very moment before he leaves the mosque, and an imam with unrestricted leave may appoint whomever he wishes even one not otherwise authorized to appoint.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Rows must be continuous with room for prostration between them, praying alone behind the rows requires repetition, a latecomer finding no place prays alongside the imam rather than in his row, and only the imam's hujja may step level with the imam.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidna Sulayman, answering the book's own author Sayyidna Ali ibn Sulayman, rules that women praying behind a screen need only one glance at the men's garments before entering the sanctified state when the place is not connected, and none at all when it is connected by an opening or lattice — any looking after the sanctified state at non-kin cuts off the prayer.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: The Prophet, reported in al-Muizz's interpretation of the Shariah as leading seated after a fall from a horse, told his companions that the imam exists to be followed and that when he prays seated they must all pray seated.

points.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
points.text: An imam uncertain how much of the prayer he has completed builds on what is certain and may be corrected by the glorifications of those behind him if they are certain, but if neither he nor they know, he begins the prayer anew.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The question-and-answer book reports that Ali (ع) recited 'So be patient; the promise of God is true' during prayer not as the opening of that surah but specifically to silence and rebuke Ibn al-Kawwa, who kept raising his voice.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: In the madhhab of the Ahl al-Bayt, the long portions of al-mufassal run from al-Hujurat to al-Mujadila, the middle from al-Mujadila to 'Amma yatasa'alun', and the short from 'Amma yatasa'alun' to al-Nas.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The same source lists acts that break the covenant, including abandoning prayer or prescribed works without excuse, disbelieving a believer's oath after accusing him, fornication, killing a believer, reviling the summoner or his appointee, and refusing the summoner's call to strive with person and wealth.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Per Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, if the intention for prayer slips away — through preoccupation, forgetfulness or anything else — before one enters the prayer, the prayer afterwards does not suffice; and one may not recite inwardly what the tongue has not uttered.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: On the tashahhuds, performing the first does not excuse one from the second, but the second does suffice in place of the first.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Al-Ikhtisar gives the minimum by which prayer is completed as five limits — opening takbir, standing for the able, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the tashahhud — valid for one who forgot or did not know more, whereas one who knows the limits and deliberately omits any obligation or sunnah has no prayer and must repeat it, and the ignorant man is obliged to learn.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Postural rulings are specified by source: the woman places her hands above her knees on her thighs so as not to raise her hindquarters (al-Akhbar); those behind the imam answer 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise' quietly, except the appointed relayer who raises his voice with it and the takbir but not the tasbih (Tawil al-Daaim); and the sitter folds his left leg beneath him and keeps the right upright (Tawil al-Daaim, outward sense).

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: In the jurisprudential exchange between Shaykh Hasan ibn Mawla Adam al-Hindi and the sayyids of Yemen, the prayer of a woman who has not undergone khafd is valid and intimacy with her is permissible, and likewise for the man, though the sunnah is to hasten to it.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes those who profess walaya yet never prostrate in a single rakah, citing the Prophet's 'between the servant and unbelief is abandoning the prayer' and Ali's 'there is no portion in Islam for one who abandons the prayer' to conclude that such a person holds no share of Islam.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman divides the neglecters of prayer into two kinds — people of tribal temper absorbed in themselves with animal nature dominant, and people of arrogance and coarse insolence, especially the women — and holds both kinds to be found in every school of Islam and every religion, adding that even unbelievers, including those of India, perform some inherited worship, so that such arrogance falls under the Quranic threat against those too proud to worship God, the path on which Iblis perished.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman argues that worship benefits only the worshipper, God having no need of it, since He created jinn and mankind to worship Him for their own benefit, and that no one has a claim of walaya to the friends of God except by holding fast to the hem of the prayer.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The lists of obligations differ by source: Tawil al-Shariah gives seven — first takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, tasbih, greeting, taslim — while the Dai Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives seven as intention, first takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, taslim, and the Majalis al-Mustansiriyya gives intention, turning to the qibla, takbirat al-ihram, recitation of the Opening, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the salutation.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah forbids moving the foot or speaking from the opening takbir to the taslim, cites the Prophet on prostrating upon seven members, and prohibits reciting while bowing, disturbing pebbles, turning like a fox, squatting like a monkey, pecking like a crow, and drooping the head below the level of the back.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives the prayer four limits — place, time, purity, intention — with five daily prayers of seventeen rakahs divided into obligation and sunnah, and interprets 'the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed' esoterically to mean the one who abandons my legatee is banished from God's mercy, adding that the outward prayer itself neither forbids nor commands.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya enumerates seven obligatory prayers (residence of seventeen rakahs, travel of eleven, Friday requiring four with the imam, fear, the tawaf of obligatory Hajj, the tawaf of obligatory Umrah, and the prayer over the bier which binds every Muslim who knows until one undertakes it) and twelve sunnah prayers, matching purity's divisions to the clauses and letters of the shahada.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya lists twelve sunnahs within each of the five prayers, ending with the rule that any prayer lacking a first sitting has a qunut counted in its place, while any prayer with two tashahhud sittings has no qunut.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Ali's Four Hundred Etiquettes forbids clasping the hands while standing in prayer as resembling the People of the Book, rules that gross turning about cuts off the prayer and requires beginning again with adhan, iqama and takbir, and directs sitting between the two prostrations until the limbs are still, turning to the right on leaving the prayer, and making oneself hear the recitation when praying alone.

points.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
points.text: Answering Muhammad Ali ibn Salih al-Badri of India, the master Hibat Allah rules that since no text from the friends of God forbids reciting the two surahs of refuge in obligatory prayer, such a prayer is complete — one who recited al-Nas in the first rakah repeats it in the last, one who recited al-Ikhlas in the first recites al-Falaq in the second — but one should not deliberately recite in this manner, putting it in the position of the sunnah.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: A question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of the Pillars of Islam reports that, per the books of the guiding call, no supplication — neither the supplication of drawing near nor any other — is recited after the afternoon prayer, yet whoever does supplicate incurs no sin.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The same source rules that wiping the face at the place of prostration is permitted only after the afternoon and dawn prayers, as the masters commanded and as received from the pure Imams, and that supplication after the afternoon prayer is not prolonged though prolonging it incurs nothing.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The book on the interpretation of the Sharia sets the rule that daytime prayers are recited quietly while night prayers — including dawn, offered in the last darkness — are recited aloud.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The author of the Mustansiriyya Councils, in the Eleventh Council, follows the jurisprudence of prayer — where the outward gets exposition and the inward its sign and intimation — with the closing supplication and its seven and its twelve.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The seven are bodily postures of supplication: asking (palms facing the face), seeking refuge (backs of palms facing the face), humble submission (grasping the shoulders, done only in solitude), devotion (pointing with the index finger), entreaty (moving the finger), fervent appeal (both palms spread and raised to the sky), and abasement in the dust (turning the cheeks on the ground).

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Each of the seven supplications has a corresponding mention in the Quran, to be brought forward later, since what has been set down so far is only roots awaiting branches and fruit.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The twelve are the foundations on which answered supplication is built: prefacing it with repentance, charity, fasting or prayer (per 'To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it'), purifying intention, praising God, blessing the Prophet at start, middle and end, drawing near through the imams of religion up to the imam of one's age, seeking access through them, asking the good of both worlds, seeking refuge from the evil of both, and then asking whatever one wills.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his Four Hundred Etiquettes, teaches that God answers supplication when He is remembered, that the gates of heaven open at six times (rainfall, the advance in battle, the call to prayer, Quranic recitation, the sun's decline, and daybreak), that supplication turns back even a firmly settled decree, that it should be used to repel affliction before it descends, and that one who supplicates without deeds is an archer with no bowstring.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Ali also states that whoever recites Sura al-Ikhlas ten times and Sura al-Qadr before sunrise will be touched by no sin however hard Iblis strives.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The question-and-answer book rules on incidental acts in prayer: deliberate throat-clearing without excuse cuts off the prayer (the imam must instead be alerted by words of glorification or a gesture) and habitual deliberate throat-clearing requires repeating the prayer; a woman may not occupy herself in prayer with carrying her child to quiet him; food placed in the mouth out of necessity for pain incurs nothing; a braid wound inside the turban is permissible since the forbidden binding is turning the hair back on its root to the middle of the head.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Holding a gemstone, dirham or similar in the mouth or hand does not void the prayer if it does not prevent proper formation of the letters or fulfilment of the prayer's limits, though being free of all such things is more fitting; and the abridgment of the compiled book holds that eating or drinking in prayer, whether forgetful or deliberate, cuts off the prayer.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: The interpretation of the Sharia further holds that recitation precedes bowing, that one must not raise his voice above the imam's, that noon and afternoon are recited quietly and the night prayer aloud, that the Prophet forbade wiping over leather socks and forbade omitting the audible basmala, and that once the opening magnification is pronounced the worshipper does not speak until the salutation.

points.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his book on the inward nursing, enumerates fourteen indispensable 'doors' of prayer — ablution, opening, call to prayer, standing call, turning toward God, recitation, bowing, praise, glorification, prostration, testimony, salutation, the supplication of the standing invocation, and the supplication of the odd-numbered prayer — which are its supporting pillars and without which prayer is incomplete.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: A collection of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of the Daaim al-Islam (Pillars of Islam) supplies the first body of rulings on dress and prayer surfaces.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: On figured rugs and garments the section preserves two differing answers: one respondent permits prayer so long as the image does not occupy the worshipper's attention (except that he does not pray toward images), while another answer states that prayer on or in figured cloth is not permitted when the figures are seen, and permitted only when they are not seen.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Dyed garments and deep red cloth belong to the domain of etiquette (adab) and do not invalidate the prayer of either a man or a woman, with the sole exception that pure silk is disliked for men.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Because the whole of a woman is 'awra, any exposure of her awra during prayer invalidates it, whether she knew of the ruling or was ignorant of it — a ruling applied explicitly to the women of the people of the dawa in India who do not wear the long shift and head-veil.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: The abridgment of the Musannaf draws a distinction by sex: a man who prays with his awra uncovered unknowingly repeats the prayer only once he learns of it, whereas a free or slave woman's prayer is spoiled whether she knew or not.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Prayer is valid only in pure garments, and impurity requires stripping it off; one who has only an impure garment and no water prays in it and repeats when a clean garment or water is found, and one with two garments, one impure but unidentified, must pray the prayer in each with the intention of fulfilling the obligation.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: One who prays and afterwards finds his garment was impure must repeat the prayer, whether or not its time has passed, if he had known of the impurity beforehand.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: On head covering the sources differ in emphasis: one ruling says a man should not pray bareheaded without turban or mantle but may do so if he finds neither, while Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in the book of the obligations and limits of religion that it is lawful for a man to uncover his head and pray bareheaded.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Slave women, women under a contract of manumission, women freed at their master's death, and girls who have not yet menstruated may pray without a head covering, but one freed without knowing it must repeat every prayer she prayed uncovered after her freedom.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Idris ibn al-Hasan, answering Shaykh Yusuf ibn Ismail ibn Ibrahim al-Samati al-Hindi, grounds the surface rule in the Prophet's saying that the earth was made a place of prostration and a means of purification, concluding that prayer is not valid upon anything of the earth with which dry ablution (tayammum) is not permitted.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Obligatory prayer is not permitted upon stone, unbaked brick and the like — only supererogatory and sunna prayer — while there is no harm in prostrating upon plaster over which carrion was burned, since the fire has purified it, and the interpretation of the Sharia holds there is no prayer except upon the earth or what grows from it.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: The interpretation of the Daaim glosses disputed phrases of the source text: praying in a single thick belted shirt so that the private part does not appear when bowing; the garment worn 'like the two wings of the swallow' when nothing else is found; and the forbidden ishtimal al-samma' wrap, which is rejected because it physically prevents placing the palms, bowing, prostrating and raising the hands, leaving the prayer incomplete.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred counsels of etiquette, forbids standing before God except in a clean garment, forbids praying in a loosely draped shirt as the practice of the people of Lot, forbids prostrating upon an image or a rug containing one, forbids knotting an image-bearing dirham into the garment while praying (though coins in a clean money belt or cloth are permitted), and forbids prostrating upon heaps of wheat, barley, any edible thing, or bread.

points.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
points.text: Minor supplementary rulings are recorded: carrying wrought or unwrought gold and silver in the waistband does not affect the prayer; something in the mouth or hand is harmless if it does not impede the letters or the limits of prayer though being free of it is better; henna for adornment is commanded for women and better left by men without being sinful; prayer is invalid in camel resting places but permitted in sheep folds once swept and sprinkled; a net does not substitute for a mantle since shift and veil suffice only if thick; and a small amount of milk, butter or egg white from filth-fed animals is permitted.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The compiler reports the ruling that Friday prayer is established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them, and that if the distance is less than three miles it is established in only one, whether the mosques stand in one city or in two.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that abandoning Friday prayer is blameworthy 'whether under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer given is that praying behind the people of injustice is permissible only for the sake of dissimulation (taqiyyah).

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Support for this is drawn from al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali, who instructed that prayer behind a nasib or haruri not be counted, and that such a leader be treated as a pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have put Muawiya's governor forward to lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the compiler explains as the practice of the People of the House in dissimulation, one Imam having said 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: A distinction is drawn: 'the unjust' in the sermon means one appointed among the summoners in whom injustice has appeared — behind him prayer is still obligatory, but the people must bring the matter before the holder of authority and await his response.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited for rulings of precedence and procedure: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims excels prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a sale then made is not annulled; and detailed remedies are given for broken purity, omitted sitting between sermons, and congregations that disperse mid-prayer.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the prayer, the prayer is two cycles, the sermon is divided by a sitting, the raised voice distinguishes it from the ordinary noon prayer, and the call to stand comes after the sermon.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah further equates the conduct of respondents in the assembly of the summoner with that of the Friday congregation: silence and listening are obligatory, and the respondent may not press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who knows better how to raise his children.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle interprets the Friday prayer as pointing to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, possessor of an outward summons to his Shariah and an inward summons to its interpretation; the reduction to two cycles with the sermon substituting for the other two, and the sitting as the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Points of Conduct names three hours for seeking a need from God: Friday at the sun's zenith, when the winds blow and the gates of heaven open, and the last hour of night at dawn, when two angels call out for the repentant, the asker, and the seeker of forgiveness.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: On the festivals, 'tashriq' is glossed as the prayer of the two festivals, so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq, and it is not incumbent on the traveler except in a congregational city.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: The twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are interpreted as a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, drawn from the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks plus the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age — the local addition of a twenty-fourth being noted as a departure.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Festival practice is specified: a congregation of five including the Imam as with Friday; the washing is a prophetic practice from dawn to the sun's zenith; hands are raised at every magnification; the festival prayer is not prayed in congregation at Mina but individually, as verified from Idris ibn Hasan.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl derives al-fitr from senses of splitting open, appearing and beginning, so that fasting is silence and concealment — evidenced by Maryam's vow of a fast of silence — and the day of breaking the fast is the day secrets and hidden knowledge are manifested.

points.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
points.text: He adds that the festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, that the breaking-of-the-fast sermon uniquely follows the prayer as a sign that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles, and that every sermon opens with praise except the sermon of the day of sacrifice, which opens with four magnifications.
entities: festival of the breaking of the fast

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The author distinguishes omission from doubt: the one who commits an omission is certain of what he omitted, while the doubter is not certain of what he doubts — a confusion said to trouble many jurists.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The two prostrations of omission are called al-marghamatan ('the two that rub down the nose') because they rub down the nose of the devil when the corruption of forgetfulness is repaired by them.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The Mustansiriyya councils enumerate seven places of omission in prayer, in six of which the two prostrations are proper — including omitting a prostration, forgetting the first or second tashahhud, saluting after two rakahs of a four-rakah prayer, and rising to a fifth rakah — while the seventh, omission behind the Imam, requires none because the Imam bears it.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Doubt in prayer falls into twelve cases: where the doubt concerns an act still ahead or unsettled (bowing, number of rakahs) the worshipper builds on what is certain — the lesser — and prostrates for omission; but where the doubt arises after the act has been passed (doubting the takbir after bowing, recitation after bowing, or anything after the salaam) nothing is due.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted from his four hundred manners: whoever is certain of something and is then struck by doubt should act on his certainty, for doubt neither dispels nor diminishes certainty.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: If the doubter is certain of nothing at all — not knowing whether he added to or fell short of his prayer — he begins the prayer again from the beginning, and so likewise does the Imam.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The responsa hold that intention resides in the heart and that utterance with the tongue is merely a verbal expression, so that an act intended in the heart is complete even if the intention is never spoken — cited as stated in the Pillars, against the text that deeds are accepted only with intentions.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The prostration of omission is not multiplied: one who omits several obligations, or commits omissions repeatedly in a single prayer, owes only the two prostrations.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Where there is no explicit text stipulating a prostration of omission — as with neglecting the first tashahhud but remembering before the salaam, or repeating a single surah after the Opening — the worshipper is not required to prostrate, though he should not do such things deliberately.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: Some omissions void the prayer outright rather than being repaired: failing to sit after each pair of rakahs, adding a bowing before sitting for the tashahhud, and neglecting the bowing or the opening takbir behind the Imam, which the Imam does not bear.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: On interruption, the Prophet's reported saying that three things interrupt the prayer — a woman, a donkey, and a black dog — is set beside his own account of seeing these pass before him, when he said nothing interrupts the prayer of a believer but 'ward off what you are able'; and Ali is quoted that smiling does not interrupt the prayer while loud laughter does.

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: The latecomer who reaches the Imam in the bowing, before the Imam raises his head, attains that rakah with a single takbir serving for both opening and bowing, provided he contracts the intention in his heart — as stated by Muhammad ibn Fahd in his epistle The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided.
entities: The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided

points.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
points.text: One who joins the Imam even only for the opening takbir before the salaam must perform the two prostrations for his Imam's omission, and one praying the remainder alone prostrates for his own errors.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib is reported to have instructed that boys be taught the prayer and held to it when they reach eight years, and taught that by which God will benefit their teachers.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Ibrahim ibn Husayn al-Hamidi in عبارة البشارة reports from Amir al-Muminin that a boy sheds his milk teeth at seven, reaches maturity at fourteen, completes his physical growth at twenty-one, and completes his intellect at twenty-eight.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: مختصر الآثار directs that children be separated in their sleeping places at that stage, as a precaution since they have neared maturity and the stirring of desire.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: The governing rule for the traveler is that he shortens the prayer and breaks the fast from leaving his dwelling until he re-enters it, provided he is pressing on in the journey, as stated in مختصر الآثار by al-Numan.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: A traveler completes (does not shorten) his prayer and fast by stopping five prayer times with a blood relative of lineage or with his resident wife, but not through his wife's relatives nor through kin by nursing.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Travel distances are defined: the barid is four farsakhs, the farsakh three miles, and the mile three thousand cubits, being a thousand even paces of a single leg.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: The limit of residence that obliges praying in full is ten days, and Muhammad ibn Fahd rules in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين that one who travels a barid intending return should commit to ten days and pray in full, and may still return earlier without invalidating those prayers.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Whoever enters Mecca prays in full and does not shorten, on the basis of the Quranic words 'the resident and the visitor stand equal' — though Sayyidina Ismail ibn Hiba held that full prayer applies only within the sanctuary of the House of God and that in Mecca itself the prayer is shortened.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: أنس الأفئدة المنيبة records Amir al-Muminin ruling that six categories do not shorten prayer or fast: circuit-traveling collectors, merchants moving market to market, princes touring their emirate, hunters, shepherds seeking rain-watered land, and warriors who cut the road.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: A traveler may lead residents (saluting after two rakahs while they rise to complete) and a mutayammim may lead those who performed ablution, but both dispensations are particular to the people of the high ranks and do not extend to the rest of the hudud.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidina Sulayman's performing tayammum in Haraz, after descending from the fortress of Tayba, and then leading the congregation is cited as the precedent establishing that dispensation when a weighty matter requires it for the good of the dawa.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in كتاب الرضاع الباطن that shortening applies to the three four-rakah prayers — the first, the afternoon, and the late evening — reducing twelve rakahs by six.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: The sick man prays according to his capacity in a descending scale: seated or cross-legged with bowing and prostration, then gesturing with the head, then with the eyes, and if unable even that, with the heart.

points.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
points.text: مختصر المصنف rules that one who loses his reason through something he drank or did to himself must repeat the prayers missed in that state, whether the act was obedient or disobedient.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Responding to perplexity over a solar eclipse observed early in a month (Dhu al-Qadah 837) against the Brethren of Purity's claim that solar eclipses occur only at month's end, the answer transmitted from the author of the letters and the pure Imams is that lunar eclipses fall at the dawn of the 15th or 16th while solar eclipses may occur at the beginning or the end of the month, the matter being in God's hand.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: A latecomer who joins the imam's eclipse prayer counts his joining as the start of his own prayer, prostrates and bows along with the imam, sits poised rather than settled during the imam's testimony, and after the imam's salutation rises to complete the remaining bowings, qunut, prostration, testimony and salutation, not counting the first two prostrations made with the imam.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The book of purity rules that the eclipse prayer is prayed only when the eclipse is actually seen with the eye, never on the word of an astrologer or anyone else, and not if cloud or another veil intervenes.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: In the prayer of fear, when swords cross and spears are thrust, prayers are reduced to takbir — one takbir in place of each bowing — and the takbir is itself shortened as shortening is obligatory in it; مختصر المصنف adds that the fear prayer requires at least three men praying with three standing guard, since the word 'party' does not apply to fewer than three.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: If eclipse prayer, funeral prayer and fear coincide for the imam, he prays over the funeral and prays both the eclipse prayer and the prayer of fear.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: For the rain prayer the cited books prescribe a hundred takbirs facing the people, a hundred glorifications to the right, a hundred declarations of oneness to the left, all aloud, then a hundred praises; two sermons as at the two feasts, delivered leaning on an Arabian bow as the Messenger of God did; going out on a day other than Monday is harmless, and whoever preaches before the prayer must pray and then preach again.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The qunut is a supplication not to be abandoned deliberately: deliberate omission in the witr requires repetition, while forgetting it requires no repetition (there being no prostrations of forgetfulness in sunnah prayers), and its minimum is three glorifications or three takbirs; it is recited after the words 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.'

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: On whether the witr may be divided by salutation, the answer cites Judge al-Numan's المنتخبة that the witr may be separated by the salutation without actions or speech, though unavoidable brief speech does no harm.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: The shaf and witr may validly be prayed during the first dawn (called by the Arabs ذنب السرحان) so long as the true dawn has not spread across the sky.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd rules in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين that one who prayed shaf, witr and then dawn only to learn it was still night keeps his shaf and witr and must repeat both sunnah and obligation of dawn, unless dawn was close upon him, in which case the sunnah also stands — because the books of the friends of God permit praying it before dawn for an inner meaning.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: معالم الدين holds the witr obligatory with no dispensation for abandoning it, counting it among the appendages of the obligatory prayers even though it is a sunnah.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Praying tarawih behind an imam for the sake of protective concealment (taqiyyah) is permitted with the intention of a voluntary prayer, but the believers do not take him as a leader, and anything of the sunnah omitted for concealment must be made up; reliance in such matters is upon الدعائم as the gathering place of the questions.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman rules that Mawlana al-Sadiq gave a text for the prayer of Umm Daud only for the month of Rajab, plus the day of 'Arafah (especially when it falls on a Friday), so Qasim ibn Fir's command to his Daudi followers to pray, fast and supplicate with it in Rabi al-Awwal and Ramadan of 1042 lacks a supporting text — no practice being valid without a text, since 'little practice in a sunnah is better than much practice in an innovation.'

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim answered from Yemen to Hind in 1135 that the prayer of the prophets and Imams at times of calamity — praise and thanksgiving for what God disclosed to them, knowing nothing occurs save by decree — may be prayed by their followers at all times when sunnah and voluntary prayers are permitted, prohibition applying only to the forbidden times.

points.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
points.text: Regarding the Quranic prostration, the binding verses oblige prostration even when recited within a supplication and oblige all present to prostrate (though not a second time for a repeat in the same place), whereas for the remaining verses prostration is optional though better, and a teacher passing over the places while instructing boys has a choice.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The compiler defines the dying state (al-naz') as the moment when death draws near and the passage from this world to the hereafter is at hand, citing the book of the interpretation of the pillars.
entities: book of the interpretation of the pillars

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Asked by Shaykh Yusuf ibn Isma'il al-Samiti al-Hindi whether people may move from place to place fleeing epidemic and plague, the master Idris ibn Hasan answered that they may go wherever they wish, since the matter is in Allah's hand.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Ja'far ibn Sulayman's epistle 'The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations', written to admonish his heedless people among those of the island of Yemen after he settled among them, is the compiler's main source here for rebuking communal faults.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Against slowness in visiting the sick, the epistle cites the Pillars of Islam on the authority of the Commander of the Faithful that seventy thousand angels pray for a Muslim who visits a sick person from the hour of the visit until sunset or sunrise.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The Prophet forbade a visitor to eat in the sick person's presence, Allah rendering such a visit (in another wording, its reward) worthless, because the visitor burdens one already burdened and galls a household possibly of slender means; whoever knows this must teach those who do not.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Asked whether lifespans are fixed with Allah without increase or decrease despite books speaking of both, the answer given is that lifespans are appointed and neither increase nor decrease, while the sense of increase and decrease is valid in that what is diminished in the past cycle is added in the future one.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Asked about the saying that the wretched is he whom the Hour overtakes alive and not yet dead, the answer is that what is intended is the Hour overtaking him while he is still in the animal (bahimi) condition — not yet passed into the angelic life.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Husayn ibn Idris, answering Hasan ibn Nuh's tenth question, ruled that if a pregnant woman dies with a living formed child, a skilled woman present must extract it when possible or when the child is six months or more with hope of life; otherwise the mother is not buried until the child's death is confirmed.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: From 'Ali's four hundred points of conduct the compiler gathers counsels on death: remember death often so calamities sit lightly; fever is death's forerunner and Allah's prison that strips sins as hair is stripped from the camel's pores; and no Shi'i who has departed from a prohibition dies before an affliction in wealth, child, or self purges his sins, so that hardship at death is itself expiation and the dead of the Shi'a is a truthful witness.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Practices around the corpse such as placing weapons beside the dead or treating the night-vigil beside the body as obligatory are dismissed in the questions-and-answers book as having no reliance placed upon them, and the abridged compendium forbids shaving hair, lighting lamps, or cutting nails for the dead.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Ja'far ibn Sulayman condemns as innovation the organized wailing over the dead — women gathering for nights and days as if it were a divine prescription, with singing, diversion and play exceeding even the limits allowed at weddings — disgracing the community before Allah and His friends though they are the cream and kernel of the world.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The prohibition is supported by Ja'far ibn Muhammad's deathbed bequest that no cheek be struck and no collar torn for him (a woman who tears her collar has a rent in Hell enlarged each time she adds to it), by 'Ali's letter to Rifa'ah ibn Shaddad his judge over al-Ahwaz to forbid wailing where he holds authority, and by the Prophet's saying that two voices are accursed — howling at calamity and a voice raised at a blessing, meaning wailing and singing.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The story of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah shows the dead and dying are punished by the living's laments: he saw an angel with a fiery iron mace that struck at his head whenever a woman shrieked 'O my mountain!' or 'O my strength!' unless he answered that Allah, not he, was her mountain — the Prophet confirming, 'What ails your dead, that they suffer by the words of your living?'

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The decisive distinction drawn is that weeping is permitted while wailing and lamentation are forbidden: the Prophet wept at his child's death and explained he forbade only nawh and 'awil, weeping being tenderness and mercy Allah places in hearts; he licensed weeping at calamity, saying the soul is stricken, the eye tearful, the loss recent — but say what pleases Allah and do not speak obscenely.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: Correspondingly, singing is forbidden except in the licensed case of banquets and weddings, where the tambourine publicizes marriage and distinguishes lawful nikah from sifah — the Prophet approving music at the Banu Zurayq wedding and saying there is no secret marriage until smoke is seen or a tambourine heard.

points.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
points.text: The proper mourning conduct commanded is that households speak well over their dead, following Fatimah, who when the daughters of Hashim mourned with her at her father's death said 'Grieve with restraint and hold fast to supplication'; and whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity forfeits his reward.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The washing of the dead requires the ablution to be performed three times along with three washings, though performing the ablution at the last washing suffices, as stated in the Book of Reports; and one wounded who is not lifted from his place and lives on for a time is not washed.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: When water is scarce, the man in a state of janabah takes the water and the dead is given tayammum; yet a washer in janabah may still wash the dead, performing tayammum first if washing would harm him, when no one else is available.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Per the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif the nearest person present has the best right to wash the dead, a martyr in janabah is washed on that account, a dead man found unmarked is washed, treated with hanut and shrouded, and no hair is shaved nor nail trimmed from a corpse.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The Mukhtasar al-Athar rules that the drowned, the burned, and any severed part without which a man could not have lived are washed; detached limbs are washed, each set in its place, and buried with the body.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Answering the author from Yemen to Hind, Jafar ibn Sulayman ruled that the Pillars prescribes only an izar from navel to knee with water passed beneath it and the private parts washed by a cloth-wrapped hand, so the Daudi group's manner of drawing the wrapper between the thighs — which they impose and denounce others for omitting — is rejected because it prevents the prescribed washing.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The best shroud, per Jafar ibn Muhammad in The Pillars of Islam, is three garments — a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper — and the better course is that washing, above all of a woman, be done within a covering.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The 'ajrah mentioned by al-Qadi al-Numan is defined as gathering the shirt at the navel and tucking it into the izar's fastening, serving, like the head covering, as a mark of distinction between men and women.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Counsels require washing for whoever touches the corpse after it grows cold, which the questions-and-answers book explains as meaning after death has come and the sunnah washing has been done, because the corpse's moisture renders a living person impure.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: For conjoined twins, separation is permitted only when slight and safe; if one dies, whatever adheres to the living is cut from the dead provided the living feels no pain, but if pain is felt their life and death are counted as one.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The shroud and outfitting are the first charge on the estate — before debt and bequest — and must be taken according to the deceased's station even if the debt exceeds the estate.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Hanut is any perfume, placed on the places of prostration and named parts of the body, with wars and saffron excluded for men but used for women; camphor accompanies it, and Quran is recited seven days for people of rank and three for others.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Per the Tawil al-Daaim only the shroud and the place of washing are incensed, and Ali's Counsels forbid incensing or perfuming the dead with anything but camphor because the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage — hence one who died in ihram has head and face uncovered and no perfume brought near.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Walking before the bier is disliked only for an enemy of the family, because angels of wrath attend it, while for believers any position is permissible since angels of mercy encompass it — though walking behind remains more excellent; the call to prayer at the bier was disliked but announcing the death without a public call was permitted.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The funeral prayer is a communal obligation on every Muslim who knows of it, may be offered anywhere and even in the disliked hours or at an eclipse, with the supplication between takbirs optional for the follower; it is offered over martyrs, grave sinners, the executed, and even the suicide.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: In the absence of the imam of the age, precedence in the funeral prayer belongs to his appointed judge or officeholder, then to the highest in station among those he has advanced, and only if none is present to the most entitled guardian; and a man's prayer accords better with the teaching of the People of the House than a woman leading women.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: The dead is buried in the town where he dies and not carried elsewhere, except from open wilderness to the nearest burial ground; burial in another's land requires his leave, but once done he may claim only the value of the grave plots and may not have the bodies removed.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Baked brick, stone or whatever is available may be placed over the dead despite the dislike of the people of the outward sense, and this is to be relied on except where prudent concealment requires otherwise.

points.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib counselled visiting the graves of those who have a claim upon one and seeking provision there, since the dead rejoice at such visits, a man asking his need at his parents' graves after praying for them.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The section begins the Book of Zakat, gathering what has been handed down on the merit of giving zakat and its attendant matters.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the book of inward nursing, cites the Prophet's word that charity is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states that one whose role in the call, after discharging what is incumbent, is that his excellence appear outwardly through abundance of wealth, pays from his wealth what he wills — apart from the fitra — of obligatory rights and voluntary giving.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman draws the distinction that paying the khums excuses one from the tithe except voluntarily, while paying the tithe alone does not excuse the khums, because the tithe does not encompass the khums as the khums encompasses the tithe.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Prophet is cited as saying there is no prayer for one who does not pay zakat, and that the one who withholds zakat is in the Fire.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the Hidden Epistle, lists ten things on which God imposed zakat: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, dates, raisins, wheat, barley, and grains.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his Four Hundred Counsels says to treat the sick with charity and fortify wealth with zakat.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils' twelfth council teaches that zakat has seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, matching the number of the clauses of the testimony and its letters, and that zakat must be received by the Imam and is taken from seven things: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, crops, and minerals.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils enumerate the eight named recipients falling into seven divisions — the poor and needy, the collectors, those whose hearts are reconciled, the freeing of necks, the debt-burdened among the people of allegiance, the way of God as an obligation of sufficiency, and the wayfarer understood as those cut off from the road of guidance.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The twelve sunnahs include the passing of a year, nisabs of twenty dinars of gold, two hundred dirhams of silver, five grazing camels, thirty grazing cows and forty sheep, taking from the middling livestock, not joining what is separate nor dividing what is joined, not taking the stud animal, giving from crops below the five-awsaq nisab by bundle and handful on the day of harvest per the Quranic verse, and no zakat on dwellings, ornaments, or things for use.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: In the questions-and-answers book arranged after Daaim al-Islam, the ruling on concealing zakat from the imam is said to concern one who brings out only part of it, whereas one who withholds it entirely has abandoned the obligation altogether.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Asked whether the Prophet's saying that charity is unlawful for 'we, the people of the House' refers to the Imams or to all his descendants through Fatima, the answer given is that it refers to the Imams.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The hamala, named among the five for whom charity is lawful in Daaim al-Islam, is explained as either a penalty imposed by a tyrannical ruler or the bearing of blood money on behalf of the 'aqila.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: Interpreting Ali's covenant to Muhnaf ibn Sulaym, the answer holds that zakat is not demanded from one seized by the enemy who is not of the Shia holding to the allegiance, and that handing zakat to other than the one God commanded does not suffice, even if it is later plundered or stolen, until it reaches the guardian of the affair or his appointee.

points.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
points.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils hold that one who keeps the outward prayer and believes its inner reality yet does not spend the zakat of his wealth, the khums of his earnings, the purchase of his own self, and the redemption of his pledge falls short of those God describes as spending from what He provided them.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: In the responsa attributed to our master Idris, the obligations owed from a deceased person's estate are discharged in a fixed order: zakat first (because it is a debt upon him and not part of his wealth), then the Hajj, then the khums, then the expiation, then al-Shurwa.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The answer holds that the Hajj takes precedence over inheritance because it is a debt, and debt comes before inheritance; the remaining obligatory duties bind likewise if the wealth suffices for them and something still remains for the heir.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Khums must be brought out of the capital even where no bequest was made, and if the heirs are God-fearing it is their duty to discharge it for the deceased and so purify the wealth — but if they refuse, the answer invokes 'There is no compulsion in religion' rather than coercion.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The limit of 'means' (for al-Shurwa liability) is defined as ownership of wealth on which zakat falls due after the hawl, namely two hundred dirhams or twenty gold dinars, with each dirham reckoned at fourteen and two-fifths carats of silver and each dinar at twenty-four carats, converted into Arab and Gujarati weights.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Because the relative price of gold and silver varies by age according to people's desire, the answer counsels that the believer holding to his religion should reckon his nisab by whichever of the two coinages is the lesser in price.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Once khums has been paid from the capital, no khums is owed on profit except on what remains in hand; paying khums on the whole profit is declared a merit, not a binding obligation.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that an undivided estate is not assessed for zakat as a whole but share by share — each heir whose share reaches a nisab pays, and one whose share does not (and who has no other wealth) owes nothing — and that a debtor pays zakat only on the excess of his wealth over his debt.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Al-Akhbar reports that there is no zakat in the wealth of an orphan or of one lacking his reason, and Tawil al-Daaim interprets this to mean no zakat is due from the owner holding it for himself, while whatever of it is held for trade is valued and does bear zakat.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Tawil al-Sharia reports that Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah taught that zakat is five dirhams for five classes of poor and that it is mutual consolation, all creation being as a single soul whose limbs turn to heal an afflicted limb — adding that if anyone were untouched by defect, death would never reach him.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inner Nursing, enumerates five zakats paralleling the five prayers: the khums of earnings, the zakat of already-khums-paid wealth (one dinar in forty, owed to the Hujja while the khums is for the Imam), the tenth of crops, one head in forty of livestock, and the zakat of the soul (shurwa and fitra).

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad in al-Risala al-Maknuna sets out the graduated livestock scales — camels from five (a sheep) through bint makhad, bint labun, hiqqa and jadha, cattle at tabi and musinna, and sheep from forty — with the rule that nothing defective and not the flock's ram is taken in charity.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: On the nisab of grains, the answer distinguishes two positions: the Pillars holds that zakat is due from everything the earth brings forth (and the masters' practice, to be followed, took the tenth from little and much), while the Sharia sets the nisab at five awsaq, the wasq being sixty sa.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Al-Akhbar distinguishes land of the tenth (Arab land not advanced upon with horse or beast, and mountain land cultivated by its own people without great-river water, plus land whose warring people submitted while still on it) from land of kharaj (Sudanese and mountain lands taken and cultivated by force), and holds that a land's ruling does not change with the religion of its purchaser because the obligation attaches to the produce, not the owner.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: The Book of the Inner Nursing treats the tenth as an outward ruling by which the Messenger judged, and holds that one who truly pays a tenth while keeping back only nine tenths has discharged his outward obligation even unasked by the ruler, whereas one who withholds and keeps more than nine tenths has not truly rendered obedience to the ruler over his outward affairs.

points.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad cites Q. 8:41 to identify five stations to which the khums is directed — God and the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer — and states that khums is taken from mines, treasures, and spoils, with al-Sadiq reporting that the Prophet took his share of spoils and divided the rest among those categories.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: A fatwa collection arranged by the chapters of the Book of the Pillars addresses the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) for the fitra and taking their monetary value, and answers that the reliance is on the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: A transmitted saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The answer concedes latitude: whoever mixes his fitra from everything he ate during Ramadan has discharged it, and whoever ate nothing but barley may give barley.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: On paying the fitra before Ramadan out of fear of poverty or travel — objected to because obligatory acts may not be done outside their appointed times — the answer is that delivering it to a rightful recipient suffices, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it and the obligation is simply its delivery; the only prohibition is that one not break the fast before delivering it.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes the zakat of Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Reports state the zakat of Fitr is paid for the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion holds it due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars records that it has also been said to be paid for a child still in the womb.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The measure of the sa is given as four and a half ratls by the Meccan ratl, five ratls less a third by the Medinan ratl, and nine and a tenth by the Baghdadi ratl, with the Selected Book allowing a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The author of the Mustansiriyya sessions, in the thirteenth session, distinguishes zakat obligatory on the wealthy from zakat of Fitr, which is obligatory in every condition and even on those of small means, and enumerates seven obligations — that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and younger of his household, the free and the enslaved, the males and the females — plus twelve Sunnah practices.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Among the Sunnah practices: it is brought out from the middle sort of one's food — a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins, with half a sa sufficing only for wheat; the sa is four mudds; it is handed to the Imam or his appointee before the breaking of the fast; delay requires making it up; one lacking food gives its value in silver or gold; and a woman without a husband pays for herself and her dependents.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad's Concealed Epistle states that the Messenger of God made the fitra obligatory on every head among the Muslims — male and female, small and great, even an infant born that day and the child in the womb — a sa of wheat, dates, raisins, barley or other grain, which is why it is named the charity of the head; if paid before the prayer it counts as charity.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima draws the temporal distinction that what is brought out before sunrise counts as fitra and after sunrise as ordinary charity, and defines the meaning of fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and as offering.

points.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
points.text: Two puzzle-rulings close the section: a man owning a thousand dinars while owing a thousand dinars owes no zakat on it, and a polytheist who finds no Muslim to whom to hand his zakat has more right to it than anyone else.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as stating that fasting is a shield from the Fire covering the tongue, hearing, eyes and all limbs, so that fasting is not food and drink alone: each limb has its portion, and whoever abandons part of it diminishes the merit of his fast proportionally.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The same source is cited as holding that fasting Ramadan is obligatory upon every Muslim, man or woman, who is of age, sound of mind, healthy and resident, and that there is no fasting for a hypocrite who is disobedient to God.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Al-Idah is cited as restricting the rulings about fasting upon sighting the crescent to one who is absent from the presence of the Imam and does not know the measures of the crescents.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in his epistle The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes them for failing to honor Ramadan as God and His Messenger prescribed.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: His specific charge is that the month must be named with the word 'month' placed before it — 'the month of Ramadan', as in the Quranic phrase shahr Ramadan — and that calling it 'Ramadan' alone is unseemly, since one does not address a person dear to him without an honorific word before his name.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: He supports this by al-Qadi al-Numan's Mukhtasar al-Athar al-Sharif, which reports Imam al-Baqir Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali as saying: do not say 'Ramadan', but say as God said, 'the month of Ramadan'.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: He argues that one who has heard this saying and then turns from it makes light of God, of His noble month and of al-Baqir's weighty word, and that one who transmits the book while not acting on it falls under the Quranic censure 'why do you say what you do not do?'

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Tawil al-Shariah is cited as holding that fasting becomes obligatory upon a boy once he can tell his right hand from his left.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The fourteenth Mustansiriyya majlis divides fasting into seven obligatory kinds: Ramadan yearly; two consecutive months for deliberately breaking a fast day when no slave can be freed; two consecutive months for killing a believer by mistake when no slave can be freed, plus blood money; two consecutive months in zihar expiation when no slave can be freed; three days for a broken oath when feeding, clothing and freeing are all unavailable; ten days for one performing tamattu who finds no offering; and the fast of a vow.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: The same majlis lists twelve fasts of the practice and commendation: itikaf, Shaban, the first Thursday of each month, its middle Wednesday, its last Thursday, the three white days, the fast of Dawud (alternate days, the most rigorous), Friday joined to Thursday or Saturday but never alone, Arafah for the non-pilgrim, the boy's fast at seven years, recompense for game taken in the sacred state as ruled by the one entrusted with that ruling, and the fast for shaving the head on account of harm.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Zaid ibn Muhammad, in the Concealed Epistle, is cited as stating that God imposed fasting the month of Ramadan after prayer and zakat, commanding one month out of twelve, and that this obligatory fast is thirty days.

points.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
points.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted from his Four Hundred Manners as saying that fasting three days of every month and fasting Shaban drive away the whisperings of the breast and the disquiet of the heart.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
