points.text: The author's thesis, following the Book of Clarification, is that the reports commanding fasting by sighting the crescent are directed only to whoever is absent from the presence of the Imam and ignorant of the measures of the crescent moons.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Sulayman ibn Hasan, in his epistle the Ijadiyya, explains that after the moon has traveled twenty-eight stations from the sun it needs two further stations to overtake the sun, since the sun has itself advanced two stations and a degree, so the meeting occurs at thirty stations, which the reckoners count as one month.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The opposing claim, refuted by al-Muayyad fil-Din in the forty-second of the Wisdom Sessions, is that Ramadan is sometimes complete and sometimes deficient and that its fast depends on sighting, argued from the Prophet's words 'Fast when it is seen and break your fast when it is seen; and if it is hidden, complete thirty.'

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The first reply is contextual: the hadith was spoken when the Companions asked how they should act in the Prophet's absence, so fasting by sighting is a rule of necessity when neither the Messenger nor the Imam standing in his place is present, while in their presence one fasts and breaks fast by theirs.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Two legal grounds deny that the Prophet himself sought the crescent: Gabriel came to him morning and evening with certain tidings from heaven, making search superfluous, and he said 'I know the roads of the sky better than you know the roads of the earth,' which searching would contradict.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The rational ground is that the Prophet knew crescent risings differ by degree and by terrain (high places sight it sooner, low places later), so he could not have imposed one sighting standard on all people, since one day cannot be Shaban where the crescent is unseen and Ramadan where it is seen.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Scriptural proof is drawn from 'Fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you' — those before being the Christians, who fast by calculation not sighting — and from 'a counted number of days,' since days always counted require no observation.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The year is ordered as six complete and six deficient months running Muharram complete, Safar deficient, and so on, so that Ramadan falls as complete, confirmed by the Prophet's saying 'Shaban is never complete, and Ramadan is never deficient.'

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Shaban's deficiency is proved by its genuine mid-night, the fifteenth, with fourteen nights on either side, whereas Ramadan admits no true midpoint — the fifteenth leaves fifteen days after it and sixteen is not half of thirty.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The expiation for willfully breaking the fast — two consecutive months, sixty days, or feeding sixty poor — matches a thirty-day Ramadan; were Ramadan twenty-nine, the expiation would allow fifty-eight poor persons.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: In an anecdote from his autobiography, al-Muayyad fil-Din, before King Abu Kalijar al-Daylami, answered a Zaydi sharif who cited the Prophet's finger-counting 'We are unlettered; we do not reckon' by denying that the Prophet, honored with the ascension, would gesture like a herdsman rather than distinguish thirty from twenty-nine in speech; the Alid withdrew in shame.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: A summoner's disputational questionnaire asks who 'those before you' are, how many the counted days, and what 'witnessing the month' means, and invokes 'that you complete the count,' arguing that those who fast by crescent-rising may fail to complete thirty and so contradict the Book — against the Prophet's rule that whatever contradicts the Book of God he did not say.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The lam in 'ṣūmū li-ruʾyatihi' is read as the lam of anticipation or outcome (lām al-ʿāqiba), as in 'mothers nourish their children for death' and 'This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning,' so the hadith means: let the crescent rise while you are already fasting, and rise while you are already breaking the fast.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the epistle al-Maknuna on the eclipse prayer, holds that God made first-age creation a proof for the last age, setting the lunar eclipse at fourteen nights (sometimes thirteen) and the moon's concealment at twenty-eight nights, absent forty-eight hours before rising again.

points.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
points.text: The section closes by introducing the next text, the epistle al-Lazima on the fast of Ramadan and its proper time, by Ahmad Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, proof of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author writes in response to a brother's request to justify the Shia practice — and specifically the command issued from the Pure Presence in the year 400 requiring the fast to begin two days before the crescent was seen by eye — and names the work the necessary epistle on fasting the month of Ramadan and its time.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author charges the opponents with falling into division not through evidence but through arrogance, envy and refusal to obey those charged with the Command, to whom the Qur'an directs that all disputed matters be referred.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The disputed authority is the Prophet's narration 'Fast at its sighting and break the fast at its sighting', which is agreed among the Muslim sects and is the pillar of the argument of the people of the outward.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Because Allah created all things in pairs and the Prophet made pairing the governing principle of his law (prayer/alms, adhan/iqama, Hajj/Umrah, Safa/Marwa), the author infers that sight too is of two paired kinds.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Natural vision occurs by means of the eye and apprehends only colours and shapes, whereas vision of the soul occurs by way of knowledge through the heart and apprehends the causes hidden from the eye — evidenced by Qur'anic verses addressing the Prophet as 'seeing' the companions of the elephant, whom he never witnessed.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Vision of the soul is judged more exalted, finer and prior in apprehension — it registers the drop removed from a pool, which the eye cannot — so holding fast to it in fulfilling obligations is more binding, since to take the lesser when the more excellent is present is a judgment of ignorance.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Just as prayer binds one who knows its time without hearing the adhan, and abstinence binds one who knows dawn has broken though a barrier hides it, so entry into the fast is binding once it is known that the moon has separated from the sun after conjunction, even if light, cloud, dust or a mountain bars sight.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author argues astronomically that the month is constituted by the moon's travel from conjunction (shared degree and minute with the sun) around the sphere, and that the sun's overpowering light is merely a barrier to the eye like cloud or a wall — as shown by stars becoming visible during a solar eclipse.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Against the claim that one knows nothing until sight falls upon it, the author offers three refutations: opponents affirm Allah whom they have not seen; they judge the world originated in time by proof not eyesight; and they permit breaking the fast after thirty days without sighting — each forcing a retreat to the vision of knowledge.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The soul is an instrument of perception alongside the five senses which surpasses them all, and its perception is of two kinds: by means of the senses, and by its own essence along the path of inference — the latter needing the senses only at the first apprehension, since the image is thereafter retained.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: Since sight apprehends only shape and colour, and the crescent is not sought to learn its colour, shape, thinness or thickness — none of which is a condition of the fast — the obligation cannot attach to eyesight but to the soul's apprehension that the moon now stands west of the sun after being east of her.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: The author reads the lam in 'li-ru'yatihi' as indicating that the act precedes that for which it is done (as in 'work for the Hereafter'), so the hadith means the community is already fasting when the crescent is seen by eye.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: To the objection that the lam in 'Establish the prayer at the declining of the sun' does not require the prayer to precede the declining, the author replies that the declining too is apprehended first by the soul (point ب) and only later by sense (point ج), so there too the worshipper is already praying when sense perceives the shadow turn.

points.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
points.text: To the further objection that 'If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days' requires eyesight, the author answers by reasserting that the vision of the soul has been established as the nobler of the two.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author holds that both sightings — the vision of the soul and the sighting of the eye — are valid foundations for performing obligatory duties, but the vision of the soul is the more excellent and belongs to the possessors of knowledge, while the eye's sighting belongs to the generality, who are obliged to follow the learned, the relation between them being like that between the first and second times of a prayer.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author generalises that all matters are of two kinds, hidden and apparent: the hidden is known only by the select, the apparent by select and common alike, and each group is bound to act on what it knows — as the pre-dawn eater who knows dawn has broken must stop, while the ignorant one follows the learned.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: Against reading the hadith 'If it is obscured from you, count thirty days' as referring to eye-sighting, the author argues that eye-sighting rarely yields thirty-day months, that the Prophet could not bind his community to a doubt-ridden rule, since Allah says worship must be with sincerity ('They were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion'), and that sincerity is other than doubt and confusion.
entities: فإن غمّ عليكم فعدوا ثلاثين يوماً

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author argues that the Prophet's fixing the month at the complete number points to the vision of the soul, whose counts neither increase nor decrease, in line with 'that you may complete the count.'

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author objects that eye-sighting makes the fast differ between regions — cloud in Kirman versus clear sky in Shiraz — and that just as one prayer's time cannot differ among the people of one town, neither can the fast's time; when the time comes the fast binds the whole community whether or not an individual keeps it.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author further argues that counting thirty days requires knowing a month's first day, which is often unknown where the crescent is hidden (Tabaristan, mountains, coasts, islands), so the eye-sighting reading would make the Prophet burden his community beyond capacity, contrary to 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity'; hence either the report is unsound or must be read as the vision of the soul.
entities: لا يكلف الله نفساً إلا وسعها

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author argues from the other pillars — prayer led by the Imam, zakat collected and distributed by him (given elsewhere it must be paid again), Hajj whose rites follow the Imam, and jihad ordered by the one entrusted with the Muslims' affair — that no pillar is entrusted to the fallible community, so the fast's beginning likewise may not be settled by the community's own ijtihad apart from the one standing in the place of the Messenger.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: Answering the objection that on his principle the day of conjunction would belong partly to Shaban and partly to Ramadan, the author replies that every obligation has two causes — a preceding general one and a specific one fixing its time (day/declining sun; wealth/passage of a year; ability/the greatest day at Mecca; opposition/the leading head) — and for fasting the general cause is the moon's separation from the sun while the specific cause is the following dawn.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author reads the sun as an indication of the rank of the Speaker (Prophet) — noblest and most luminous, source of light to others, cause of growth and the cause to which all causes attach, but in the world of the soul and religion — within the interpretive call commanded by 'Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom,' wisdom having two divisions: outward work (which requires interpretation) and knowledge, the hidden worship of the soul.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author reads the moon as an indication of the rank of the Foundation (الأساس), below the Speaker, receiving more of his light than any other, illuminating the night by expounding the Prophet's sealed symbols and parables, and mediating spiritual offspring between Speaker and community — with the moon's phases mapped onto the Foundation's career: conjunction as the Prophet's instruction of Ali ('I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate'), hiddenness as his rank known only to the elect, the crescent as the explicit designation near the Prophet's death, its faintness as the community's disagreement over his Imamate, and its fullness at fourteen days as the universal recognition of his Imamate at the passing of the seven repetitions at the cycle's end.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author reads the Ramadan verses interpretively: Ramadan as the noblest month stands for the Foundation (since the Quran was in fact revealed over twenty-three years, the outward sense of 'the month in which the Quran was sent down' yields contradiction), 'Whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it' means whoever attends the Foundation's assembly must keep silent and follow him, and 'whoever is sick or on a journey' excepts the one who speaks to receive benefit — a doubter or learner.
entities: لا ترفعوا أصواتكم فوق صوت النبي

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author defends the people of truth's entering the Ramadan fast of the year 400 two days before the eye-sighting, on the grounds that the conjunction fell on Monday night, the moon stood only about six degrees from the sun so the eye could not reach it, the Shawwal conjunction fell on Wednesday night making Wednesday the festival, and Ramadan is thirty days without deficiency ('Shaban was never complete nor Ramadan deficient'), confirmed by 'the day of your fasting is the day of your sacrifice,' the sacrifice at Mecca having fallen on Monday.
entities: ما تم شعبان ولا نقص رمضان

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: To the objection that his reasoning uses the forbidden science of the stars, the author answers that it would be an 'unjust division' to allow astronomical inference for the qibla and prayer times but forbid it for the fast, and that the Prophet forbade it only for one who begins with astronomy before the divine and revealed sciences, which leads to the doctrine of Ptolemy's followers who ascribe divinity to the heavenly bodies; when the revealed sciences come first, such knowledge increases certainty in Allah's oneness, as the Quran's oaths by the stars show.

points.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
points.text: The author concludes that sighting is of two kinds, that choosing the more excellent is the better course, and that the Prophet's lam in 'لرؤيته' meant the sighting of knowledge — which requires that people already be fasting when the crescent is seen by the eye — and seals the treatise with praise, prayer upon the Prophet, Ali, the pure Imams as 'moons amid the darkness,' and the Imam of the age al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: Reporting from 'some of the noble books', the author states that faith has eight levels (مراتب).

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The first of the eight levels of faith is charity (الإحسان) toward parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is a relative, the nearby neighbor, the companion at one's side, the traveler, and those whom one's faith obligates one to care for — a level the author says is established in the Book of God.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The quoted source asserts that whoever undertakes the worship of God and the call of the People of the House without knowledge and without action cannot rightly bear the name of faith, and holds no bond with God nor covenant or honor with His guardian, having departed from faith.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: Quoting the fourth of the Mustansiriyya Councils (the Councils of Exposition and Wisdom), the author reports that the Imams of religion are seven, recurring in the world as the days of the week recur until the rising of the Qa'im, while twelve proofs (hujjas) are spread throughout the world — and this constitutes knowledge of the sum of the limits (hudud) of the testimony.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The author distinguishes knowing the limits of the testimony from fulfilling the rights owed to those limits: the latter consists of upholding seven obligations of religion and twelve practices incumbent upon the God-fearing, mirroring the seven Imams and twelve proofs.

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The seven obligations of religion are guardianship (walaya), purity (tahara), prayer (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting (sawm), pilgrimage (hajj), and struggle (jihad).

retained.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
retained.text: The twelve practices are honoring parents, maintaining kinship ties, protecting the neighbor, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, truthfulness in one's home, good conduct with one's spouse, kindness to dependents, spreading the greeting of peace, feeding others, keeping the bond among the brethren, and visiting the sick — and the author states these twelve are not obligatory upon women.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: On the same authority, 'and their father was righteous' is taken to mean an Imam, and 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' to mean the Imams among God's servants, so that 'the righteous' in scripture is a technical designation for the Imams.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: The Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah, in a Friday sermon, likened himself in the physical world to the Pen in the spiritual world, setting four ranks beneath him each preceded by a spiritual rank guiding it upward, so that the earthly hierarchy faces and inscribes what it derives from the spiritual world as a pen inscribes a tablet.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: 'Ali answers that what is not God's is a partner, what is not with God is injustice, and what God does not know is that the Messiah is His son — citing 'Do you inform God of what He does not know?' — the point being that what does not exist is not an object of divine knowledge.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: The Roman envoy responds by professing that there is no god but God, that Muhammad is His Messenger, and that 'Ali is his guardian (wali), and 'Ali has al-Hasan and al-Husayn distribute the money among the Muslims.

retained.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
retained.text: Ibn al-Asfar, receiving the answers through Muawiya, testifies that they could only come from the mine of prophecy and the seat of the message and refuses Muawiya even a single dirham — a foreign witness against Muawiya's claim.

retained.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
retained.text: The author, citing the twenty-third of the Mustansiriya councils, states that the revelation of peace divides into seven sections above (from God and His angels) and twelve sections below (from human beings).

retained.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
retained.text: In the twenty-fourth assembly it is stated that the offering of peace is an obligatory Sunnah of Islam expressing affection and submission, and that al-Salam is one of the names of God, possessed of majesty and honor.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Al-Muizz li Din Allah, in his Sunday supplication, ranks beneath the Foundation (al-Asas) the Terminus (al-Mutimm) facing Israfil, beneath the Terminus the After (al-Lahiq) facing Michael, and beneath the After the Wing (al-Janah) facing Gabriel.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Al-Muizz states that these three ranks deliver to the respondents from the Speaker and the Foundation in the corporeal world, just as three deliver from the two principles — the Pen and the Tablet — in the spiritual world; the author glosses these three as the Grandfather (al-Jadd), the Opener (al-Fath), and the Imagination (al-Khayal), identified with Israfil, Michael, and Gabriel.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: In his Friday supplication al-Muizz enumerates the hudud as Speaker, Foundation, Terminus, After, Wing, Authorized (ma'dhun) and Respondent (mustajib), together with twelve proofs ranked across twelve regions (jaza'ir), which the author links to the Quranic 'over it are nineteen.'

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Ali prohibits exaggeration (ghuluw) concerning the Imams, requiring believers to say 'we are servants under a Lord' while permitting them to say of the Imams' excellence whatever they wish — a boundary that condemns excess without limiting praise of merit.

retained.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
retained.text: Ali teaches that both errors are remediable through the Imams: the one who exaggerates returns to them, and they themselves raise up the one who falls short (al-muqassir).

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: In the seventeenth Mustansiriya council, righteousness toward parents is named the first of the twelve practices that correspond to the number of the letters of the testimony, the seven obligatory rights corresponding to its seven clauses having already been explained.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The eighteenth council divides righteousness toward parents into seven obligatory parts and twelve manners, and identifies three pairs of parents: the bodily parents who caused his form to come into being and nourished him, the two parents in religion who caused his form in knowledge (the Imam of the age and his proof), and the two fathers of the community who convey the divine sciences (the Prophet and the legatee, and the Imams of their progeny), citing 'I and you, O Ali, are the two fathers of this community.'

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The twenty-fourth council names three obligatory rights that God will not accept unless discharged in full: the right of God (to come out from what He forbade and enter into what He commanded), the right of parents (thankfulness for what has passed and obedience in what remains), and the right of the child (to be raised with tenderness, nourished, and taught the Book and wisdom); Ali adds that whoever goes against his parents has been undutiful to them.

retained.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
retained.text: The nineteenth council divides relatives into twelve categories (children; full brothers, al-ashiqqa'; paternal half-brothers, banu al-'allat; maternal half-brothers, al-akhyaf; paternal grandfathers and grandmothers; maternal grandfathers and grandmothers; paternal uncles and aunts; maternal uncles and aunts), with anyone related through one of these taking that one's ruling, and defines the commanded tie as keeping the bond, giving, drawing near, and loving even when the relatives cut off, withhold, push away, or abandon — and Ali states there is no binding oath in the severing of kinship.

retained.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
retained.text: The obligatory knowledge no believer may leave unlearned is enumerated as: knowledge of God's oneness and His transcendence above likeness, above the stripping of attributes, and above nonexistence; acknowledgment of all messengers first to last and of their delivery of the message; acknowledgment of Muhammad as Seal of the Prophets and affirmation of what he brought; acknowledgment of the Imams of his progeny whose guardianship and obedience God joined to His own in 'Obey God, and obey the Messenger, and those vested with authority among you'; and recognition of the Imam of the age with submission to his command and taking knowledge from him.

retained.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
retained.text: This obligatory knowledge rests on the premise that God has never left the earth without a proof against His servants and an Imam calling to His obedience, supported by 'On the day We shall call every people by their Imam' and 'You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide'; whoever affirms this is bound to follow the guide, ask the people of remembrance, and take from them, and his rank is raised in proportion to what he then learns.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: The Trusted of the Imam, the Banner of Islam (al-Muayyad), in the fifth council of his Majalis al-Bayan and Majalis al-Hikma (the Councils of al-Mustansiriyya), teaches that Islam is built upon seven obligations to which twelve practices are attached, and that each individual obligation likewise contains its own seven obligations and twelve practices.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: The seven obligations of the lesser purity (ablution) are given as pure water, intention, washing the face, washing the hands, wiping the head, wiping the feet, and order — order being that one begins with what God began by mentioning.

retained.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
retained.text: The greater purity — washing of the whole body — is likewise divided into seven obligations (washing from janabah, from menstruation, of the unbeliever entering Islam, of one recovering from unconsciousness, from the blood of nifas, after immersion in impurity, and of the dead, this last being an obligation on the living until one of them performs it) and twelve practices (Friday; al-Fitr; al-Adha; ihram; entering the Haram; entering the Kabah; entering Madinah; the day of Arafah; the nights of the nineteenth, twenty-first and twenty-third of Ramadan; and after washing the dead).

retained.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl in al-Risalah al-Maknunah divides purity and filth into two kinds: outward purity by outward water cleansing urine and excrement, and inward purity by inward water — which is knowledge — cleansing the inward filth of doubt and ignorance.

retained.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
retained.text: The same author reads the seven elements of wudhu as seven bounds — three Sunnah (rinsing the mouth, drawing in water, istinja), two washings and two wipings, one of each bounded and one unbounded — and takes the face, containing the seven openings, as bearing the meaning of the Speaker, since a person is known by his face just as no one is known except through his prophet and there is no deliverance except by turning toward him.

retained.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
retained.text: Asked for the inner likeness of ghusl from janabah, since marital relations are a likeness of imparting and receiving, the answer given is that the washing is a likeness of the removal of doubt, and doubt arises only at the moment of imparting and receiving.

retained.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
retained.text: In answers of Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris to Sheikh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi, Ali's saying 'whomever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him' is interpreted esoterically: water purifies and is not itself purified, and so is the knowledge of the Imam — whomever it does not purify, God does not purify.

retained.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
retained.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, writing from Yemen in his letter al-Sayf al-aqta fi ibtal al-bida, argues that God placed men's adornment in the beard and women's in the length of their head hair, so that a woman's shaving of her head — or even of the edges around the crown and the temples — is a disfigurement of her form and an inversion of the divinely appointed order.

retained.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
retained.text: Jafar condemns a double inversion of practice: girls are being circumcised within ten to forty days when Ali forbade it before seven years, while boys' circumcision — commanded to be hastened, ideally on the seventh day — is deferred, in some regions to nearly twenty years, a delay shamed by the People of the Book who circumcise on the seventh day in obedience to Moses.

retained.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
retained.text: The texts set the least of menstruation at three days, the most at ten days, and the least of purity at ten days; blood beyond ten days makes the woman a mustahadah if she is in doubt, while a certain woman who distinguishes menstrual blood from istihadah blood may continue to abstain without making up prayers.

retained.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
retained.text: The mustahadah is defined as a woman whose blood does not cease but is distinguishable — thick and turbid in menstruation, thin otherwise — so that she abstains from prayer, the mosque and her husband while the menstrual blood is present, and resumes all of these with ablution for each appearance of the remaining flow.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: One who abandons the prescribed prayer for a long period without excuse is 'not counted a Muslim' during that period and none of his lawful deeds is accepted — citing the Prophet's 'between the servant and disbelief is only the abandonment of prayer' and Ali's 'prayer is the pillar of religion, the first deed God examines' and 'no share in Islam for one who abandons prayer'.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: The author qualifies that 'disbelief' here means only that his deeds are not accepted, since he stands in a disbeliever's position; in practice — poll tax, killing, enslaving his offspring, ritual impurity, his slaughtered meat — his ruling remains that of a Muslim, because the two testimonies place him within the rulings of Islam.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Upon sincere repentance (tawba nasuh, Q66:8) the abandoner becomes truly Muslim and his deeds are accepted; he need not make up the prayers missed before repenting (though he is rewarded if he does), but deliberately broken Ramadan fasts from that period require both making up and expiation.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, in the book of the interpretation of the Sharia, defines the five times by hidden indications — Dhuhr when a shadow equals its object, 'Asr when double, Maghrib at the setting of the disc, Isha' al-Akhirah at the vanishing of the white twilight, Fajr from daybreak to near sunrise — and notes the times are hidden while the prayers are manifest, making ten: five outward and five inward.

retained.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
retained.text: Al-Nu'man further sets prayer's four boundaries — time, qibla, wudu, intention — and its seven obligatory elements: takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, glorification, tashahhud, and sealing.

retained.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
retained.text: Al-Hakim's syllogism concludes that since Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus are in the Garden but are not its youths, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn are masters of its youth while their father is better than they, it is established that Ali is the best of humankind together with the Prophet — whereupon the shaykh assented and al-Hakim told the dai to give the call as he wished, for none would oppose him.

retained.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
retained.text: Proof four reasons that God granted Moses's request for Aaron as minister, brother, sharer in his task and holder of joint authority, and that since God's way admits no change or alteration (35:43, 17:77) and Muhammad was told to follow earlier prophets' guidance, Muhammad was obliged to appoint Ali in the same role — confirmed by the hadith 'Ali stands to me in the station of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.'

retained.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
retained.text: Proof five argues from the Guardianship verse (5:55–56), read as revealed concerning Ali, that he shares with the Messenger guardianship over the believers, a station only the best of human beings after the Messenger could hold — reinforced by the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir Khumm, 'Whoever's master I am, this Ali is his master.'

retained.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
retained.text: Both the Q&A compilation and Muhammad ibn al-Fahd resolve the grave-and-mosque problem by order of construction: if the mosque or domed structure was built first and burial followed, prayer in it is permitted, but if it was built on account of a pre-existing grave it takes the ruling of a cemetery and prayer in it is never permitted.

retained.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
retained.text: Al-Majalis al-Mustansiriyya grades prayer in seven ascending ranks of merit: the house counts as one prayer, the market mosque twelve, the tribal mosque twenty-five, the congregational mosque one hundred, the Farthest Mosque one thousand, the Mosque of the Messenger ten thousand, and the Sacred House of God one hundred thousand.

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: The compiler states that twelve categories of men may not lead prayer — the sick leading the healthy, the leper, the one with white leprosy, the madman, one on whom a prescribed penalty has been carried out, the child of adultery, the bedouin leading emigrants, the fettered leading the unfettered, one who performed dry ablution leading those who used water, the mute leading speakers, a traveler leading residents, and one hostile to the Prophet's household leading its followers — while each of these may lead others in his own condition.

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: Reported from Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, precedence in leading prayer follows a ranked order — earliest in emigration, then best reciter, then most learned in jurisprudence, then eldest — with the owner of a mosque having better right in his mosque, and the Imam or whomever he appoints having the strongest right of all, while a woman leading women stands among them rather than ahead.

retained.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
retained.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidna Sulayman, answering the book's own author Sayyidna Ali ibn Sulayman, rules that women praying behind a screen need only one glance at the men's garments before entering the sanctified state when the place is not connected, and none at all when it is connected by an opening or lattice — any looking after the sanctified state at non-kin cuts off the prayer.

retained.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
retained.text: Al-Ikhtisar gives the minimum by which prayer is completed as five limits — opening takbir, standing for the able, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the tashahhud — valid for one who forgot or did not know more, whereas one who knows the limits and deliberately omits any obligation or sunnah has no prayer and must repeat it, and the ignorant man is obliged to learn.

retained.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
retained.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya enumerates seven obligatory prayers (residence of seventeen rakahs, travel of eleven, Friday requiring four with the imam, fear, the tawaf of obligatory Hajj, the tawaf of obligatory Umrah, and the prayer over the bier which binds every Muslim who knows until one undertakes it) and twelve sunnah prayers, matching purity's divisions to the clauses and letters of the shahada.

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: The seven are bodily postures of supplication: asking (palms facing the face), seeking refuge (backs of palms facing the face), humble submission (grasping the shoulders, done only in solitude), devotion (pointing with the index finger), entreaty (moving the finger), fervent appeal (both palms spread and raised to the sky), and abasement in the dust (turning the cheeks on the ground).

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: The twelve are the foundations on which answered supplication is built: prefacing it with repentance, charity, fasting or prayer (per 'To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it'), purifying intention, praising God, blessing the Prophet at start, middle and end, drawing near through the imams of religion up to the imam of one's age, seeking access through them, asking the good of both worlds, seeking refuge from the evil of both, and then asking whatever one wills.

retained.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
retained.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in his book on the inward nursing, enumerates fourteen indispensable 'doors' of prayer — ablution, opening, call to prayer, standing call, turning toward God, recitation, bowing, praise, glorification, prostration, testimony, salutation, the supplication of the standing invocation, and the supplication of the odd-numbered prayer — which are its supporting pillars and without which prayer is incomplete.

retained.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
retained.text: A collection of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of the Daaim al-Islam (Pillars of Islam) supplies the first body of rulings on dress and prayer surfaces.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that abandoning Friday prayer is blameworthy 'whether under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer given is that praying behind the people of injustice is permissible only for the sake of dissimulation (taqiyyah).

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle interprets the Friday prayer as pointing to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, possessor of an outward summons to his Shariah and an inward summons to its interpretation; the reduction to two cycles with the sermon substituting for the other two, and the sitting as the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: The twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are interpreted as a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, drawn from the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks plus the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age — the local addition of a twenty-fourth being noted as a departure.

retained.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl derives al-fitr from senses of splitting open, appearing and beginning, so that fasting is silence and concealment — evidenced by Maryam's vow of a fast of silence — and the day of breaking the fast is the day secrets and hidden knowledge are manifested.

retained.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
retained.text: The Mustansiriyya councils enumerate seven places of omission in prayer, in six of which the two prostrations are proper — including omitting a prostration, forgetting the first or second tashahhud, saluting after two rakahs of a four-rakah prayer, and rising to a fifth rakah — while the seventh, omission behind the Imam, requires none because the Imam bears it.

retained.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
retained.text: Doubt in prayer falls into twelve cases: where the doubt concerns an act still ahead or unsettled (bowing, number of rakahs) the worshipper builds on what is certain — the lesser — and prostrates for omission; but where the doubt arises after the act has been passed (doubting the takbir after bowing, recitation after bowing, or anything after the salaam) nothing is due.

retained.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
retained.text: The governing rule for the traveler is that he shortens the prayer and breaks the fast from leaving his dwelling until he re-enters it, provided he is pressing on in the journey, as stated in مختصر الآثار by al-Numan.

retained.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
retained.text: The sick man prays according to his capacity in a descending scale: seated or cross-legged with bowing and prostration, then gesturing with the head, then with the eyes, and if unable even that, with the heart.

retained.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
retained.text: The decisive distinction drawn is that weeping is permitted while wailing and lamentation are forbidden: the Prophet wept at his child's death and explained he forbade only nawh and 'awil, weeping being tenderness and mercy Allah places in hearts; he licensed weeping at calamity, saying the soul is stricken, the eye tearful, the loss recent — but say what pleases Allah and do not speak obscenely.

retained.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
retained.text: Answering the author from Yemen to Hind, Jafar ibn Sulayman ruled that the Pillars prescribes only an izar from navel to knee with water passed beneath it and the private parts washed by a cloth-wrapped hand, so the Daudi group's manner of drawing the wrapper between the thighs — which they impose and denounce others for omitting — is rejected because it prevents the prescribed washing.

retained.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
retained.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inner Nursing, enumerates five zakats paralleling the five prayers: the khums of earnings, the zakat of already-khums-paid wealth (one dinar in forty, owed to the Hujja while the khums is for the Imam), the tenth of crops, one head in forty of livestock, and the zakat of the soul (shurwa and fitra).

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: The author of the Mustansiriyya sessions, in the thirteenth session, distinguishes zakat obligatory on the wealthy from zakat of Fitr, which is obligatory in every condition and even on those of small means, and enumerates seven obligations — that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and younger of his household, the free and the enslaved, the males and the females — plus twelve Sunnah practices.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: Among the Sunnah practices: it is brought out from the middle sort of one's food — a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins, with half a sa sufficing only for wheat; the sa is four mudds; it is handed to the Imam or his appointee before the breaking of the fast; delay requires making it up; one lacking food gives its value in silver or gold; and a woman without a husband pays for herself and her dependents.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad's Concealed Epistle states that the Messenger of God made the fitra obligatory on every head among the Muslims — male and female, small and great, even an infant born that day and the child in the womb — a sa of wheat, dates, raisins, barley or other grain, which is why it is named the charity of the head; if paid before the prayer it counts as charity.

retained.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
retained.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima draws the temporal distinction that what is brought out before sunrise counts as fitra and after sunrise as ordinary charity, and defines the meaning of fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and as offering.

retained.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
retained.text: The fourteenth Mustansiriyya majlis divides fasting into seven obligatory kinds: Ramadan yearly; two consecutive months for deliberately breaking a fast day when no slave can be freed; two consecutive months for killing a believer by mistake when no slave can be freed, plus blood money; two consecutive months in zihar expiation when no slave can be freed; three days for a broken oath when feeding, clothing and freeing are all unavailable; ten days for one performing tamattu who finds no offering; and the fast of a vow.

retained.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
retained.text: The same majlis lists twelve fasts of the practice and commendation: itikaf, Shaban, the first Thursday of each month, its middle Wednesday, its last Thursday, the three white days, the fast of Dawud (alternate days, the most rigorous), Friday joined to Thursday or Saturday but never alone, Arafah for the non-pilgrim, the boy's fast at seven years, recompense for game taken in the sacred state as ruled by the one entrusted with that ruling, and the fast for shaving the head on account of harm.

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: The author's thesis, following the Book of Clarification, is that the reports commanding fasting by sighting the crescent are directed only to whoever is absent from the presence of the Imam and ignorant of the measures of the crescent moons.

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: The first reply is contextual: the hadith was spoken when the Companions asked how they should act in the Prophet's absence, so fasting by sighting is a rule of necessity when neither the Messenger nor the Imam standing in his place is present, while in their presence one fasts and breaks fast by theirs.

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: The year is ordered as six complete and six deficient months running Muharram complete, Safar deficient, and so on, so that Ramadan falls as complete, confirmed by the Prophet's saying 'Shaban is never complete, and Ramadan is never deficient.'

retained.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
retained.text: The lam in 'ṣūmū li-ruʾyatihi' is read as the lam of anticipation or outcome (lām al-ʿāqiba), as in 'mothers nourish their children for death' and 'This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning,' so the hadith means: let the crescent rise while you are already fasting, and rise while you are already breaking the fast.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author writes in response to a brother's request to justify the Shia practice — and specifically the command issued from the Pure Presence in the year 400 requiring the fast to begin two days before the crescent was seen by eye — and names the work the necessary epistle on fasting the month of Ramadan and its time.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author charges the opponents with falling into division not through evidence but through arrogance, envy and refusal to obey those charged with the Command, to whom the Qur'an directs that all disputed matters be referred.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Because Allah created all things in pairs and the Prophet made pairing the governing principle of his law (prayer/alms, adhan/iqama, Hajj/Umrah, Safa/Marwa), the author infers that sight too is of two paired kinds.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Natural vision occurs by means of the eye and apprehends only colours and shapes, whereas vision of the soul occurs by way of knowledge through the heart and apprehends the causes hidden from the eye — evidenced by Qur'anic verses addressing the Prophet as 'seeing' the companions of the elephant, whom he never witnessed.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Vision of the soul is judged more exalted, finer and prior in apprehension — it registers the drop removed from a pool, which the eye cannot — so holding fast to it in fulfilling obligations is more binding, since to take the lesser when the more excellent is present is a judgment of ignorance.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Just as prayer binds one who knows its time without hearing the adhan, and abstinence binds one who knows dawn has broken though a barrier hides it, so entry into the fast is binding once it is known that the moon has separated from the sun after conjunction, even if light, cloud, dust or a mountain bars sight.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: Since sight apprehends only shape and colour, and the crescent is not sought to learn its colour, shape, thinness or thickness — none of which is a condition of the fast — the obligation cannot attach to eyesight but to the soul's apprehension that the moon now stands west of the sun after being east of her.

retained.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
retained.text: The author reads the lam in 'li-ru'yatihi' as indicating that the act precedes that for which it is done (as in 'work for the Hereafter'), so the hadith means the community is already fasting when the crescent is seen by eye.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author holds that both sightings — the vision of the soul and the sighting of the eye — are valid foundations for performing obligatory duties, but the vision of the soul is the more excellent and belongs to the possessors of knowledge, while the eye's sighting belongs to the generality, who are obliged to follow the learned, the relation between them being like that between the first and second times of a prayer.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author generalises that all matters are of two kinds, hidden and apparent: the hidden is known only by the select, the apparent by select and common alike, and each group is bound to act on what it knows — as the pre-dawn eater who knows dawn has broken must stop, while the ignorant one follows the learned.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: Against reading the hadith 'If it is obscured from you, count thirty days' as referring to eye-sighting, the author argues that eye-sighting rarely yields thirty-day months, that the Prophet could not bind his community to a doubt-ridden rule, since Allah says worship must be with sincerity ('They were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion'), and that sincerity is other than doubt and confusion.
entities: فإن غمّ عليكم فعدوا ثلاثين يوماً

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author argues that the Prophet's fixing the month at the complete number points to the vision of the soul, whose counts neither increase nor decrease, in line with 'that you may complete the count.'

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author further argues that counting thirty days requires knowing a month's first day, which is often unknown where the crescent is hidden (Tabaristan, mountains, coasts, islands), so the eye-sighting reading would make the Prophet burden his community beyond capacity, contrary to 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity'; hence either the report is unsound or must be read as the vision of the soul.
entities: لا يكلف الله نفساً إلا وسعها

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author argues from the other pillars — prayer led by the Imam, zakat collected and distributed by him (given elsewhere it must be paid again), Hajj whose rites follow the Imam, and jihad ordered by the one entrusted with the Muslims' affair — that no pillar is entrusted to the fallible community, so the fast's beginning likewise may not be settled by the community's own ijtihad apart from the one standing in the place of the Messenger.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: Answering the objection that on his principle the day of conjunction would belong partly to Shaban and partly to Ramadan, the author replies that every obligation has two causes — a preceding general one and a specific one fixing its time (day/declining sun; wealth/passage of a year; ability/the greatest day at Mecca; opposition/the leading head) — and for fasting the general cause is the moon's separation from the sun while the specific cause is the following dawn.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author reads the sun as an indication of the rank of the Speaker (Prophet) — noblest and most luminous, source of light to others, cause of growth and the cause to which all causes attach, but in the world of the soul and religion — within the interpretive call commanded by 'Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom,' wisdom having two divisions: outward work (which requires interpretation) and knowledge, the hidden worship of the soul.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author reads the moon as an indication of the rank of the Foundation (الأساس), below the Speaker, receiving more of his light than any other, illuminating the night by expounding the Prophet's sealed symbols and parables, and mediating spiritual offspring between Speaker and community — with the moon's phases mapped onto the Foundation's career: conjunction as the Prophet's instruction of Ali ('I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate'), hiddenness as his rank known only to the elect, the crescent as the explicit designation near the Prophet's death, its faintness as the community's disagreement over his Imamate, and its fullness at fourteen days as the universal recognition of his Imamate at the passing of the seven repetitions at the cycle's end.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author reads the Ramadan verses interpretively: Ramadan as the noblest month stands for the Foundation (since the Quran was in fact revealed over twenty-three years, the outward sense of 'the month in which the Quran was sent down' yields contradiction), 'Whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it' means whoever attends the Foundation's assembly must keep silent and follow him, and 'whoever is sick or on a journey' excepts the one who speaks to receive benefit — a doubter or learner.
entities: لا ترفعوا أصواتكم فوق صوت النبي

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: To the objection that his reasoning uses the forbidden science of the stars, the author answers that it would be an 'unjust division' to allow astronomical inference for the qibla and prayer times but forbid it for the fast, and that the Prophet forbade it only for one who begins with astronomy before the divine and revealed sciences, which leads to the doctrine of Ptolemy's followers who ascribe divinity to the heavenly bodies; when the revealed sciences come first, such knowledge increases certainty in Allah's oneness, as the Quran's oaths by the stars show.

retained.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
retained.text: The author concludes that sighting is of two kinds, that choosing the more excellent is the better course, and that the Prophet's lam in 'لرؤيته' meant the sighting of knowledge — which requires that people already be fasting when the crescent is seen by the eye — and seals the treatise with praise, prayer upon the Prophet, Ali, the pure Imams as 'moons amid the darkness,' and the Imam of the age al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author states that he composed the book at the repeated request of a senior figure of the dawa, to gather into one place what lies scattered through the books of the saints and their learned callers — the paired and authoritative books, the brief compositions on Sharia matters, and expansive treatments of juristic paths and legal opinions — so that their contents would be made more accessible.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author names the book إسعاف الطالب في جميع المطالب ('The Student's Aid in All Demands') and dates the start of composition to the seventh of Rajab al-Asabb in the year 1051 of the Prophetic migration.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author writes from within the Tayyibi Ismaili tradition, invoking the Prophet, 'Ali, Fatima al-Batul, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, the pure Imams, and the caller of his own age, the dai Jafar ibn Sulayman and his successor the dai Muhammad ibn al-Fahd, in service to the Imam al-Tayyib.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author disclaims personal credit: whatever in the work is correct derives from the substance of his patron the caller and his successor, while whatever is a slip or error comes from his own shortness of reach.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author announces that he will next treat the distinction between faith (iman) and Islam — what each encompasses — and what lies beyond them.

dropped.section_title: 1. The Eight Levels of Faith
dropped.text: The author cites 'Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred precepts that the Children of Israel divided into seventy-two sects and this community will divide into seventy-three, of which one is in the Garden and the rest in the Fire.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Foster-Suckling, reads the Qur'anic phrase 'God is his master, and Gabriel, and the righteous of the believers' as designating 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Imam of every believing man and woman.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In the account from Uns al-Afidah al-Muniba, the king of Rum sends a messenger with money to test Muhammad's successor with three questions: what is not God's, what is not with God, and what God does not know.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: Abu Bakr and 'Umar both fail the test and, rather than admitting ignorance, accuse the questioner of disbelief — a failure 'Abdullah ibn Abbas explicitly criticises before directing the company to 'Ali.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In the narration from Abu al-Jarud via al-Harith al-Awar, Muawiya secretly sends a Syrian to 'Ali in al-Rahba with eleven questions relayed from Ibn al-Asfar, who had promised to follow and pay tribute to whoever could answer them.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: 'Ali detects the stranger as an outsider before he speaks, grants him safety for wartime acts on the principle that 'when war lays down its burdens, there is no harm in it,' and denounces Muawiya and the nation that severed his kinship and denied him his right.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: 'Ali defers the answering to al-Hasan, who resolves all eleven questions — including that truth and falsehood are four fingers apart (what the eye sees is true, what the ear hears is largely false), that the moon's light was once like the sun's until God erased it per the verse on the two signs, and that the hardest of ten things ascends from stone through iron, fire, water, cloud, wind, angel, Angel of Death, death, to the command of God.

dropped.section_title: 2. Three Questions from the King of Rum
dropped.text: In a further narration, 'Ali resolves 'Umar's four unasked questions: true dreams occur while the soul is loosed in the kingdom and false ones as it returns (per the verse on God taking souls in sleep), instinctive love and hatred trace to souls created two thousand years before bodies that knew or rejected one another in the air, and forgetting comes from a film over the heart like the film of the moon — after which 'Umar concedes 'You have spoken truly, O Abu al-Hasan.'

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The seven higher forms of peace are enumerated from Qur'anic verses: God's own 'Peace be upon you'; 'O Noah, descend in peace from Us'; 'their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace'; 'they will be met therein with greeting and peace'; the angels' entering with peace from every gate; the command that believers pray for and submit to the Prophet; and 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin'.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The author identifies Yasin as the Prophet Muhammad, and therefore 'the family of Yasin' as the family of Muhammad, making the seventh Qur'anic peace a peace upon the Imams of the Prophet's house.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Among the twelve human forms, the first four are named: the greeting of the people of the right hand ('Peace be upon you for your patience'), the greeting on entering houses/the mosque, the peace concluding the prayer, and the believer's 'peace' when addressed by the ignorant.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The Sunnah fixes an order of precedence in initiating the greeting: camel-rider to horse-rider, horse-rider to donkey-rider, donkey-rider to the walker, the walker to the one standing, and the one standing both initiates and returns it.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The return of a greeting is divided into three kinds — the virtuous reply (greeting back with something better), the complete reply (responding in kind, per 'return it with something better, or return it as it is'), and the just reply.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The just reply applies to dhimmis, who do not initiate the greeting; if one does, the answer is 'And upon you', because some were reported to say 'al-sam alaykum' (death be upon you) instead of 'al-salam alaykum', so that whoever said good receives its like and whoever said evil receives its like.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: The Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah is reported to pray on Sunday for the lower borders, the five — the spokesman, the foundation, the culmination, the successor, and the wing — and on Saturday over the seven days and twelve months.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Saints of the religion are reported to pray across the days of the week for the proclaimers and their gates, the imams of their stations, their proofs and preachers, and specifically for the seven proclaimers, seven culminations, seven caliphs and twelve successors, asking to be admitted to every good granted them and spared every evil they were spared.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: Amir al-Mu'minin in his Four Hundred Counsels commands returning a greeting with something better or in kind, shaking the hand of an enemy who dislikes it (citing 'Repel with that which is better...'), and replying to 'May God greet you with peace' with 'You are the peace of God, and the finest of abodes and stations'.

dropped.section_title: 3. The Grammar of Peace
dropped.text: From the book of questions of Shaykh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi with answers from Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, it is ruled that peace should be proclaimed aloud to shaykhs and teachers (better than the Indian custom of bowing or lowering the head), while audibility in returning greetings or in blessing a sneezer is a courtesy and not an obligation — except that returning a greeting itself is required, whether aloud or silently.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen, in the book of the Esoteric Nursing, interprets the Quranic verse 'the earth is inherited by My righteous servants' as referring to the Imams among God's servants.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: On the verse promising to make 'those made weak in the land' Imams and heirs, Jafar bin Mansour al-Yemen identifies 'those made weak' as the descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib, weakened in the person of Ali himself, who is the proof (hujja) of Muhammad, the earth being his likeness.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Sayings ascribed to Ali in the supplication of victory and awe invoke numbered groups — six transmitted, seven beheld, nine signs, ten words, twenty-one, eight encircling the Throne, eleven prostrating, twelve bowing — and seven Imams, seven successors, seven witnesses, seven substitutes.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Ali is reported in the Four Hundred Manners as saying that whoever holds fast to the Imams joins the truth and whoever holds to another way is undone.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Ali's commandments to the Imams' followers require working as the Imams work, relying on pious restraint (wara'), avoiding those who revile them, not praising them openly before the enemy, truthfulness, patience, and not burdening the Imams with intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Further maxims from the Four Hundred Manners warn that disputation bequeaths doubt, that speech is to be reckoned among deeds, that sin withholds sustenance, that the best deed of the believer is awaiting the relief (intizar al-faraj), and that blessed is he admonished by another's example.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: Muhammad bin Tahir's supplication seeks nearness to God through the Imams' gates, proofs, preachers, authorized ones, respondents of their cycles, and all who follow or shelter with them.

dropped.section_title: 4. Guardians, Proofs, and the Limits of Praise
dropped.text: The nineteenth Mustansiriya council divides the commanded ties of kinship into seven and twelve, identifying the seven as the Imams of the religion — the 'kin' whose affection the Quran names as the Prophet's only reward — recurring like the days of Friday.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred manners, warns believers not to despise weak brothers (whoever despises a believer is belittled and detested by God and will not be joined with him on the Day of Resurrection unless he repents), not to force a brother to ask when his need is already known, and to visit, be tender, and give freely rather than be like the hypocrite who describes what he does not do.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali is quoted as saying the Muslim is the mirror of his Muslim brother, so that a brother's slip is met with guidance, counsel and gentleness rather than a group banding against him, and discord is condemned because it leads a person away from the path.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Ali forbids backbiting on the authority of the Qur'anic rebuke 'Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?', and urges that meeting believers with a handshake and a bright face causes the burdens each carried to lift by the time they part.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: A recorded question from Shaykh Shimon bin Muhammad al-Ghuri al-Hindi about the Indian custom of asking neighbors for water, salt and food when one lacks them at the moment (though able to buy) was answered by Sayyidina Hassan bin Idris bin al-Hassan bin Abdullah al-Ala: there is no harm in it, since it belongs to the purity of affection and the excellence of brotherhood.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: From the two Qur'anic verses enjoining goodness toward both parents, the council draws the point that in both places it is the mother's deed alone (carrying in hardship, weakness upon weakness) that is laid to the child's account, so she whom God distinguished by mention must be distinguished with honor and righteousness.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: The seal of righteousness toward parents is a person's righteousness toward his own soul: making the truth plain to it and establishing it therein, magnifying it so as to awaken its longing, placing fear in it, dealing gently with it, delivering it from what would destroy it and rescuing it from what has bound it.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: The twelve manners toward parents are listed: honoring their dwelling, rising for them, answering their call, lowering one's voice, magnifying and not rebuking them, lowering the wing of humility in mercy, not walking ahead of them in light or darkness, not opposing their command, saying no word of complaint, desiring life for them in old age as they desired it for him in childhood, and providing for their needs as they provided for his.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: The twentieth council, building on parents and kinship, divides safeguarding the neighbor into seven ranks graded by how many rights each holds — the kin-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship, faith), the kin non-believer neighbor (neighborliness, kinship), the believing stranger-neighbor (neighborliness, faith), the companion at your side who differs in religion and creed (neighborliness), the companion aboard ship (right of nearness), the one who shares your litter, and the one who sits with you to receive wisdom, whose sanctity is the most binding of all.

dropped.section_title: 5. Parents, Kin, and the Neighbor at Your Side
dropped.text: Twelve manners of neighborliness are enumerated — not peering into or eavesdropping on the neighbor's house, not disclosing what one learns of him, not letting him hear or see what he would hate, not withholding a household implement he asks for, not acting haughtily when higher in station nor envying when he is above, helping when he seeks help, covering his 'awrah if exposed, causing him no injury, and bearing his injury with patience — these being called the deeds of a people whose hearts God has tested for piety.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, forbids silence until nightfall except in the remembrance of God, forbids reverting to desert life after the migration, and holds that a man of sound mind does not recite the Quran in a state of ritual impurity until he purifies himself for it.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib warns believers not to let the Murjiah overcome them with their opinion, marking a category of teachers whose word must be refused.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: In the book of questions of Sheikh Shamoun ibn Muhammad Ghori al-Hindi answered by Badr al-Din Hasan ibn Idris, the questioner asks whether al-Sadiq's reported licensing of al-Shafii — cited from Hamid al-Din's al-Hadi wal-Mustahdi, al-Numan's al-Daaim, and Idris ibn al-Hasan's Zahr al-Maani — meant al-Shafii later changed like al-Mughirah and Abu al-Khattab, or whether ignorant men falsely claimed his school as others falsely claimed the Imamate of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and Abdullah ibn Muawiyah.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: The answer given is qualified, not general: al-Sadiq had indeed granted al-Shafii license, but solely on account of al-Shafii's acknowledgment of the excellence of the Ahl al-Bayt and for no other reason.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Asked how the Prophet's saying that whoever looks into his brother's book without permission is as one looking into the Fire can stand when members of a school freely read one another's books, the answer distinguishes the book of inner truth (haqiqa), which may be looked into only by permission of the one who granted access, from all other books, where refraining is mere good manners and not binding.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: A borrower who finds damage or disorder in a borrowed Quran or other book may repair it without the owner's permission, but is under no obligation to do so.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Books of the dawah left by a deceased man may not be used to settle his debts even when his other goods are insufficient, because they belong to the dawah and are not inherited property.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Yemeni callers answering Indian sheikhs rule that those licensed to read religious benefits may read to women through a screen so the woman hears without being seen, and that no man may be alone with a woman unless another woman is with her or another man with him.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Ali holds that the worth of every man is what he has mastered of knowledge, and the Messenger of God holds that seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim man and woman.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Ali forbids measuring religion by analogy, declaring that a people will come who do so and that they are religion's enemies, the first analogical reasoner having been Iblis; instead, discourse one does not recognize must be referred back to the Imams and suspended there.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: Al-Qadi al-Numan in Mafatih al-Nimah reports al-Sadiq drawing a distinction between referring an obscure teaching back to the Imams — bringing it to them so they may establish its proof and disclose its interpretation — and throwing it back at them by calling it false and turning away.

dropped.section_title: 6. What Must Be Learned, What Must Be Concealed
dropped.text: On concealment and precaution, Ali warns that whoever divulges the Imams' secret will be made by God to taste the cold of iron.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The author cites a Book of Question and Answer arranged by the order of the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, in which the questions come from teachers of the Indian lands and the answers from the summoners (duat) of the Yemeni lands.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Answering an Indian question, the Yemeni respondent rules that the prohibition on urinating beneath fruit-bearing trees covers both trees on which fruit is actually present and trees whose property it is to bear fruit.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The respondent rules that although greeting and speaking are forbidden to one in a state of hadath, once he has risen from that place — having cleansed himself with a stone or otherwise — he may be greeted, must return the greeting, and may speak.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The respondent permits reusing a stone or clod of earth previously used for cleansing after urination, once it has dried, provided no impurity and no moisture are evident upon it.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as listing the nullifiers of ablution: sleep, whatever issues from the front or rear passage (whether a stone or wind), an enema, fainting, insanity, and the disappearance of the glans into the front passage of a living or dead person.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Tawil al-Daaim is cited for the rule that one who interrupts his ablution may build upon what he has already done, so long as the water has not dried upon the limbs already washed.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
