dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is also cited for the concession that one whose hands are amputated above the elbows, leaving nothing of them, is released from the obligation of washing the hands.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: In that council walaya is named the first and most excellent of the obligations, and it is stated that in every allusion made by these numbers the ranking of the friends of God is the utmost aim and intention.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: The twelve practices of ablution are enumerated as istinja, washing the hands before entering them into the vessel, pronouncing God's name on sitting down, rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, moving the ring so water reaches beneath it, combing water through the beard, wetting the eyes, giving the right limbs precedence over the left, wiping the ears inside and out, the second and third washings of the face (the first being the obligation), and the siwak.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, commands cleansing with water from foul odor and prescribes set invocations on entering the privy and on looking at what has passed from one, the latter grounded in the Prophet's report that an angel turns the servant's neck so he looks at it and asks: this is what you were eager for — consider where you took it from and what it has come to.

dropped.section_title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
dropped.text: Ali is also cited in the same context for the rule that when sleep mingles with the heart, ablution becomes obligatory.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: A ruling reported in the question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam holds that prayer is not permitted while a man knowingly carries impurity, so one who prayed having forgotten the istinja must wash and repeat the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The same source rules that uncovering oneself for wudhu or washing in a screened place where no one sees is permissible and the purity obtained is valid, the concealment reported of some Imams being a matter of excellence of manners rather than obligation.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah lists twelve manners of the wudhu governing the privy, including entering with sandals and the left foot first, covering the head, not facing or turning the back to the qiblah, leaning on the left leg, not lingering, cleansing with the left hand using three fresh stones rather than dung or worn bone, keeping silent within, and leaving with the right foot first.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Kitab al-Idah reports the Prophet saying Gabriel commanded him on God's behalf to wash the two hollows beside the chin in ablution — the sides of the tuft below the lower lip — these being "the neglected place."

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The author reports sayings of Ali ibn Abi Talib from his Four Hundred Manners on purification, including that rinsing the mouth and drawing in water is Sunnah purification of mouth and nose, that istinja with cold water cuts off piles, that ablution after purity is ten good deeds, and that one should say the basmalah and the prayer to be among the repentant and the purified before touching water.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The questions and answers distinguish the istinja as both a Sunnah practice that must not be deliberately abandoned — whose omission through forgetfulness does not spoil wudhu or require repeating a prayer already performed — and as obligatory insofar as the removal of impurity is itself obligatory.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: For one with a wound or boil that water cannot touch, the answer given is that he wipes over bandages and coverings for wudhu, and performs tayammum if removal would harm him through cold or injury or if he is sick; for the greater purification he pours water in a stream, and performs tayammum if he fears for himself, whether traveling or at home.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: On water, the rulings hold that abundant water above the Shariah measure which overpowers impurity remains purifying, whereas a vessel whose water has shown a quality of impurity becomes impure and is not restored by pouring more water in a stream unless it rises above the measure after the vessel is purified; running water and a pool eight cubits in length and breadth remain valid.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Used water and used dust are declared pure and purifying, so that purification with them is permitted once and many times, against the practice of ordinary people who do not permit a second use.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: The saying "whoever the sea does not purify, may God not purify him" is interpreted to mean that water purifies and is not itself purified, and likewise the knowledge of the Imam: whomever it does not purify, nothing else will.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Majalis al-Bayan enumerates seven obligations of wudhu (pure water, intention, washing face, washing hands, wiping head, wiping feet, and the Quranic order), twelve of its Sunnah acts, seven obligatory forms of ghusl, twelve Sunnah forms of ghusl, and twelve places where prayer is disliked.

dropped.section_title: 8. The Manners of the Washing Place
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah reports the Prophet forbidding wiping over the socks and forbidding the abandonment of saying the basmalah aloud, and Ali is quoted that there is no dissimulation in drinking intoxicants or in wiping over the socks.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: The section's material is drawn from a compiled book of questions and answers arranged according to the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, with further material from Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, al-Risala al-Maknuna, Tawil al-Shariah, and the Four Hundred Manners of Ali ibn Abi Talib.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Against the report in some Shariah books that one who performs tayammum out of fear of cold must later wash and repeat the prayer, the answering dai rules that whoever fears water will harm him — resident or traveler, weak man or sick — performs tayammum, prays, and owes nothing further and no repetition.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Doubt itself triggers obligation: one who revives from unconsciousness not knowing his condition, and one who wakes finding traces of semen (wet or dry) without recalling emission, must perform the ghusl.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: For the one in janabah and the menstruating or post-natally bleeding woman, removing hair or nails is disliked — better left until purification — and neither may deliberately recite the Quran, nor Quranic matter embedded in supplications or books, nor the basmalah with the intention of Quranic recitation.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Al-Risala al-Maknuna grounds ghusl in Quran 'if you are junub, purify yourselves' and the Prophet's 'beneath every hair is janabah', and glosses junub as 'one far from a thing', concluding that the obedience of one in janabah is void and false.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Ali is reported in the Four Hundred Manners as forbidding the Muslim to sleep while junub or without purity (using tayammum if no water), because the believer's spirit ascends to God, who blesses it and either forms it beautifully if its term has come or returns it to the body with trusted angels.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Vomit does not render impure what it falls upon (though washing the place is better), and ground once urinated upon becomes ruled pure for prayer and tayammum when the impurity's substance and smell are gone — since sun and light purify it — provided it is not ground set aside as a privy.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Ali's ruling that touching a corpse 'after it has grown cold' obliges ghusl is interpreted to mean after it has become impure, so contact with its moisture makes the living person impure, while the corpse-washer's own washing is from the Sunnah.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Items that cannot be rubbed or wrung three times are purified by passing the hand over them until impurity and smell are gone, then lifting from the water and letting it drip, repeated three times; heavier items are trodden with the feet and pressed out, likewise three times.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: A Muslim nursing woman's milk is pure for her and others (Walid Izz al-Din Maad ibn Abdullah ibn Ali), since milk is like saliva and every Muslim's saliva is pure; and small amounts of impurity — wet hair, the milk or butter of filth-eating animals, egg white — are excused.
entities: Izz al-Din Maad ibn Abdullah ibn Ali

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Despite the verse 'the polytheists are nothing but impurity', the Imams permitted prayer in garments polytheists have made so long as they have not worn them or visible impurity has not appeared — including cloth sprinkled with impure water during weaving that has since dried — whereas what they have bleached or washed with soap is pure only by washing.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Against the common people's view that a large garment whose ends do not move together may be prayed upon at its pure part, the dai rules that prayer upon a partly impure garment or bedding is not permitted at all; tayammum covers ritual impurity, not impure garments, and the sick man must have his garments washed by another.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Idris ibn al-Hasan, answering Sheikh Yusuf ibn Ismail al-Samti al-Hindi, rules that whatever ground tayammum is not valid from may not be prayed upon (citing 'the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a purification'), and that the Indian scruple against sweeping houses and shops at night is unreliable and blameless to violate.
entities: Yusuf ibn Ismail ibn Ibrahim al-Samti al-Hindi

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: A vessel licked by a dog — and likewise by a pig — is washed seven times, one of them with earth; and if impurity falls into one of two indistinguishable vessels, neither may be used and one performs tayammum and prays.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: Ali's Four Hundred Manners are cited for a body of cleanliness practices as Sunnah and purification — trimming the mustache and nails, washing the head with mallow, depilatory paste every fifteen days, plucking the armpits, feast-day bathing, washing garments, avoiding dogs, not relieving oneself on roads or into standing water or the wind (for water and air have their folk), and cleansing foul odor since God hates the servant who offends those sitting near him.

dropped.section_title: 9. Major Impurity and the Cleanliness of Things
dropped.text: On long uncombed hair, Hasan ibn Idris rules there is no defect if it is parted into two halves, though leaving it unparted is unfitting, and doing so deliberately in defiance of the ruling voids the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author reports that using a split bamboo cane or similar to scrape the tongue after the siwak, as most people of India do, is permitted, since the siwak itself is the mainstay; he also records that one must not clean between the teeth with a knotted stalk of dried grass, and that using the siwak while in janaba (major ritual impurity) is disliked.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author cites Sharh al-Akhbar defining rayhan as every fragrant plant, with the myrtle (al-as) singled out by that name, and Ta'wil al-Da'a'im defining it as the tips of sweet-scented plants at blossoming — a comprehensive name for fragrant plants, most often given to myrtle because it is the most lasting and strongest.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author quotes Ali ibn Abi Talib's four hundred points of etiquette that the tooth-stick pleases the Lord, sweetens the mouth, and belongs to the sunna.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Tayammum requires dust: on a smooth rock fixed in the ground it is valid only if dust lies on it, not otherwise.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author draws the distinction that tayammum is not permitted to a settled (non-traveling) person except for cause, whereas a traveler far from water, or unable to reach it before the prayer time lapses, or endangered in person or property by going to it, performs tayammum.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: A traveler who forgets an owed ghusl from a night of Ramadan and finds no water may use tayammum for both prayer and fast; likewise a woman purified from menses before sunset in Ramadan, or a man with a nocturnal emission, who fear harm from washing, may perform tayammum and fast without making up the day.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author records a series of tayammum cases: one who dies on a journey without water is given tayammum; one who fears illness from ablution performs tayammum; a menstruating traveler's wife once pure may do tayammum and become lawful to her husband; an imam in janaba with water for only one may do tayammum and lead others who have done so; a man with water only for ablution but impurity on his garment washes the garment and does tayammum; a junub with water insufficient for ghusl does tayammum at noon and uses the water for ablution at afternoon prayer since he is by then pure; where a corpse and a junub compete for one washing's water, the junub washes and the corpse is given tayammum; and a Christian or Zoroastrian wife purified from menses on a journey is taught the tayammum by her husband.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Citing Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, the author adds that finding water breaks the tayammum and returns the man to janaba, that a new convert without water performs tayammum and prays, that one made impure while sleeping in the Prophet's mosque should perform tayammum before passing through it or the sanctuary, and that a sound person performs tayammum on behalf of an invalid who cannot.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author records that one in minor impurity may do tayammum for the funeral prayer if he fears missing it; that one who prayed with tayammum while forgetting water in his baggage repeats with ablution if time remains but is discharged if the time has gone out; that al-Muntakhaba directs one who finds no earth to beat felts and garments and use that dust even if none is seen to fly; and that Ta'wil al-Da'a'im requires a man trapped in a crush to pray with tayammum and then repeat the prayer once he can reach water.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: In a reported case two men performed tayammum together and only one prayer was valid: the man who asked to be taught prayed validly, while his teacher, who struck the earth for him, did not, because he formed no intention for himself — establishing that intention (niyya) is indispensable.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author rules that the dung of any animal not lawful to eat is impure, so neem oil pressed from stones passed through crows' droppings may not be eaten, sold, or bought, even though no impurity is visible in it.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: Where a liquid such as honey, clarified butter, olive oil or sesame oil holds an animal with flowing blood that has died in it, it may not be eaten nor fed to animals lawful to eat, though soap may be made from it and sold only if the buyer is told of its corruption, and a garment washed with such soap must be rinsed with pure water; reports add that it may be fed to dogs and non-edible beasts, that a pot with a dead mouse has its broth poured off and its meat washed and eaten, and that food is still edible if one or two grains of mouse droppings are removed but not if three come out.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author reconciles the report that the leavings of a menstruating woman, a Jew, a Christian, beasts of prey and riding animals do no harm with the ruling that a dog's lapping is impure by appealing to moisture and to water above the legal limit, and elsewhere holds that the leavings of a Jew, Christian, Magian or cat falling into a small vessel leave it valid for purification so long as no saliva is apparent.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: On unbelievers' foodstuffs the author distinguishes the prohibition of their slaughtered animals — forbidden only because God's name is not pronounced and the animal is not turned to the qibla — from their other food, which is lawful in itself but defiled wherever they have touched it with their moisture or wet implements, so that avoidance is obligatory when an alternative exists but need removes the restriction except for their slaughter and their moisture.

dropped.section_title: 10. Tooth-Stick, Dust, and the Purity of Food
dropped.text: The author cites Hasan ibn Nuh's questions to Husayn ibn Idris that the slaughter of the People of the Book may be eaten if a Muslim observed the qibla and the divine name, and cites the Yemeni masters' answers to Hasan al-Hindi that eating the cooking of a serving girl careless about ritual purity is permitted; and holds that betel with a small harmless amount of lime, like water with a little earth, is not forbidden unless gross and harmful.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: The section is built from a question-and-answer compilation arranged according to the chapter order of Qadi al-Numan's Daaim al-Islam, supplemented by letters and rulings of later dignitaries.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: On circumcision the rule given is that no uncircumcised person is left so in Islam even at eighty years of age, and the same insistence is extended to the circumcision of girls (khafd) for a woman who has grown old.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Qadi al-Numan, answering his district governor al-Khattab ibn Wasim, qualifies the rule: a man born circumcised — as some prophets are reported to have been — is exempt, and one whose glans or most of it is already exposed is not compelled, though it is recommended for a young man that remaining skin be cut away.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: A reported saying of Ali instructs women not to take the girls' circumcision to the utmost but to leave something of it, which the answer glosses as better for the husband's inclination toward her; a further opinion holds that the prayer and the marital intercourse of an uncircumcised woman are nonetheless valid, the sunna being merely to hasten to it.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Hair of the head must be parted into two halves from front to back — the Indian custom of parting toward the middle is rejected — and deliberate defiance of this ruling is said to corrupt the prayer, while mere negligence does not.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Trimming is permitted only from the two sides of the beard (al-aridayn) and body hair may be shaved, shortened or plucked freely, but nothing may be removed from the beard itself.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Defined terms are supplied for the Prophet's prohibition on a menstruating woman taking up a qassa or jumma: the jumma is hair plaited from the side locks to the nape, the qassa is cutting the head's hair leaving about a quarter at the front, and the qunzua — hair gathered with portions left standing — is likewise forbidden.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Engraving the skin with henna dye is forbidden, but dyeing the teeth, filing uneven teeth level (for women), and piercing the ears of women and infant girls for ornaments are all permitted, and Indian popular scruples about spouses sharing one comb or about combing on Friday night are dismissed as having no reliance placed upon them.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Henna for a man is not sinful but is judged unfitting: it is better for him to leave it absent a cause, since henna, like jewelry, was appointed for women.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Jafar's proof for that prohibition is an a fortiori argument from Qadi al-Numan's ihram rulings: since the bald man passes the razor over his head while the woman released from ihram only cuts from the ends of her hair and shaves none of it, shaving can never be lawful for her as a standing custom.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: Jafar rules that girls' circumcision must be done in concealment — known only to the girl, the operator and a few household women — and that the public gatherings, hospitality and call to prayer used for it in Yemen belong only to the purification of male children and offend against modesty, which the Prophet made part of faith.

dropped.section_title: 11. Bodies, Hair, and the Reform of Custom
dropped.text: The author reports that he himself put questions from the Island of Hind to Jafar in Yemen, who ruled that a girl dying below seven is not to be circumcised since the set limit may not be transgressed — a ruling Muhammad ibn Fahd al-Mukarrami independently confirms — whereas a male child who dies uncircumcised is, by preferred sunna, circumcised after death.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The author states that the material in this section is drawn largely from a previously mentioned book of questions and answers whose compiler arranged it following the chapter order of دعائم الإسلام.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The answer given is that if impure garments, carrion skins, or skins of beasts of prey cling to the body while either is wet, the body must be washed, and the same applies to garments washed by the hands of polytheists.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On the authority of تأويل الدعائم, the goat's hair is not to be shorn except after slaughter — if shorn while the animal is alive it counts as carrion — a ruling stated to apply to the goat in particular, whereas sheep's wool may be shorn for use while the animal lives.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The answer regarding wool, fleece or hair shorn from a lawful animal while alive is that prayer is not permitted in it until it has been washed, yet the material itself is not impure.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Concerning vessels made of carrion skins in Waghar used to transport ghee or oil to Ahmedabad, the answer is that the contents become impure and one may not pray in a garment they touch, that selling or buying the ghee or the soap made from it is permitted provided the buyer is told it is impure, but that selling or buying the carrion skins themselves is unlawful.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: From مختصر المصنف: a broken bone may be patched only with the bone of a properly slaughtered animal whose flesh is eaten; one who used carrion bone, non-edible animal bone, or human bone must remove it and repeat every prayer, compelled by the ruling authority if known, but it is not removed after death if he died in ignorance.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On menstruation, the husband may touch the whole body of the menstruating woman short of intercourse, though it is better he avoid what is beneath the wrapper worn from navel to knees, for fear the fluid reach her womb.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On the term of nifas the author reports divergent positions: Hasan ibn Nuh and several books reckon it by the woman's accustomed duration; a book of the Sharia of the people of the House gives a minimum of twenty days, a middle of forty and a maximum of sixty; and al-Numan's المنتخبة has her wait up to two months and then, if blood persists, count herself mustahadah and make up the abandoned prayers and fasts by precaution.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: The author gives his own decisive ruling that the postpartum woman, once clean of blood, becomes pure after twenty days, thereafter relying on her custom and judging any excess blood as istihadah if its character has changed.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: From تأويل الدعائم: a man who approaches a menstruating woman must seek forgiveness and repent, with charity recommended; the same falls on the woman if she consented, nothing on her if compelled, and if she concealed her menstruation the sin falls on her alone and not on the unknowing husband.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: In the answer of Hasan ibn Idris to Shaykh Shimon ibn Muhammad Ghuri al-Hindi, nifas may be less than forty days though forty must be reckoned, and Muhammad ibn al-Fahd held that blood seen after ten days makes a woman a mustahadah who washes (or performs tayammum) for each prayer time as she is able.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: Hasan ibn Idris answers that neither the menstruating woman nor the one in janaba may recite any portion of the Quran, whether in supplications or books, nor recite the basmala with the intention of Quranic recitation.

dropped.section_title: 12. Skins, Blood, and Waiting Periods
dropped.text: On istibra: marriage to a woman with whom one has fornicated requires prior clearing of the womb; مختصر المصنف sets the withdrawal at two months; كتاب الأخبار transmits forty-five nights for a mature woman who has not menstruated and nine months for such a virgin deflowered by the seller; and by the maxim "the child belongs to the bed and the fornicator gets the stone," the fornicator has no claim in the child's lineage.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The author cites Ali ibn Abi Talib's 'four hundred precepts' to establish prayer's merits and conditions: night prayer benefits body and earns God's pleasure, the worshipper receives only that portion of prayer to which he attended, and laziness, drowsiness, looking aside, and toying with the beard are to be avoided.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Quoting Ali, prayer is 'the offering (qurban) of every godfearing person' and no deed is more beloved to God than prayer, so worldly affairs must not distract from its appointed times, God having reproached in Q107 those 'neglectful of their prayer' — i.e., heedless of its times.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: From a book of legal riddle-questions the author reports three cases: the drunkard for whom prayer is impermissible (Q4:43) yet who is not excused for omitting it; the emigrant whose prayer behind a bedouin (a'rabi) is invalid since bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy; and the swimmer unable to reach land, who owes an obligatory prayer without bowing or prostration.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: On precedence, the answer given is that one who remembers missed prayers (al-fawa'it) during a current prayer's time must pray the missed ones first if time allows, and he sins if, with room in the time and no hindrance, he neglects them for the current prayer.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The section systematically distinguishes ada (performance within its time) from qada (making up after the time has passed), applying the distinction to sunnah and nafilah prayers — e.g., remaining sunnah is made up once its time (before the obligatory prayer) has passed, and the optional prayer is ada so long as its time has not lapsed.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: The sunnah of Maghrib is the stated exception to the rule that sunnah precedes the obligatory prayer: it is prayed after the obligatory Maghrib and still counts as ada, provided nothing separates the two, or if a slight interruption occurred and the congregation had not finished it.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: A contrasting case is drawn: one otherwise constant in prayer who misses obligatory prayers out of necessity may not perform the sunnah or optional prayers of the current time until he has first made up the missed obligatory prayer.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Prayer at the end of the time with certainty is better than at its beginning with doubt; prayer performed before the time has entered must be repeated; missed prayers may be made up whenever remembered except at sunrise, the meridian, and sunset, and voluntary prayer at those moments is makruh on Friday and other days alike.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Imam al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah is reported as ruling that the Fajr prayer belongs neither to the night nor the day prayers — for if it were of the night the faster could still eat, and if of the day its recitation would not be aloud — it being the middle prayer of five, and no prayer follows it because it is a call after a call with no call after it.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Ja'far ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the Book of the Inward Nursing, gives the witr as three units with fixed surahs (al-A'la, al-Kafirun, al-Ikhlas) and the qunut after rising from bowing, followed after a separation by two units prayed seated reciting al-Falaq and al-Nas specifically, then the dawn prayer of four units — two voluntary and two obligatory — identified as the middle prayer of Q2:238.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim, answering Muhammad 'Ali ibn Salih al-Badri from Yemen to Hind in 1145 AH, rules that making up prayer follows the rule of the fast — only men make up on behalf of men — and that an aged man too weak to make up prays what he can while another makes up on his behalf with expiation.

dropped.section_title: 13. The Pillar of Religion and Its Appointed Hours
dropped.text: Muhammad ibn al-Fahd ibn Salah's epistle rules that a bequest for making up a deceased's missed worship is applied in order — obligatory prayer portions, then shaf' and witr, then the sunan — with prayer advanced before the obligatory fast if the wage is insufficient.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Answering a question about a man appointed by a tyrannical sultan as prayer leader, muezzin or teacher on a salary drawn from the port levy or jizya, the compiled answer is that such money comes from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) and is lawful for him to consume only if it is administered according to the judgment of one appointed by the friends of God.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Idah reports from Jafar ibn Muhammad ibn Ali that giving the call while walking or mounted is permissible provided that at the moment of the testimony one faces the qibla, while the author states that the books attributed to the Ahl al-Bayt agree that the iqama is valid only while standing on the ground.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf instructs the muezzin to say inwardly, after the twofold testimony to Muhammad's messengership, 'I bear witness that Ali is the friend of God,' and after 'Come to the best of deeds,' 'The family of Muhammad are the best of humankind.'

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf further holds that one present in the mosque at the call should not leave before praying, except for a necessity with intent to return in time or to perform ablution, and if he misses the congregation he prays alone or with another congregation without fault.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Tawil al-Sharia holds that the muezzin may give the adhan without purity but the iqama requires purity, that he faces the qibla and forms intention first, and that the supererogatory prayer is joined to the adhan while the obligatory prayer is prayed only after the iqama.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Idris ibn Sayyidina Hasan records in the sixth part of Uyun al-Akhbar that in the caliphate of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah the muezzins added to the call the testimony that 'our mawla Ali is the friend of God' and the proclamation that Muhammad and Ali are the best of humankind and their kindred the best of kindred, in confirmation of the Prophet's declaration at Ghadir, 'Whoever's master I am, Ali is his master.'

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Against the claim, related from Abu Bakr, that 'we are the kindred of the Messenger of God,' the text holds that Ibn Abbas identified the near kindred as Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn alone, and that Abu Bakr's only link to the Prophet was the remote one of Quraysh, a point supported by al-Kumayt's verse naming Banu Hashim as the Prophet's clan.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The common objection is stated: many concede that Muhammad is the best of humankind but deny it of Ali, since humankind includes the prophets.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The first answer to that objection is that all Muslims agree, on the verse 'You were the best community brought forth for the people,' that Muhammad's community surpasses earlier communities which themselves contained prophets and favoured friends of God — so the same comparative logic must be granted for Ali.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: Supporting reports are cited: the hadith of the two weighty things from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, likening the Book and the Prophet's kindred to Noah's ark in which boarding means salvation and holding back means drowning, and the saying 'Ali is the best of humankind, and whoever refuses this has disbelieved.'

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The narrated confrontation at al-Gharafa has al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah adjudicate between the preacher of Atfih, who rejected the new call, and the dai who gave it, by getting the preacher to confirm as sound the reports that al-Hasan and al-Husayn are the masters of the youth of the Garden, that their father is better than the two of them, and that the people of the Garden are youths who do not grow old.

dropped.section_title: 14. The Disputed Words of the Call
dropped.text: The author announces that he will next reproduce in full the epistle of his sayyid and mawla and father Muhammad ibn Fahd, entitled al-Muriba amma jarat bihi al-mubahatha, which frames the dispute between those who hold the added words of the call impermissible and unnarrated and those who hold them commanded by the Noble Book and binding on whoever obeys those whose command must be obeyed.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The section is framed as a recorded debate: one jurist challenges another over why his school alone says in the call to prayer 'Muhammad and Ali are the best of human beings, and their kindred are the best of kindred,' and the respondent undertakes to answer.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The respondent's first reply is that by Quran 41:46 and 6:164 the formula, if righteous, benefits only its users and, if wrong, harms only them, so no other group is burdened by it — a reply the questioner accepts while still demanding a plain proof.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The questioner concedes as established that Muhammad is the best of human beings because he is master of the messengers, but denies that Ali's likeness to him in that excellence is established, and demands proof — so only Ali's rank is actually in dispute.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proof one argues from the Purification verse (33:33) that the people of the household are equal to the Prophet in purity, and since Ali is the most excellent of them and the Prophet's guardian and successor, likeness to the Prophet is established for him.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proofs two, three and six argue from 'Peace be upon the family of Yasin' (37:130), 'You are the best community brought forth for humankind' (3:110), and 'those who believe and do righteous deeds are the best of creation' (98:7) that these verses address the Prophet's household, and since Ali is first and most excellent among them he is the best of human beings.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Proofs seven and eight argue from 3:33–34 (God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran) and 44:30–32 (God chose the Children of Israel above the worlds) that, since Muhammad is more excellent than all prophets, his family surpasses the family of every prophet in every era, and Ali is the most excellent of that family.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: An objection is reported from opponents of the school: that Umar's removal of 'Hayya ala khayr al-amal' from the adhan is unproven from their books, was in any case a sound exercise of judgment, and that if it were an error then adding 'I testify that our master Ali is the guardian of God' would equally be an error, since adder and subtractor are alike.
entities: Ashhadu anna mawlana Aliyyan waliyy Allah

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The author replies that even conceding both addition and subtraction to be error, the two are not of equal degree, for four reasons: the subtractor misled vastly more people; he preceded al-Hakim by over four centuries and the earlier misleader is more culpable; he not only subtracted but added the ugly sentence 'prayer is better than sleep,' setting prayer against sleep as though comparing a sword to wood; and he dropped the Prophet's phrase from all five prayers while attaching his own only to the dawn prayer.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: The author rejects as void slander the ascription of the guardianship phrase to al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, noting that the Twelver Shia, though differing from him in school, also use it in the call to prayer.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: Against the claim that Umar's subtraction is absent from the opponents' books, the author answers that the disputed soundness and fabricated reports of Sahih al-Bukhari, the other five, and al-Mishkat relieve the people of truth of any need to refute them, and that al-Qadi al-Numan's narration from Jafar al-Sadiq predates those compilations, which may well have suppressed the report to avoid censure.

dropped.section_title: 15. Eight Proofs for the Best of Human Beings
dropped.text: On the origin of the added phrase, the author holds that the testimony to guardianship issued from Ali himself about himself once the office passed to him after the Prophet, just as the Prophet testified to his own prophethood and God testified concerning His own oneness (3:18).

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The compilation cites the Prophet's saying that the earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification except the bathhouse, the cemetery, and the latrine, and the answer affirms that in the outward sense of the Sharia one does not pray in those places at all and no mosque is built beside graves.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: A decisive distinction is drawn between a mosque given over to public use (waqf) and one kept private: a private mosque within a house may be pulled down, relocated or absorbed into the house, while a publicly dedicated mosque may not be demolished by its owner, though nothing is owed if it collapses on its own.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: A man building a congregational or other mosque on his own property does as he wishes and need not seek the governor's permission.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The 'neighbor of the mosque' is defined as one who hears the call to prayer, and while the prayer of any man without congregation counts as a single prayer, it is specifically disliked for the neighbor of the mosque to pray alone at home without an excuse.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The greeting prayer of the mosque is owed only in a mosque open to the people, not in a private place of prayer, and not while an obligatory prayer is owed or outside the times when supererogatory prayer is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: The compilation's answer holds that one who leaves the mosque for a need and returns prays the greeting again, whereas Muhammad ibn al-Fahd rules in his epistle that going out only to the mosque's courtyard or forecourt does not require repeating it, since those areas lie within the mosque's bounds.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Two imams do not lead the same prayer at one time in one assembly, and the leading of prayer is not held in one mosque more than once — except that an imam whose state is broken may appoint a substitute, and a separate congregation praying on the roof is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: One ignorant of the qibla exerts his judgment and prays; if he learns of his error during the prayer and time is short he turns toward the House and completes it provided he was between east and west, but if his back was to the Kaaba only repetition suffices — and if two (or four) directions are equally confused he prays toward both together.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Tawil al-Daaim rules that bringing weapons into mosques is not permitted in the outward sense except for the imam of the mosque on Friday, while Ali is quoted forbidding praying with a sword before one because the qibla is a place of safety.

dropped.section_title: 16. Where a Muslim Stands to Pray
dropped.text: Majalis al-Bayan lists twelve places where prayer is disliked: cemetery, slaughterhouse, bathhouse, latrine, resting places of camels, facing a sleeping person, without a screen, wet impure ground, upon food, places of worship, churches, and Magian houses unless sprinkled with water.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The compiler defines the محدود, whose leadership is barred, as one upon whom the prescribed legal penalty has actually been carried out, and defines the barred 'fettered' man as one bound on the legs or anywhere else.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: A slave learned in jurisprudence may lead when no one more learned is present, and he leads whoever is below him in rank even if they are free men — though when the slave's master is present in the slave's own dwelling the master has the stronger right to lead.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Taqiyya licenses modification but not abandonment of ritual elements: one may omit ربنا لك الحمد before outsiders, and may recite the basmala aloud only so far as to hear himself, but such omission is forbidden for any cause other than taqiyya.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: An imam whose recitation is so distorted that it alters the meanings of the Quran — as by a wrong vowel turning a verse of mercy into one of punishment — may not lead and spoils the prayer, whether the defect comes from lost teeth or ignorance of the points of articulation; and one who recites well is obliged to lead when the people call on him.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Sources differ in degree on the blind imam: al-Ikhtisar and al-Qadi al-Numan permit his leading when there is need and he is set straight, but not as a standing imam, while al-Muntakhaba adds that he may lead only if set straight on a given day; Mukhtasar al-Athar reports that the People of the House disliked his imamate along with that of the leper, the child of adultery, the castrated, the owned slave, the bedouin, the penalized, and the madman.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Two imams are not to be gathered in one undivided place unless the later one is the more excellent — as when a higher licence-holder prays a second congregation of the same prayer in the same house — while a partition removes the objection entirely.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: A follower must never precede the imam in any act, returning to his prior position if he does so by forgetfulness, and the Prophet is reported in al-Majalis al-Hatimiyya as warning that whoever raises his head before the imam risks God transforming his head into a donkey's.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: If an imam's ablution breaks, the prayer is saved only if a substitute is put forward at that very moment before he leaves the mosque, and an imam with unrestricted leave may appoint whomever he wishes even one not otherwise authorized to appoint.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: Rows must be continuous with room for prostration between them, praying alone behind the rows requires repetition, a latecomer finding no place prays alongside the imam rather than in his row, and only the imam's hujja may step level with the imam.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: The Prophet, reported in al-Muizz's interpretation of the Shariah as leading seated after a fall from a horse, told his companions that the imam exists to be followed and that when he prays seated they must all pray seated.

dropped.section_title: 17. Who May Lead, and Who May Not
dropped.text: An imam uncertain how much of the prayer he has completed builds on what is certain and may be corrected by the glorifications of those behind him if they are certain, but if neither he nor they know, he begins the prayer anew.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: The question-and-answer book reports that Ali (ع) recited 'So be patient; the promise of God is true' during prayer not as the opening of that surah but specifically to silence and rebuke Ibn al-Kawwa, who kept raising his voice.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: In the madhhab of the Ahl al-Bayt, the long portions of al-mufassal run from al-Hujurat to al-Mujadila, the middle from al-Mujadila to 'Amma yatasa'alun', and the short from 'Amma yatasa'alun' to al-Nas.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: The same source lists acts that break the covenant, including abandoning prayer or prescribed works without excuse, disbelieving a believer's oath after accusing him, fornication, killing a believer, reviling the summoner or his appointee, and refusing the summoner's call to strive with person and wealth.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Per Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, if the intention for prayer slips away — through preoccupation, forgetfulness or anything else — before one enters the prayer, the prayer afterwards does not suffice; and one may not recite inwardly what the tongue has not uttered.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: On the tashahhuds, performing the first does not excuse one from the second, but the second does suffice in place of the first.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Postural rulings are specified by source: the woman places her hands above her knees on her thighs so as not to raise her hindquarters (al-Akhbar); those behind the imam answer 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise' quietly, except the appointed relayer who raises his voice with it and the takbir but not the tasbih (Tawil al-Daaim); and the sitter folds his left leg beneath him and keeps the right upright (Tawil al-Daaim, outward sense).

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: In the jurisprudential exchange between Shaykh Hasan ibn Mawla Adam al-Hindi and the sayyids of Yemen, the prayer of a woman who has not undergone khafd is valid and intimacy with her is permissible, and likewise for the man, though the sunnah is to hasten to it.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes those who profess walaya yet never prostrate in a single rakah, citing the Prophet's 'between the servant and unbelief is abandoning the prayer' and Ali's 'there is no portion in Islam for one who abandons the prayer' to conclude that such a person holds no share of Islam.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman divides the neglecters of prayer into two kinds — people of tribal temper absorbed in themselves with animal nature dominant, and people of arrogance and coarse insolence, especially the women — and holds both kinds to be found in every school of Islam and every religion, adding that even unbelievers, including those of India, perform some inherited worship, so that such arrogance falls under the Quranic threat against those too proud to worship God, the path on which Iblis perished.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman argues that worship benefits only the worshipper, God having no need of it, since He created jinn and mankind to worship Him for their own benefit, and that no one has a claim of walaya to the friends of God except by holding fast to the hem of the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: The lists of obligations differ by source: Tawil al-Shariah gives seven — first takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, tasbih, greeting, taslim — while the Dai Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives seven as intention, first takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, taslim, and the Majalis al-Mustansiriyya gives intention, turning to the qibla, takbirat al-ihram, recitation of the Opening, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the salutation.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah forbids moving the foot or speaking from the opening takbir to the taslim, cites the Prophet on prostrating upon seven members, and prohibits reciting while bowing, disturbing pebbles, turning like a fox, squatting like a monkey, pecking like a crow, and drooping the head below the level of the back.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives the prayer four limits — place, time, purity, intention — with five daily prayers of seventeen rakahs divided into obligation and sunnah, and interprets 'the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed' esoterically to mean the one who abandons my legatee is banished from God's mercy, adding that the outward prayer itself neither forbids nor commands.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya lists twelve sunnahs within each of the five prayers, ending with the rule that any prayer lacking a first sitting has a qunut counted in its place, while any prayer with two tashahhud sittings has no qunut.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Ali's Four Hundred Etiquettes forbids clasping the hands while standing in prayer as resembling the People of the Book, rules that gross turning about cuts off the prayer and requires beginning again with adhan, iqama and takbir, and directs sitting between the two prostrations until the limbs are still, turning to the right on leaving the prayer, and making oneself hear the recitation when praying alone.

dropped.section_title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
dropped.text: Answering Muhammad Ali ibn Salih al-Badri of India, the master Hibat Allah rules that since no text from the friends of God forbids reciting the two surahs of refuge in obligatory prayer, such a prayer is complete — one who recited al-Nas in the first rakah repeats it in the last, one who recited al-Ikhlas in the first recites al-Falaq in the second — but one should not deliberately recite in this manner, putting it in the position of the sunnah.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: A question-and-answer book arranged by the chapters of the Pillars of Islam reports that, per the books of the guiding call, no supplication — neither the supplication of drawing near nor any other — is recited after the afternoon prayer, yet whoever does supplicate incurs no sin.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The same source rules that wiping the face at the place of prostration is permitted only after the afternoon and dawn prayers, as the masters commanded and as received from the pure Imams, and that supplication after the afternoon prayer is not prolonged though prolonging it incurs nothing.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The book on the interpretation of the Sharia sets the rule that daytime prayers are recited quietly while night prayers — including dawn, offered in the last darkness — are recited aloud.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The author of the Mustansiriyya Councils, in the Eleventh Council, follows the jurisprudence of prayer — where the outward gets exposition and the inward its sign and intimation — with the closing supplication and its seven and its twelve.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Each of the seven supplications has a corresponding mention in the Quran, to be brought forward later, since what has been set down so far is only roots awaiting branches and fruit.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his Four Hundred Etiquettes, teaches that God answers supplication when He is remembered, that the gates of heaven open at six times (rainfall, the advance in battle, the call to prayer, Quranic recitation, the sun's decline, and daybreak), that supplication turns back even a firmly settled decree, that it should be used to repel affliction before it descends, and that one who supplicates without deeds is an archer with no bowstring.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Ali also states that whoever recites Sura al-Ikhlas ten times and Sura al-Qadr before sunrise will be touched by no sin however hard Iblis strives.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The question-and-answer book rules on incidental acts in prayer: deliberate throat-clearing without excuse cuts off the prayer (the imam must instead be alerted by words of glorification or a gesture) and habitual deliberate throat-clearing requires repeating the prayer; a woman may not occupy herself in prayer with carrying her child to quiet him; food placed in the mouth out of necessity for pain incurs nothing; a braid wound inside the turban is permissible since the forbidden binding is turning the hair back on its root to the middle of the head.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: Holding a gemstone, dirham or similar in the mouth or hand does not void the prayer if it does not prevent proper formation of the letters or fulfilment of the prayer's limits, though being free of all such things is more fitting; and the abridgment of the compiled book holds that eating or drinking in prayer, whether forgetful or deliberate, cuts off the prayer.

dropped.section_title: 19. Supplication, Speech, and Silence
dropped.text: The interpretation of the Sharia further holds that recitation precedes bowing, that one must not raise his voice above the imam's, that noon and afternoon are recited quietly and the night prayer aloud, that the Prophet forbade wiping over leather socks and forbade omitting the audible basmala, and that once the opening magnification is pronounced the worshipper does not speak until the salutation.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: On figured rugs and garments the section preserves two differing answers: one respondent permits prayer so long as the image does not occupy the worshipper's attention (except that he does not pray toward images), while another answer states that prayer on or in figured cloth is not permitted when the figures are seen, and permitted only when they are not seen.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Dyed garments and deep red cloth belong to the domain of etiquette (adab) and do not invalidate the prayer of either a man or a woman, with the sole exception that pure silk is disliked for men.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Because the whole of a woman is 'awra, any exposure of her awra during prayer invalidates it, whether she knew of the ruling or was ignorant of it — a ruling applied explicitly to the women of the people of the dawa in India who do not wear the long shift and head-veil.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: The abridgment of the Musannaf draws a distinction by sex: a man who prays with his awra uncovered unknowingly repeats the prayer only once he learns of it, whereas a free or slave woman's prayer is spoiled whether she knew or not.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Prayer is valid only in pure garments, and impurity requires stripping it off; one who has only an impure garment and no water prays in it and repeats when a clean garment or water is found, and one with two garments, one impure but unidentified, must pray the prayer in each with the intention of fulfilling the obligation.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: One who prays and afterwards finds his garment was impure must repeat the prayer, whether or not its time has passed, if he had known of the impurity beforehand.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: On head covering the sources differ in emphasis: one ruling says a man should not pray bareheaded without turban or mantle but may do so if he finds neither, while Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in the book of the obligations and limits of religion that it is lawful for a man to uncover his head and pray bareheaded.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Slave women, women under a contract of manumission, women freed at their master's death, and girls who have not yet menstruated may pray without a head covering, but one freed without knowing it must repeat every prayer she prayed uncovered after her freedom.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Idris ibn al-Hasan, answering Shaykh Yusuf ibn Ismail ibn Ibrahim al-Samati al-Hindi, grounds the surface rule in the Prophet's saying that the earth was made a place of prostration and a means of purification, concluding that prayer is not valid upon anything of the earth with which dry ablution (tayammum) is not permitted.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Obligatory prayer is not permitted upon stone, unbaked brick and the like — only supererogatory and sunna prayer — while there is no harm in prostrating upon plaster over which carrion was burned, since the fire has purified it, and the interpretation of the Sharia holds there is no prayer except upon the earth or what grows from it.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: The interpretation of the Daaim glosses disputed phrases of the source text: praying in a single thick belted shirt so that the private part does not appear when bowing; the garment worn 'like the two wings of the swallow' when nothing else is found; and the forbidden ishtimal al-samma' wrap, which is rejected because it physically prevents placing the palms, bowing, prostrating and raising the hands, leaving the prayer incomplete.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred counsels of etiquette, forbids standing before God except in a clean garment, forbids praying in a loosely draped shirt as the practice of the people of Lot, forbids prostrating upon an image or a rug containing one, forbids knotting an image-bearing dirham into the garment while praying (though coins in a clean money belt or cloth are permitted), and forbids prostrating upon heaps of wheat, barley, any edible thing, or bread.

dropped.section_title: 20. What the Worshipper Wears and Stands Upon
dropped.text: Minor supplementary rulings are recorded: carrying wrought or unwrought gold and silver in the waistband does not affect the prayer; something in the mouth or hand is harmless if it does not impede the letters or the limits of prayer though being free of it is better; henna for adornment is commanded for women and better left by men without being sinful; prayer is invalid in camel resting places but permitted in sheep folds once swept and sprinkled; a net does not substitute for a mantle since shift and veil suffice only if thick; and a small amount of milk, butter or egg white from filth-fed animals is permitted.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: The compiler reports the ruling that Friday prayer is established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them, and that if the distance is less than three miles it is established in only one, whether the mosques stand in one city or in two.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Support for this is drawn from al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali, who instructed that prayer behind a nasib or haruri not be counted, and that such a leader be treated as a pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have put Muawiya's governor forward to lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the compiler explains as the practice of the People of the House in dissimulation, one Imam having said 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: A distinction is drawn: 'the unjust' in the sermon means one appointed among the summoners in whom injustice has appeared — behind him prayer is still obligatory, but the people must bring the matter before the holder of authority and await his response.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited for rulings of precedence and procedure: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims excels prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a sale then made is not annulled; and detailed remedies are given for broken purity, omitted sitting between sermons, and congregations that disperse mid-prayer.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the prayer, the prayer is two cycles, the sermon is divided by a sitting, the raised voice distinguishes it from the ordinary noon prayer, and the call to stand comes after the sermon.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah further equates the conduct of respondents in the assembly of the summoner with that of the Friday congregation: silence and listening are obligatory, and the respondent may not press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who knows better how to raise his children.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Points of Conduct names three hours for seeking a need from God: Friday at the sun's zenith, when the winds blow and the gates of heaven open, and the last hour of night at dawn, when two angels call out for the repentant, the asker, and the seeker of forgiveness.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: On the festivals, 'tashriq' is glossed as the prayer of the two festivals, so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq, and it is not incumbent on the traveler except in a congregational city.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: Festival practice is specified: a congregation of five including the Imam as with Friday; the washing is a prophetic practice from dawn to the sun's zenith; hands are raised at every magnification; the festival prayer is not prayed in congregation at Mina but individually, as verified from Idris ibn Hasan.

dropped.section_title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
dropped.text: He adds that the festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, that the breaking-of-the-fast sermon uniquely follows the prayer as a sign that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles, and that every sermon opens with praise except the sermon of the day of sacrifice, which opens with four magnifications.
entities: festival of the breaking of the fast

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The author distinguishes omission from doubt: the one who commits an omission is certain of what he omitted, while the doubter is not certain of what he doubts — a confusion said to trouble many jurists.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The two prostrations of omission are called al-marghamatan ('the two that rub down the nose') because they rub down the nose of the devil when the corruption of forgetfulness is repaired by them.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted from his four hundred manners: whoever is certain of something and is then struck by doubt should act on his certainty, for doubt neither dispels nor diminishes certainty.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: If the doubter is certain of nothing at all — not knowing whether he added to or fell short of his prayer — he begins the prayer again from the beginning, and so likewise does the Imam.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The responsa hold that intention resides in the heart and that utterance with the tongue is merely a verbal expression, so that an act intended in the heart is complete even if the intention is never spoken — cited as stated in the Pillars, against the text that deeds are accepted only with intentions.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The prostration of omission is not multiplied: one who omits several obligations, or commits omissions repeatedly in a single prayer, owes only the two prostrations.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Where there is no explicit text stipulating a prostration of omission — as with neglecting the first tashahhud but remembering before the salaam, or repeating a single surah after the Opening — the worshipper is not required to prostrate, though he should not do such things deliberately.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: Some omissions void the prayer outright rather than being repaired: failing to sit after each pair of rakahs, adding a bowing before sitting for the tashahhud, and neglecting the bowing or the opening takbir behind the Imam, which the Imam does not bear.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: On interruption, the Prophet's reported saying that three things interrupt the prayer — a woman, a donkey, and a black dog — is set beside his own account of seeing these pass before him, when he said nothing interrupts the prayer of a believer but 'ward off what you are able'; and Ali is quoted that smiling does not interrupt the prayer while loud laughter does.

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: The latecomer who reaches the Imam in the bowing, before the Imam raises his head, attains that rakah with a single takbir serving for both opening and bowing, provided he contracts the intention in his heart — as stated by Muhammad ibn Fahd in his epistle The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided.
entities: The Broad Road of the Path of Guidance for the Rightly Guided

dropped.section_title: 22. Forgetting, Doubting, and Beginning Again
dropped.text: One who joins the Imam even only for the opening takbir before the salaam must perform the two prostrations for his Imam's omission, and one praying the remainder alone prostrates for his own errors.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib is reported to have instructed that boys be taught the prayer and held to it when they reach eight years, and taught that by which God will benefit their teachers.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Ibrahim ibn Husayn al-Hamidi in عبارة البشارة reports from Amir al-Muminin that a boy sheds his milk teeth at seven, reaches maturity at fourteen, completes his physical growth at twenty-one, and completes his intellect at twenty-eight.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: مختصر الآثار directs that children be separated in their sleeping places at that stage, as a precaution since they have neared maturity and the stirring of desire.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: A traveler completes (does not shorten) his prayer and fast by stopping five prayer times with a blood relative of lineage or with his resident wife, but not through his wife's relatives nor through kin by nursing.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Travel distances are defined: the barid is four farsakhs, the farsakh three miles, and the mile three thousand cubits, being a thousand even paces of a single leg.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: The limit of residence that obliges praying in full is ten days, and Muhammad ibn Fahd rules in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين that one who travels a barid intending return should commit to ten days and pray in full, and may still return earlier without invalidating those prayers.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Whoever enters Mecca prays in full and does not shorten, on the basis of the Quranic words 'the resident and the visitor stand equal' — though Sayyidina Ismail ibn Hiba held that full prayer applies only within the sanctuary of the House of God and that in Mecca itself the prayer is shortened.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: أنس الأفئدة المنيبة records Amir al-Muminin ruling that six categories do not shorten prayer or fast: circuit-traveling collectors, merchants moving market to market, princes touring their emirate, hunters, shepherds seeking rain-watered land, and warriors who cut the road.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: A traveler may lead residents (saluting after two rakahs while they rise to complete) and a mutayammim may lead those who performed ablution, but both dispensations are particular to the people of the high ranks and do not extend to the rest of the hudud.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sayyidina Sulayman's performing tayammum in Haraz, after descending from the fortress of Tayba, and then leading the congregation is cited as the precedent establishing that dispensation when a weighty matter requires it for the good of the dawa.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states in كتاب الرضاع الباطن that shortening applies to the three four-rakah prayers — the first, the afternoon, and the late evening — reducing twelve rakahs by six.

dropped.section_title: 23. Children, Travelers, and the Sick
dropped.text: مختصر المصنف rules that one who loses his reason through something he drank or did to himself must repeat the prayers missed in that state, whether the act was obedient or disobedient.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Responding to perplexity over a solar eclipse observed early in a month (Dhu al-Qadah 837) against the Brethren of Purity's claim that solar eclipses occur only at month's end, the answer transmitted from the author of the letters and the pure Imams is that lunar eclipses fall at the dawn of the 15th or 16th while solar eclipses may occur at the beginning or the end of the month, the matter being in God's hand.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: A latecomer who joins the imam's eclipse prayer counts his joining as the start of his own prayer, prostrates and bows along with the imam, sits poised rather than settled during the imam's testimony, and after the imam's salutation rises to complete the remaining bowings, qunut, prostration, testimony and salutation, not counting the first two prostrations made with the imam.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The book of purity rules that the eclipse prayer is prayed only when the eclipse is actually seen with the eye, never on the word of an astrologer or anyone else, and not if cloud or another veil intervenes.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: In the prayer of fear, when swords cross and spears are thrust, prayers are reduced to takbir — one takbir in place of each bowing — and the takbir is itself shortened as shortening is obligatory in it; مختصر المصنف adds that the fear prayer requires at least three men praying with three standing guard, since the word 'party' does not apply to fewer than three.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: If eclipse prayer, funeral prayer and fear coincide for the imam, he prays over the funeral and prays both the eclipse prayer and the prayer of fear.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: For the rain prayer the cited books prescribe a hundred takbirs facing the people, a hundred glorifications to the right, a hundred declarations of oneness to the left, all aloud, then a hundred praises; two sermons as at the two feasts, delivered leaning on an Arabian bow as the Messenger of God did; going out on a day other than Monday is harmless, and whoever preaches before the prayer must pray and then preach again.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The qunut is a supplication not to be abandoned deliberately: deliberate omission in the witr requires repetition, while forgetting it requires no repetition (there being no prostrations of forgetfulness in sunnah prayers), and its minimum is three glorifications or three takbirs; it is recited after the words 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.'

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: On whether the witr may be divided by salutation, the answer cites Judge al-Numan's المنتخبة that the witr may be separated by the salutation without actions or speech, though unavoidable brief speech does no harm.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: The shaf and witr may validly be prayed during the first dawn (called by the Arabs ذنب السرحان) so long as the true dawn has not spread across the sky.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
