dropped.text: Muhammad ibn Fahd rules in لاحبة سبيل الهدى للمهتدين that one who prayed shaf, witr and then dawn only to learn it was still night keeps his shaf and witr and must repeat both sunnah and obligation of dawn, unless dawn was close upon him, in which case the sunnah also stands — because the books of the friends of God permit praying it before dawn for an inner meaning.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: معالم الدين holds the witr obligatory with no dispensation for abandoning it, counting it among the appendages of the obligatory prayers even though it is a sunnah.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Praying tarawih behind an imam for the sake of protective concealment (taqiyyah) is permitted with the intention of a voluntary prayer, but the believers do not take him as a leader, and anything of the sunnah omitted for concealment must be made up; reliance in such matters is upon الدعائم as the gathering place of the questions.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman rules that Mawlana al-Sadiq gave a text for the prayer of Umm Daud only for the month of Rajab, plus the day of 'Arafah (especially when it falls on a Friday), so Qasim ibn Fir's command to his Daudi followers to pray, fast and supplicate with it in Rabi al-Awwal and Ramadan of 1042 lacks a supporting text — no practice being valid without a text, since 'little practice in a sunnah is better than much practice in an innovation.'

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Hibat Allah ibn Ibrahim answered from Yemen to Hind in 1135 that the prayer of the prophets and Imams at times of calamity — praise and thanksgiving for what God disclosed to them, knowing nothing occurs save by decree — may be prayed by their followers at all times when sunnah and voluntary prayers are permitted, prohibition applying only to the forbidden times.

dropped.section_title: 24. Eclipse, Fear, Rain, and the Night Vigil
dropped.text: Regarding the Quranic prostration, the binding verses oblige prostration even when recited within a supplication and oblige all present to prostrate (though not a second time for a repeat in the same place), whereas for the remaining verses prostration is optional though better, and a teacher passing over the places while instructing boys has a choice.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The compiler defines the dying state (al-naz') as the moment when death draws near and the passage from this world to the hereafter is at hand, citing the book of the interpretation of the pillars.
entities: book of the interpretation of the pillars

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Asked by Shaykh Yusuf ibn Isma'il al-Samiti al-Hindi whether people may move from place to place fleeing epidemic and plague, the master Idris ibn Hasan answered that they may go wherever they wish, since the matter is in Allah's hand.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Ja'far ibn Sulayman's epistle 'The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations', written to admonish his heedless people among those of the island of Yemen after he settled among them, is the compiler's main source here for rebuking communal faults.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in the Nullifying of Innovations

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Against slowness in visiting the sick, the epistle cites the Pillars of Islam on the authority of the Commander of the Faithful that seventy thousand angels pray for a Muslim who visits a sick person from the hour of the visit until sunset or sunrise.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The Prophet forbade a visitor to eat in the sick person's presence, Allah rendering such a visit (in another wording, its reward) worthless, because the visitor burdens one already burdened and galls a household possibly of slender means; whoever knows this must teach those who do not.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Asked whether lifespans are fixed with Allah without increase or decrease despite books speaking of both, the answer given is that lifespans are appointed and neither increase nor decrease, while the sense of increase and decrease is valid in that what is diminished in the past cycle is added in the future one.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Asked about the saying that the wretched is he whom the Hour overtakes alive and not yet dead, the answer is that what is intended is the Hour overtaking him while he is still in the animal (bahimi) condition — not yet passed into the angelic life.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Husayn ibn Idris, answering Hasan ibn Nuh's tenth question, ruled that if a pregnant woman dies with a living formed child, a skilled woman present must extract it when possible or when the child is six months or more with hope of life; otherwise the mother is not buried until the child's death is confirmed.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: From 'Ali's four hundred points of conduct the compiler gathers counsels on death: remember death often so calamities sit lightly; fever is death's forerunner and Allah's prison that strips sins as hair is stripped from the camel's pores; and no Shi'i who has departed from a prohibition dies before an affliction in wealth, child, or self purges his sins, so that hardship at death is itself expiation and the dead of the Shi'a is a truthful witness.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Practices around the corpse such as placing weapons beside the dead or treating the night-vigil beside the body as obligatory are dismissed in the questions-and-answers book as having no reliance placed upon them, and the abridged compendium forbids shaving hair, lighting lamps, or cutting nails for the dead.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Ja'far ibn Sulayman condemns as innovation the organized wailing over the dead — women gathering for nights and days as if it were a divine prescription, with singing, diversion and play exceeding even the limits allowed at weddings — disgracing the community before Allah and His friends though they are the cream and kernel of the world.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The prohibition is supported by Ja'far ibn Muhammad's deathbed bequest that no cheek be struck and no collar torn for him (a woman who tears her collar has a rent in Hell enlarged each time she adds to it), by 'Ali's letter to Rifa'ah ibn Shaddad his judge over al-Ahwaz to forbid wailing where he holds authority, and by the Prophet's saying that two voices are accursed — howling at calamity and a voice raised at a blessing, meaning wailing and singing.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The story of 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah shows the dead and dying are punished by the living's laments: he saw an angel with a fiery iron mace that struck at his head whenever a woman shrieked 'O my mountain!' or 'O my strength!' unless he answered that Allah, not he, was her mountain — the Prophet confirming, 'What ails your dead, that they suffer by the words of your living?'

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: Correspondingly, singing is forbidden except in the licensed case of banquets and weddings, where the tambourine publicizes marriage and distinguishes lawful nikah from sifah — the Prophet approving music at the Banu Zurayq wedding and saying there is no secret marriage until smoke is seen or a tambourine heard.

dropped.section_title: 25. The Sickbed and the Sound of Mourning
dropped.text: The proper mourning conduct commanded is that households speak well over their dead, following Fatimah, who when the daughters of Hashim mourned with her at her father's death said 'Grieve with restraint and hold fast to supplication'; and whoever strikes his thigh at a calamity forfeits his reward.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The washing of the dead requires the ablution to be performed three times along with three washings, though performing the ablution at the last washing suffices, as stated in the Book of Reports; and one wounded who is not lifted from his place and lives on for a time is not washed.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: When water is scarce, the man in a state of janabah takes the water and the dead is given tayammum; yet a washer in janabah may still wash the dead, performing tayammum first if washing would harm him, when no one else is available.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Per the Mukhtasar of al-Musannif the nearest person present has the best right to wash the dead, a martyr in janabah is washed on that account, a dead man found unmarked is washed, treated with hanut and shrouded, and no hair is shaved nor nail trimmed from a corpse.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The Mukhtasar al-Athar rules that the drowned, the burned, and any severed part without which a man could not have lived are washed; detached limbs are washed, each set in its place, and buried with the body.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The best shroud, per Jafar ibn Muhammad in The Pillars of Islam, is three garments — a shirt neither buttoned nor hemmed, a wrapping sheet, and a waist wrapper — and the better course is that washing, above all of a woman, be done within a covering.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The 'ajrah mentioned by al-Qadi al-Numan is defined as gathering the shirt at the navel and tucking it into the izar's fastening, serving, like the head covering, as a mark of distinction between men and women.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Counsels require washing for whoever touches the corpse after it grows cold, which the questions-and-answers book explains as meaning after death has come and the sunnah washing has been done, because the corpse's moisture renders a living person impure.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: For conjoined twins, separation is permitted only when slight and safe; if one dies, whatever adheres to the living is cut from the dead provided the living feels no pain, but if pain is felt their life and death are counted as one.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The shroud and outfitting are the first charge on the estate — before debt and bequest — and must be taken according to the deceased's station even if the debt exceeds the estate.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Hanut is any perfume, placed on the places of prostration and named parts of the body, with wars and saffron excluded for men but used for women; camphor accompanies it, and Quran is recited seven days for people of rank and three for others.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Per the Tawil al-Daaim only the shroud and the place of washing are incensed, and Ali's Counsels forbid incensing or perfuming the dead with anything but camphor because the dead man is in the position of one consecrated for pilgrimage — hence one who died in ihram has head and face uncovered and no perfume brought near.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Walking before the bier is disliked only for an enemy of the family, because angels of wrath attend it, while for believers any position is permissible since angels of mercy encompass it — though walking behind remains more excellent; the call to prayer at the bier was disliked but announcing the death without a public call was permitted.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The funeral prayer is a communal obligation on every Muslim who knows of it, may be offered anywhere and even in the disliked hours or at an eclipse, with the supplication between takbirs optional for the follower; it is offered over martyrs, grave sinners, the executed, and even the suicide.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: In the absence of the imam of the age, precedence in the funeral prayer belongs to his appointed judge or officeholder, then to the highest in station among those he has advanced, and only if none is present to the most entitled guardian; and a man's prayer accords better with the teaching of the People of the House than a woman leading women.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: The dead is buried in the town where he dies and not carried elsewhere, except from open wilderness to the nearest burial ground; burial in another's land requires his leave, but once done he may claim only the value of the grave plots and may not have the bodies removed.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Baked brick, stone or whatever is available may be placed over the dead despite the dislike of the people of the outward sense, and this is to be relied on except where prudent concealment requires otherwise.

dropped.section_title: 26. Washing, Shrouding, Carrying, Burying
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib counselled visiting the graves of those who have a claim upon one and seeking provision there, since the dead rejoice at such visits, a man asking his need at his parents' graves after praying for them.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The section begins the Book of Zakat, gathering what has been handed down on the merit of giving zakat and its attendant matters.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman, in the book of inward nursing, cites the Prophet's word that charity is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman states that one whose role in the call, after discharging what is incumbent, is that his excellence appear outwardly through abundance of wealth, pays from his wealth what he wills — apart from the fitra — of obligatory rights and voluntary giving.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Mansur al-Yaman draws the distinction that paying the khums excuses one from the tithe except voluntarily, while paying the tithe alone does not excuse the khums, because the tithe does not encompass the khums as the khums encompasses the tithe.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Prophet is cited as saying there is no prayer for one who does not pay zakat, and that the one who withholds zakat is in the Fire.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the Hidden Epistle, lists ten things on which God imposed zakat: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, dates, raisins, wheat, barley, and grains.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib in his Four Hundred Counsels says to treat the sick with charity and fortify wealth with zakat.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils' twelfth council teaches that zakat has seven obligations and twelve sunnahs, matching the number of the clauses of the testimony and its letters, and that zakat must be received by the Imam and is taken from seven things: gold, silver, camels, cows, sheep, crops, and minerals.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils enumerate the eight named recipients falling into seven divisions — the poor and needy, the collectors, those whose hearts are reconciled, the freeing of necks, the debt-burdened among the people of allegiance, the way of God as an obligation of sufficiency, and the wayfarer understood as those cut off from the road of guidance.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The twelve sunnahs include the passing of a year, nisabs of twenty dinars of gold, two hundred dirhams of silver, five grazing camels, thirty grazing cows and forty sheep, taking from the middling livestock, not joining what is separate nor dividing what is joined, not taking the stud animal, giving from crops below the five-awsaq nisab by bundle and handful on the day of harvest per the Quranic verse, and no zakat on dwellings, ornaments, or things for use.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: In the questions-and-answers book arranged after Daaim al-Islam, the ruling on concealing zakat from the imam is said to concern one who brings out only part of it, whereas one who withholds it entirely has abandoned the obligation altogether.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Asked whether the Prophet's saying that charity is unlawful for 'we, the people of the House' refers to the Imams or to all his descendants through Fatima, the answer given is that it refers to the Imams.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The hamala, named among the five for whom charity is lawful in Daaim al-Islam, is explained as either a penalty imposed by a tyrannical ruler or the bearing of blood money on behalf of the 'aqila.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: Interpreting Ali's covenant to Muhnaf ibn Sulaym, the answer holds that zakat is not demanded from one seized by the enemy who is not of the Shia holding to the allegiance, and that handing zakat to other than the one God commanded does not suffice, even if it is later plundered or stolen, until it reaches the guardian of the affair or his appointee.

dropped.section_title: 27. The Wealth That Is Not Yours
dropped.text: The Mustansiriyya Councils hold that one who keeps the outward prayer and believes its inner reality yet does not spend the zakat of his wealth, the khums of his earnings, the purchase of his own self, and the redemption of his pledge falls short of those God describes as spending from what He provided them.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: In the responsa attributed to our master Idris, the obligations owed from a deceased person's estate are discharged in a fixed order: zakat first (because it is a debt upon him and not part of his wealth), then the Hajj, then the khums, then the expiation, then al-Shurwa.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The answer holds that the Hajj takes precedence over inheritance because it is a debt, and debt comes before inheritance; the remaining obligatory duties bind likewise if the wealth suffices for them and something still remains for the heir.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Khums must be brought out of the capital even where no bequest was made, and if the heirs are God-fearing it is their duty to discharge it for the deceased and so purify the wealth — but if they refuse, the answer invokes 'There is no compulsion in religion' rather than coercion.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The limit of 'means' (for al-Shurwa liability) is defined as ownership of wealth on which zakat falls due after the hawl, namely two hundred dirhams or twenty gold dinars, with each dirham reckoned at fourteen and two-fifths carats of silver and each dinar at twenty-four carats, converted into Arab and Gujarati weights.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Because the relative price of gold and silver varies by age according to people's desire, the answer counsels that the believer holding to his religion should reckon his nisab by whichever of the two coinages is the lesser in price.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Once khums has been paid from the capital, no khums is owed on profit except on what remains in hand; paying khums on the whole profit is declared a merit, not a binding obligation.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that an undivided estate is not assessed for zakat as a whole but share by share — each heir whose share reaches a nisab pays, and one whose share does not (and who has no other wealth) owes nothing — and that a debtor pays zakat only on the excess of his wealth over his debt.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Al-Akhbar reports that there is no zakat in the wealth of an orphan or of one lacking his reason, and Tawil al-Daaim interprets this to mean no zakat is due from the owner holding it for himself, while whatever of it is held for trade is valued and does bear zakat.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Tawil al-Sharia reports that Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah taught that zakat is five dirhams for five classes of poor and that it is mutual consolation, all creation being as a single soul whose limbs turn to heal an afflicted limb — adding that if anyone were untouched by defect, death would never reach him.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad in al-Risala al-Maknuna sets out the graduated livestock scales — camels from five (a sheep) through bint makhad, bint labun, hiqqa and jadha, cattle at tabi and musinna, and sheep from forty — with the rule that nothing defective and not the flock's ram is taken in charity.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: On the nisab of grains, the answer distinguishes two positions: the Pillars holds that zakat is due from everything the earth brings forth (and the masters' practice, to be followed, took the tenth from little and much), while the Sharia sets the nisab at five awsaq, the wasq being sixty sa.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Al-Akhbar distinguishes land of the tenth (Arab land not advanced upon with horse or beast, and mountain land cultivated by its own people without great-river water, plus land whose warring people submitted while still on it) from land of kharaj (Sudanese and mountain lands taken and cultivated by force), and holds that a land's ruling does not change with the religion of its purchaser because the obligation attaches to the produce, not the owner.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: The Book of the Inner Nursing treats the tenth as an outward ruling by which the Messenger judged, and holds that one who truly pays a tenth while keeping back only nine tenths has discharged his outward obligation even unasked by the ruler, whereas one who withholds and keeps more than nine tenths has not truly rendered obedience to the ruler over his outward affairs.

dropped.section_title: 28. Gold, Herds, and Harvest
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad cites Q. 8:41 to identify five stations to which the khums is directed — God and the Messenger, the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer — and states that khums is taken from mines, treasures, and spoils, with al-Sadiq reporting that the Prophet took his share of spoils and divided the rest among those categories.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: A fatwa collection arranged by the chapters of the Book of the Pillars addresses the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) for the fitra and taking their monetary value, and answers that the reliance is on the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: A transmitted saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: The answer concedes latitude: whoever mixes his fitra from everything he ate during Ramadan has discharged it, and whoever ate nothing but barley may give barley.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: On paying the fitra before Ramadan out of fear of poverty or travel — objected to because obligatory acts may not be done outside their appointed times — the answer is that delivering it to a rightful recipient suffices, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it and the obligation is simply its delivery; the only prohibition is that one not break the fast before delivering it.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes the zakat of Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Reports state the zakat of Fitr is paid for the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion holds it due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars records that it has also been said to be paid for a child still in the womb.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: The measure of the sa is given as four and a half ratls by the Meccan ratl, five ratls less a third by the Medinan ratl, and nine and a tenth by the Baghdadi ratl, with the Selected Book allowing a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house.

dropped.section_title: 29. The Charity of the Head
dropped.text: Two puzzle-rulings close the section: a man owning a thousand dinars while owing a thousand dinars owes no zakat on it, and a polytheist who finds no Muslim to whom to hand his zakat has more right to it than anyone else.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited as stating that fasting is a shield from the Fire covering the tongue, hearing, eyes and all limbs, so that fasting is not food and drink alone: each limb has its portion, and whoever abandons part of it diminishes the merit of his fast proportionally.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: The same source is cited as holding that fasting Ramadan is obligatory upon every Muslim, man or woman, who is of age, sound of mind, healthy and resident, and that there is no fasting for a hypocrite who is disobedient to God.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Al-Idah is cited as restricting the rulings about fasting upon sighting the crescent to one who is absent from the presence of the Imam and does not know the measures of the crescents.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Jafar ibn Sulayman, in his epistle The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes them for failing to honor Ramadan as God and His Messenger prescribed.
entities: The Sharpest Sword in Nullifying Innovations

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: His specific charge is that the month must be named with the word 'month' placed before it — 'the month of Ramadan', as in the Quranic phrase shahr Ramadan — and that calling it 'Ramadan' alone is unseemly, since one does not address a person dear to him without an honorific word before his name.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: He supports this by al-Qadi al-Numan's Mukhtasar al-Athar al-Sharif, which reports Imam al-Baqir Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali as saying: do not say 'Ramadan', but say as God said, 'the month of Ramadan'.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: He argues that one who has heard this saying and then turns from it makes light of God, of His noble month and of al-Baqir's weighty word, and that one who transmits the book while not acting on it falls under the Quranic censure 'why do you say what you do not do?'

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Tawil al-Shariah is cited as holding that fasting becomes obligatory upon a boy once he can tell his right hand from his left.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Zaid ibn Muhammad, in the Concealed Epistle, is cited as stating that God imposed fasting the month of Ramadan after prayer and zakat, commanding one month out of twelve, and that this obligatory fast is thirty days.

dropped.section_title: 30. A Shield Against the Fire
dropped.text: Ali ibn Abi Talib is quoted from his Four Hundred Manners as saying that fasting three days of every month and fasting Shaban drive away the whisperings of the breast and the disquiet of the heart.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Sulayman ibn Hasan, in his epistle the Ijadiyya, explains that after the moon has traveled twenty-eight stations from the sun it needs two further stations to overtake the sun, since the sun has itself advanced two stations and a degree, so the meeting occurs at thirty stations, which the reckoners count as one month.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The opposing claim, refuted by al-Muayyad fil-Din in the forty-second of the Wisdom Sessions, is that Ramadan is sometimes complete and sometimes deficient and that its fast depends on sighting, argued from the Prophet's words 'Fast when it is seen and break your fast when it is seen; and if it is hidden, complete thirty.'

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Two legal grounds deny that the Prophet himself sought the crescent: Gabriel came to him morning and evening with certain tidings from heaven, making search superfluous, and he said 'I know the roads of the sky better than you know the roads of the earth,' which searching would contradict.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The rational ground is that the Prophet knew crescent risings differ by degree and by terrain (high places sight it sooner, low places later), so he could not have imposed one sighting standard on all people, since one day cannot be Shaban where the crescent is unseen and Ramadan where it is seen.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Scriptural proof is drawn from 'Fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you' — those before being the Christians, who fast by calculation not sighting — and from 'a counted number of days,' since days always counted require no observation.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Shaban's deficiency is proved by its genuine mid-night, the fifteenth, with fourteen nights on either side, whereas Ramadan admits no true midpoint — the fifteenth leaves fifteen days after it and sixteen is not half of thirty.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The expiation for willfully breaking the fast — two consecutive months, sixty days, or feeding sixty poor — matches a thirty-day Ramadan; were Ramadan twenty-nine, the expiation would allow fifty-eight poor persons.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: In an anecdote from his autobiography, al-Muayyad fil-Din, before King Abu Kalijar al-Daylami, answered a Zaydi sharif who cited the Prophet's finger-counting 'We are unlettered; we do not reckon' by denying that the Prophet, honored with the ascension, would gesture like a herdsman rather than distinguish thirty from twenty-nine in speech; the Alid withdrew in shame.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: A summoner's disputational questionnaire asks who 'those before you' are, how many the counted days, and what 'witnessing the month' means, and invokes 'that you complete the count,' arguing that those who fast by crescent-rising may fail to complete thirty and so contradict the Book — against the Prophet's rule that whatever contradicts the Book of God he did not say.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: Zayd ibn Muhammad, in the epistle al-Maknuna on the eclipse prayer, holds that God made first-age creation a proof for the last age, setting the lunar eclipse at fourteen nights (sometimes thirteen) and the moon's concealment at twenty-eight nights, absent forty-eight hours before rising again.

dropped.section_title: 31. The Quarrel Over the Crescent
dropped.text: The section closes by introducing the next text, the epistle al-Lazima on the fast of Ramadan and its proper time, by Ahmad Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani, proof of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The disputed authority is the Prophet's narration 'Fast at its sighting and break the fast at its sighting', which is agreed among the Muslim sects and is the pillar of the argument of the people of the outward.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The author argues astronomically that the month is constituted by the moon's travel from conjunction (shared degree and minute with the sun) around the sphere, and that the sun's overpowering light is merely a barrier to the eye like cloud or a wall — as shown by stars becoming visible during a solar eclipse.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: Against the claim that one knows nothing until sight falls upon it, the author offers three refutations: opponents affirm Allah whom they have not seen; they judge the world originated in time by proof not eyesight; and they permit breaking the fast after thirty days without sighting — each forcing a retreat to the vision of knowledge.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: The soul is an instrument of perception alongside the five senses which surpasses them all, and its perception is of two kinds: by means of the senses, and by its own essence along the path of inference — the latter needing the senses only at the first apprehension, since the image is thereafter retained.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: To the objection that the lam in 'Establish the prayer at the declining of the sun' does not require the prayer to precede the declining, the author replies that the declining too is apprehended first by the soul (point ب) and only later by sense (point ج), so there too the worshipper is already praying when sense perceives the shadow turn.

dropped.section_title: 32. Two Kinds of Sight
dropped.text: To the further objection that 'If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days' requires eyesight, the author answers by reasserting that the vision of the soul has been established as the nobler of the two.

dropped.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
dropped.text: The author objects that eye-sighting makes the fast differ between regions — cloud in Kirman versus clear sky in Shiraz — and that just as one prayer's time cannot differ among the people of one town, neither can the fast's time; when the time comes the fast binds the whole community whether or not an individual keeps it.

dropped.section_title: 33. The Sun, the Moon, and the Order of Obedience
dropped.text: The author defends the people of truth's entering the Ramadan fast of the year 400 two days before the eye-sighting, on the grounds that the conjunction fell on Monday night, the moon stood only about six degrees from the sun so the eye could not reach it, the Shawwal conjunction fell on Wednesday night making Wednesday the festival, and Ramadan is thirty days without deficiency ('Shaban was never complete nor Ramadan deficient'), confirmed by 'the day of your fasting is the day of your sacrifice,' the sacrifice at Mecca having fallen on Monday.
